review: There is a question Pixar has been quietly building toward for thirty years, and Toy Story 5 finally asks it out loud: what happens when the world stops believing in play? Not the toys - the world. And more uncomfortably: what does that say about us, the generation that grew up with these films, and now watches children scroll past the things that once made childhood feel infinite? Stanton does not pretend the answer is simple. The film takes a genuine social problem - childhood loneliness, the replacement of imaginative play by screens, the way technology solves some things while quietly eroding others - and refuses to flatten it into a villain. The result is a film that is chill in pace, rich in layers, and emotionally precise in a way that never announces itself. You don't cry because the music tells you to. You feel things because the film is honest. ""Pixar takes a question that philosophers, parents and sociologists can't resolve - and builds a film around it. The answer it offers isn't a solution. It's something better: an emotion you can carry with you."" At the center of it all is Jessie - and this is unambiguously her film. She inherits the franchise's emotional weight and carries it with a complexity that surprises. She is warm, relentlessly optimistic on the surface, and quietly struggling underneath. She doesn't lead from strength - she leads because the alternative is giving up. There is a single scene, late in the film, that redefines her entire arc in one image, with no dialogue, no musical swell. It is the kind of moment that makes you sit still for a few seconds after it happens. One of the finest sequences Pixar has ever crafted. What makes Toy Story 5 exceptional is not any single element but the balance of all of them. The humor is genuinely funny without undercutting the emotion. The romance is light-handed and earned. The nostalgia is present but never weaponized. And beneath everything runs a philosophical undercurrent - a real, unresolved question about what we lose when imagination is replaced by consumption - that gives the film a weight rare in mainstream animation. Visually, it is among Pixar's best work. The voice performances are outstanding across the board. The pacing is confident - it knows when to breathe. The ending is predictable in the best sense: you feel it coming, and it still lands. For those of us who grew up with Woody and Buzz, this film does something quietly profound. It makes us realize we are no longer on the child's side of the story. We are on the toys' side now - watching, hoping, unable to intervene. And Jessie, with her stubborn, undefeated optimism, becomes the answer to a question we didn't know we were asking. One of Pixar's greatest films. On par with the fourth - possibly better. Time will tell. ⚠ SPOILERS BELOW Two scenes define this film and deserve to be named. The first: a sleepover, four girls in one bedroom, each alone on a screen. Same room, same silence, different worlds. No commentary, no reaction shot. Pixar simply holds the image - and from the toys' point of view, it is one of the most quietly devastating things the franchise has ever shown. We live in this reality every day. Seeing it through the eyes of something that only wants to be played with makes it impossible to look away. The second is Jessie's scene beneath the tree. I will not describe it in full - it needs to be experienced. What I will say is this: it is a single image, no dialogue, no music cue, that answers thirty years of the franchise's deepest question about love, memory, and whether any of it mattered. It is the best scene Pixar has made in a decade. Possibly ever.

review: The traditional toys face an existential threat with the arrival of modern technology. With children increasingly glued to screens, the older playthings find themselves sidelined in favour of a sleek new tablet character named Lilypad. As the electronic world threatens to take over completely, Jessie is forced to contemplate a massive dilemma, leaving questions over whether she will turn her back on her oldest companions to embrace the digital age. It is miles better than the fourth instalment and a refinement, though it still feels like a somewhat curious release. The current lack of originality in Hollywood means they naturally chose to revisit an old favourite, but it is undeniably better than expected. The film is heartfelt, genuinely funny, and packed with the usual mix of humour and high-stakes hijinx. It also carries a surprisingly deep, if frightening, message about children and technology that mirrors the modern world perfectly. While the story is amusing, it does feel a bit more geared toward kids than the earlier films, perhaps lacking some of those clever, dual-meaning jokes that parents used to enjoy. Joan Cusack shines brightly here, and it was wonderful to see Jessie finally get the central focus she deserves. However, the reason this cannot score any higher is the treatment of Tom Hanks as Woody and Tim Allen as Buzz. They seem to be here merely as whipping boys, which is a shame given they are what made this franchise so eternally loved. This is a fun, amusing movie that managed to pack out the cinema, which was a lovely sight to see. It handles its emotional beats well and delivers an entertaining ride, even if the treatment of its two original icons leaves a bit of a sour taste. It is a strong return to form, but it is safe to say nobody needs a sixth film; some new ideas from Pixar would be most welcome. 7/10.

review: I walked into the theater with very low expectations, and while the film never completely won me over, I ended up having a genuinely good time watching it. Once again, Pixar demonstrates why it remains one of the most accomplished animation studios in the industry. Years of experience and craftsmanship are evident in every frame. Although parts of the story occasionally feel forced, the film's central message is clear and surprisingly relevant: the challenges of childhood in an increasingly digital world. What makes the film particularly interesting is its lack of a traditional villain. Instead of focusing on a single antagonist, it addresses a broader issue-the consequences of leaving children at the mercy of the digital age. It's a different approach, but one that allows the message to resonate more naturally. Pixar also understands its audience remarkably well. While the film is marketed toward children, much of its emotional weight is aimed at the adults who grew up with Woody and Buzz and are now entering parenthood themselves. Parents will likely empathize with Bonnie's situation, while others may find her character more frustrating than relatable. The film also explores themes of love and relationships in ways that sometimes feel as though Pixar took inspiration from some of the internet's most imaginative fan theories. This is far from one of Pixar's best films, but neither is it the disaster many feared it would be. Its execution may be uneven, but its foundation is solid, and above all, it succeeds in delivering what audiences seek most: entertainment.

review_title: this movie never deserved the hate
review: I honestly don't understand the hate this movie got before it even came out. People were calling it unnecessary, saying it would ruin the franchise, calling it trash, and some were even talking about boycotting it. The amount of drama surrounding this movie was honestly ridiculous. A lot of the arguments online reminded me of how people will argue about absolutely anything. It's like cancelling Eminem for swearing. Everyone already knows what they're getting, yet people still find reasons to be angry. Instead of waiting to watch the movie and judging it fairly, many people had already decided they hated it months before seeing it. The Sonic 3 and Mufasa: The Lion King conflict made everything even worse. People were constantly comparing movies, picking sides, and acting like they had to choose one over another. Then Toy Story 5 got dragged into all the drama too. Instead of enjoying movies, people were turning everything into an argument. It felt completely unnecessary. Movies are supposed to be entertainment, not internet wars. Meanwhile, I was just excited to watch another Toy Story movie. After watching it, I can confidently say that I never understood the hate. This movie is gold. What makes Toy Story 5 work so well is that it remembers why people fell in love with the franchise in the first place. It has heart, humor, adventure, and charm. The movie feels like a true Toy Story film and doesn't forget what made the previous movies special. The animation is absolutely beautiful. Every detail looks incredible, and it shows just how far animation has come since the first Toy Story. Some scenes genuinely looked stunning on the big screen. The comedy is great, the emotional moments work, and the movie never feels boring. It constantly gives you something to enjoy. Whether it's a funny moment, an exciting scene, or a heartfelt interaction, there's always something happening. One thing I really appreciated is that the movie feels like it was made by people who genuinely care about the franchise. It doesn't feel lazy or unnecessary like many people claimed before release. It feels like a movie that actually had effort and passion put into it. The funniest part is that many of the people who spent months hating the movie ended up liking it after they actually watched it. That's why I think movies should be judged after you've seen them, not before. At the end of the day, I had an amazing time watching Toy Story 5. The characters are still lovable, the animation is incredible, the humor works, and the movie reminded me why Toy Story remains one of the greatest animated franchises ever made. This movie is gold.

review: ...well, maybe not NEED. But that doesn't change the fact that "Toy Story 5" is still a really solid sequel that also offers a thoughtful and fleshed out look at the advantages and consequences of technology. Focusing this story on Jessie was perhaps the best thing the filmmakers could have done to make this story as compelling as possible. It's refreshing to see more of her struggles and how she processes change, and Joan Cusack gives a fantastic vocal performance as usual. The focus on Jessie does come at the expense of the other characters' screen time (pun intended), but it's worth it to see her get a film to herself. The new characters, while rather underused, are good as well, and the voice cast is uniformly excellent. Ultimately, "Toy Story 5" is nowhere near the best of this series, and I can't imagine anyone thinking it is. There's an entire subplot that feels more like Pixar's attempt at the Minions than anything else, and some overused toilet humor that gets old very quickly. Nonetheless though, this is still a very fun time at the movies that's well worth taking the entire family to see. You may even shed a tear.

Still, it was a no brainer to watch it because I love the franchise. Toy Story 5 is not a bad sequel, however I find the content lacking more than the other movies. All in all a nice sequel, but the weakest of the five.

review: Toy Story 5 would be a much more deserving spin-off titled Jessie: From the Toy Story World than that awful Lightyear movie, it introduces fresh ideas and new charms to the Toy Story franchise, at first, i wasn't entirely sure about it, i never disliked it, but as the story progressed, i began to understand where it was going, and in the end, it worked. I think it's fair to say that this has the most challenging conflict in the franchise, especially because it feels very relatable to what many people are going through in real life today, is it as exciting or as memorable as the previous movies? No, but on its own, it's still a good one, even the weakest Toy Story movie has never been a bad one. This is a new chapter of the franchise, some people may find Woody's presence underwhelming, but i understand the decision, his story has already been told and concluded, Jessie, on the other hand, more than deserves to take center stage, and this film finally gives her that opportunity well enough. The new device toys are also a great addition, i actually like them more than some of the new characters from the previous movie, the film also gives us a more complete look at Jessie's backstory, which was nice to see. Overall, Pixar did it again, thankfully, the problems that hurt Lightyear didn't carry over to Toy Story 5, it's still a charming, funny, and enjoyable movie set in this beloved toy world, in the end, Toy Story 5 is simply a good Jessie movie.

review_title: toy story 5 a poignant story of purpose and friendship in the digital age
review: As a casual fan of Toy Story, the film series has never failed to deliver quality entertainment. The first movie was so groundbreaking for its originality, the second was probably the best sequel ever made for its character depth, and third was indeed a satisfying closing chapter to Andy's story. As for the fourth movie, I will defend it because of the emotional beats and themes it wanted to convey in Woody's journey. So as I went into the theater, the main question that I had for the fifth one was whether or not it could justify its existence - and yes it did like how I felt with the fourth. Toy Story 5 is a worthy installment to the franchise because of an emotional voice performance by Joan Cusack, the consistent animation that Pixar always maintained, and a poignant story on friendship, technology and meaning in life. Joan Cusack leads the story in the most charming and emotional way possible throughout the story. Her role as Jessie made us love her even more as a character as she strives to make her role as Bonnie's toy meaningful through her ups and downs. It is so nice to hear the old voices of Tom Hanks and Tim Allen as Woody and Buzz Lightyear once more. They may not be the main stars of the movie, but their supporting roles elevate Jessie to grow in her own story. The new voice performances of Greta Lee and Conan O'Brien as Lilypad and SmartyPants respectively made their characters easily interesting and likeable. With Lilypad, we understand her perspective of what she thinks is forming friends through technology and social media which made her realize the actions she did. SmartyPants, alongside his friends Snappy and Atlas, were easily likeable once they saw what fun really is and where Jessie is coming from. And yes, most of the characters we met along the way have some lines here and there but the movie made it clear that it is focused on Jessie and her character arc. The movie shows how Pixar never fails to maintain its technical craftsmanship as shown in its creative animation, with Randy Newman's great score. It comes as no surprise that whether a movie is good or bad, Pixar always delivers great animation. Whether it is in a suburban area of a neighborhood, a house near a barn just outside of the city, or even in a deserted island, the studio knows how to set the production design immersive. I also have to acknowledge how Pixar was able to make the smallest details look so realistic like on Jessie's hat and Buzz's toy design and even Woody's new outfit to name a few. Randy Newman returning once again to score for the film franchise knows how to tug in our heartstrings. Whether it was using old scores from previous movies and mixing it with new ones, it added an emotional layer to the dramatic scenes as well as heightening the adventure sequences that could be a tearjerker and nostalgic for the fans. For the most part, Jennifer Jew's editing skills were able to know how to transition from one subplot to another with proper fades in and out. However, there were certain scenes that could have finished first before jumping back to a new one, instead of playing one scene and then all of a sudden cut in the middle of it and switched to the previous scene. But of course, what really justified the movie's existence, at least for me, are the poignant emotions and themes about finding meaning and friendship that the movie wanted to say. Considering that this is Jessie's story, it helps the audience to see why she acts that way and how she will do anything to be with Bonnie despite the rise of technology. It really does tug at my heartstrings as to how Jessie gets the realization of what meaning she does bring as a toy not just to Bonnie but even to Blaze as well as her previous owner Emily. The movie also invites a very simple yet relevant discussion as to how technology and social media can make people cave into the pressure. And yet, it does not give this binary answer but rather explores a profound way of using technology alongside the importance of toys in forming real friendships whether its through online or offline. For the most part, in terms of adventure, it is fun to see how Jessie, Woody and Buzz try to handle the situation as they go up against technology. Whether that is through Jessie getting used to a new environment just like Woody in the third movie, or the loveable back and forth bickering between Woody and Buzz, it is hard not to smile and laugh with their antics. Narrative-wise, the major issue in its storytelling is the convenient moments, especially with one subplot that involves so many Buzz Lightyears until it actually does connect in the climax. Toy Story 5 does justify its existence in telling a new story as a fifth installment of the franchise. The emotional narrative about Jessie and how she searches for purpose in the rise of technology gives a fresh perspective from the toys in their sense of fun and belongingness. Despite not reaching the same level of greatness as the first and second movies, it at least offers a poignant adventure with Woody, Jessie and Buzz once again. Overall, with the release of the fifth movie, it does imply that the Toy Story franchise can grow along with its audience in a meaningful way.

review: I really wish I liked Toy Story 5 more than I did. And trust me, I know. Between this and The Mandalorian and Grogu, I can already see the "you hate fun" allegations coming. I promise that's not what's happening here. Because I wanted to love this so badly. I'm a Toy Story 4 defender. I know that's not the majority opinion, but I loved that movie. I loved that it pushed these characters into messy, existential territory and asked questions about purpose, identity, change, and what it means to move on. On top of that, Toy Story 3 is a straight up masterpiece -- especially that ending. So when I heard Andrew Stanton - the guy who made WALL-E (my favourite Pixar movie) - was directing a Toy Story movie about technology and childhood in the modern age, I thought, "Oh, this thing is about to ruin me emotionally." Instead, I walked out thinking... "That was okay." And for most movies, that's enough. For Toy Story? I don't know if it is. Because here's the thing: I actually agree with almost everything this movie has to say. I loved how nuanced it was about technology. It would've been so easy to make a two-hour "technology = bad" lecture, and it never does that. It acknowledges that technology can connect us. It can teach us. It can bring people together. I mean, I use technology every day. You're literally reading my thoughts because of it. But it also understands that something gets lost when screens replace connection instead of complementing it. It understands that friendships fade sometimes without anyone meaning for them to. That attention spans are changing. That childhood looks different now than it did twenty years ago. And maybe most importantly, it understands that a child's imagination is a gift technology can never replace. I genuinely think what this movie has to say about toys versus tech is smart, timely, and handled with way more grace than I expected. I just don't think that, by itself, is enough. Because the name Toy Story means something to me. I don't go into these movies hoping they're good. I go into them hoping they'll wreck me. I want the ugly crying from Toy Story 3. I want the existential spiral of Toy Story 4. I want to walk out of the theater staring at the ceiling thinking about growing older and letting go and whether being loved for a season is enough. And this movie never quite got there for me. There is one stretch involving Jessie that absolutely did. It's actually my favourite part of the movie. Jessie makes for a really compelling emotional center, and there's a realization she comes to that genuinely caught me off guard. For about ten minutes, I felt that familiar ache in my chest and thought, "There it is. There's the movie I was looking for." Then it moved on. And I wish it had stayed there a little longer. Because as much as I appreciated Jessie's role in the story, I couldn't shake the feeling that this franchise is starting to repeat itself. This was the first Toy Story movie where I found myself thinking, "How many times are we going to revisit abandonment?" And I hate even writing that. Because abandonment is the beating heart of this series. Andy leaving. Emily leaving. Bonnie moving on. These movies understand that loving someone means accepting they won't need you forever. But for the first time, it felt less revelatory and more recycled. The juggling act with all these characters doesn't help either. The gang fades into the background more than I'd like, and Buzz continues to feel increasingly flanderized. And as much as I appreciated Jessie stepping into the spotlight, Woody just has too much gravity to function as a supporting player. Every time he disappeared from the movie, I found myself waiting for him to come back. There are still so many things I liked here. These voices feel like reuniting with old friends every single time. Conan O'Brien absolutely steals the show in a role I never would've predicted. The humor mostly works. Randy Newman still knows exactly which emotional buttons to press with the score (though I missed hearing "You've Got a Friend in Me" this time around). And even if I found the animation a little less impressive than Toy Story 4, Pixar's craftsmanship remains undeniable. Plus the new Taylor Swift song written for the movie was very fitting and deserves a Best Original Song nomination at the Oscars next year! So maybe that's why this review sounds harsher than I actually feel. Because I don't think Toy Story 5 is bad. I think it's good. I think it's thoughtful. I think it's sweet. I think it fully justifies its existence and has something genuinely worthwhile to say about technology, friendship, peer pressure, and the importance of human connection in a world that feels increasingly designed to pull us apart. I also think it's the first Toy Story movie that left me more appreciative than emotional. And maybe that's the real disappointment. Not that Pixar made a bad Toy Story movie. But that, after decades of excellence, they finally made one that was just okay. A 3½-star Toy Story movie is still better than most animated films. I just never thought I'd walk out of one saying, "I wish I loved it more."

review: For me, Toy Story 5 is easily the weakest entry in the franchise. Going into the movie, I was actually excited by the idea of toys facing off against technology. On paper, the "tech vs. Toys" concept sounded like a fresh and interesting direction for the series. Unfortunately, I felt the execution was disappointing, and the overall plot ended up being the film's biggest problem. One of my biggest issues was the decision to make Jessie the central character. While I like Jessie as a character, she just didn't work for me as the main focus of a Toy Story movie. The series has always had a certain heart and soul that came from the dynamic between Woody, Buzz, and the rest of the gang, and shifting that focus made the movie feel like it had lost some of its identity. Combined with the weak plot, it left the film feeling disconnected from what made the franchise special in the first place. I also wasn't a fan of what they did with Buzz. His characterization felt very different from previous movies, and the direction they took him didn't work for me. On the positive side, it was great to see Woody back, and he remained one of the highlights of the film. Another disappointment was the emotional side of the story. Previous Toy Story movies always managed to hit me emotionally, whether through their themes, character moments, or endings. Toy Story 5 never really reached those same heights. I didn't feel nearly as connected to the story as I did with the earlier films. That said, the movie definitely has its strengths. The humor is still strong, and many of the jokes landed well, just like in the previous entries. Visually, the film looks fantastic, with impressive animation and beautifully detailed environments throughout. I also enjoyed the Buzz army concept. It was fun, different, and added some entertaining moments to the movie. However, the way the various storylines came together felt rushed. In fact, much of the film felt rushed, as if it was trying to juggle too many ideas without giving them enough time to develop properly. Ultimately, that's what hurts the movie the most. The overall plot never fully comes together, and despite some enjoyable moments, it just didn't feel like a true Toy Story movie to me. The tech-versus-toys premise had a lot of potential, but the execution never lived up to the concept. Between the underwhelming story, the lack of emotional impact, the changes to Buzz, and the decision to center the film around Jessie, the movie felt like it had lost some of the soul that made the franchise so beloved. While I still had fun watching it and appreciated the laughs, visuals, and Woody's return, the experience was far more underwhelming than I expected.

review: I watched Toy Story 5 on its opening day, and honestly, I left the cinema extremely disappointed. I would not call it a complete disaster, but it simply does not feel like the Toy Story we once knew and loved. The biggest problem is the story. It feels empty, forced, and strangely soulless. The idea of toys competing with modern technology and tablets is actually relevant and full of potential, but the film barely does anything interesting with it. There is no satisfying conclusion to that conflict, and by the end, it feels as though the main theme has simply been forgotten. A lot of the characters are pushed aside or treated like they no longer matter. Woody, who has always been my favourite character alongside Buzz, is barely involved and spends most of the film in the background. Buzz does not receive much attention either. Despite being called Toy Story, this is essentially Jessie's movie. Before watching it, you should be prepared for a story focused almost entirely on her, while many of the characters people love are reduced to minor appearances. Even the way some characters are removed from the story feels incredibly lazy. Bo Peep appears and then simply disappears. The rest of the toys are placed in a box and spend half the movie sitting there, leaving Jessie and Bullseye to deal with everything on their own. It does not feel like a natural development of the story, but rather as if the writers simply needed to get everyone out of the way so Jessie could become the sole main character. The film also spends a lot of time exploring Jessie, even though we already know her personality and tragic past from the previous movies. I do not think her character needed this much additional explanation, especially when it came at the expense of Woody, Buzz, and the rest of the group. Another major disappointment was the atmosphere. I did not hear any memorable music, and the warmth, emotion, and sense of adventure that defined the earlier films are almost completely gone. The movie feels like it was made because another sequel had to be released, not because the creators had a genuinely meaningful story to tell. That is what frustrates me the most: the central idea could have worked. Technology replacing traditional toys is a strong and timely concept, and it could have led to a much deeper, more emotional story. Unfortunately, the potential was wasted on a weak plot, an unsatisfying ending, and a strange lack of focus on the characters who made this franchise special. It is not completely terrible, and there are still a few enjoyable moments, but compared with the previous films, this is a very low point for the series.

review_title: the sequel i never thought we needed but i'm glad we got
review: I'll be honest: I never thought Toy Story needed a fifth movie. After Toy Story 4, I genuinely believed the franchise was over. Woody had found his new purpose, Buzz had his goodbye, and it felt like the perfect place to stop. So when Toy Story 5 was announced, I expected another unnecessary sequel made purely because the name sells tickets. I was completely wrong. This movie proved why it deserved to exist. The biggest surprise is making Jessie the emotional center of the story. It was a brilliant decision because she's always been one of the franchise's strongest characters, and finally giving her the spotlight pays off. Her journey feels incredibly relatable, especially as she struggles to understand that kids today grow up differently than previous generations. The film's biggest strength is how realistic its message is. Toy Story 3 was about accepting that your kid grows up. Toy Story 5 asks an even harder question: what happens when kids don't even play with toys the way they used to? Tablets, phones, and technology have completely changed childhood, and Pixar doesn't ignore that reality. Bonnie's imagination sequences were absolutely gorgeous. The new visual style during her playtime almost felt inspired by The Wild Robot and Puss in Boots: The Last Wish. I honestly hope Pixar experiments with animation like this more often because it adds so much personality. There are also some wonderful callbacks for longtime fans. Hearing Bullseye finally talk-even if only within Bonnie's imagination-felt like a fun nod to one of the original ideas for Toy Story 2. I also loved spotting one of the old scrapped toy concepts hidden in the background. Those little Easter eggs show how much respect the filmmakers have for the franchise's history. The new characters were also surprisingly enjoyable. Smarty Pants starts off a little annoying, but he really grows on you. Snappy and Atlas were hilarious additions, and together they brought a fresh energy to the story without replacing the classic toys. Lilypad is an interesting antagonist because she isn't evil. She genuinely believes she's helping Bonnie, but her arrogance and belief that she's better than everyone else make her a very believable modern villain. Ironically, though, I don't think she's the real villain. The real villains are Bonnie's classmates. Watching those kids mock Bonnie for still loving toys and calling her a crybaby was honestly harder to watch than anything Lilypad did. That's a very real kind of cruelty that many kids experience growing up. Jessie's emotional journey is easily the best part of the movie. After Bonnie rejects her, watching Jessie blame herself for children growing up was heartbreaking. Her frustration eventually causes her to push Smarty Pants away, and you immediately see how much she regrets it. It reminds us that growing up isn't anyone's fault. It's simply part of life. Bullseye once again proves he's one of the most loyal characters in the entire franchise. He barely needs words to show how much he cares. Then came the scene that completely broke me. Learning that Emily named her own daughter Jessie after the toy she loved as a child was one of the sweetest moments Pixar has ever created. I wasn't expecting that, and it genuinely made me cry. I also loved finally seeing Buzz and Jessie openly express how much they love each other. Their relationship has quietly developed since Toy Story 2, so seeing them finally kiss-and even hearing they're officially married-felt like a satisfying payoff that longtime fans have waited years for. And of course... Woody returns. Every moment between Woody and Buzz put a smile on my face. Their callbacks to the original movie, especially Woody joking, "Buzz! Look, an alien!" instantly brought me back to 1995. It's nostalgic without feeling forced. The ending is exactly what I wanted. Bonnie making a genuine new friend who still enjoys playing with toys reminds us that imagination never truly disappears. It just finds new ways to grow. Was Toy Story 5 necessary? No. Did it earn its place in the franchise? Absolutely. This isn't just another sequel. It's a thoughtful continuation that respects everything that came before while saying something meaningful about childhood today. I went in expecting disappointment and walked out completely won over. Pixar somehow made me care about these toys all over again.

review: 🏆85% A very enjoyable continuation to Toy Story. Besides Jessie's arc, I'm not really sure I'd call this film necessary, though I do think it brings a great message to this current generation. I think this movie is a good way for new audiences to get into Toy Story, so there could likely be a sixth film. Even though Jessie's arc felt earned here, every other character doesn't get all that much to do when compared to her; you can tell this was pretty much Jessie's movie. Woody does literally nothing useful the whole film, and he continuously gets made fun of by everyone. We also get this stuff with Buzz liking Jessie, which makes sense since we saw stuff like that within the previous films, but it felt mostly irrelevant in this film. Buzz and Jessie's relationship felt much more relevant in the third film rather than this one. The movie is definitely not perfect, and it's no Toy Story 1, 2, or 3. review: I'm not bothered that people adored the fourth Toy Story, whether they were hopelessly nostalgic adults or excitable tots. It was quite emotional and, what's more, one of the best-animated movies in Pixar's already amazing roster (albeit maybe a little TOO realistic-looking at times). What bothers me is that people got fooled twice: With Toy Story 4, many apologists basically went, "Ok it kiiind of weakens the finality of Toy Story 3, but after that ending, it's pretty clear that we're not getting another one! Woody leaves the rest of the gang, for Stinky Pete's sake! This time it's REALLY time to move on!" But to me, it was obvious in the other direction: Of course Disney is gonna put out another one where Woody says sike, comes back, and brings us to meet a new set of side characters that you, too, can get in stores now and/or see again on streaming. Surely others saw this coming? Even if I didn't know that Disney has been pumping out Toy Story short films in the years since 2019's supposed "second grand finale" (including a bunch of Forky shorts designed, ironically, to give parents something to keep their iPad babies occupied with), I'd know that Pixar hasn't moved on from this universe. Here, Sheriff Woody (Tom Hanks) is living his life as a lost toy when he is asked to rejoin Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen), Jessie (Joan Cusack), and the others after little Bonnie starts to become enamored with a tablet voiced by Greta Lee, who taunts our heroes by pointing out that they are a thing of the past; that social media is the key to Bonnie making friends. Being a Disney joint -- aka the same company that produced the aforementioned Forky clips on Disney+ -- the satire of the iPad Kids era obviously doesn't bite TOO hard, and Lilypad (whose main enemy becomes Jessie, sort of mirroring the original Buzz-Woody rivalry) isn't truly evil in the end. The alternative may have been a decidedly "Boomer-y" text, but what of it, at this point? (My family and I recently had a discussion about how history will show that we should have listened to the Old Man Yelling At Clouds.) Despite a fair few impressive shots, some tear-jerking moments, and -- I confess -- sweet reunions, it often plays like one of the recent short adventures, stretched out to feature length, and/or spliced together with another story in which Buzz yet again faces doppelgängers. In the end, however, we're left with a sequel that hits pretty hard, possibly more so than movie 4. (On the flipside, it lacks the previous film's fascinating experimentation with artificial camera lenses.) Randy Newman's music is still sterling, of course, but he seems to have recycled a few tracks, not just from Toy Story but from Monsters Inc. I didn't laugh at all of the jokes, but the part where Bullseye suddenly receives the voice of Alan Cumming was pretty special. On that note, though, the most disappointing thing about the past few movies (besides the fact that their climaxes fall short of the first three) has been the lack of memorable side character moments. Back in Toy Story 2, even Utility Belt Buzz and Emperor Zurg had arcs. In 5, this is barely the case for Woody and Buzz, almost as if this series ought to have ended about 16 years ago. (Doug Walker, of all people, made the interesting point that this movie could've just as well been named Jessie the Cowgirl.) I will say that, aside from a certain spin-off, there is no outright bad Toy Story film. Movie 5 is no exception, and it has enough heart that some will yet again believe they're watching a tremendous conclusion. Critics have remarked that it does supply logical thematic progression and feels more organic than certain other Disney addenda, as well as getting a crucial thing right: being largely for -- and about -- the parents. All we need now is for Pixar to visualize the Western that Andy saw when he was a kid; the film that, supposedly, got him interested in cowboy dolls. "But wait," I hear you say, "didn't they already show Woody's Roundup in Toy Story 2? Don't we already know what inspired the toyline?" Yes, and we also already learned that Buzz Lightyear came from the 2D-animated Buzz Lightyear of Star Command, but Disney/Pixar went ahead and made 2022's Lightyear anyway. Again: Have you learned nothing?

review_title: fun but not the best this franchise can be
review: Those kids that bully Bonnie are the real villains of this film and should have been dealt with. Anyway, this film always had a lot to battle, especially in taking on the gigantic issue that is children and tech, which by and large is quite a depressing issue. The numerous shots and sequences where kids are entranced by technology, and completely shut out from the imagination and the world, hits hard, but does create a weird tone for the film. In some ways I wish the film was bolder and able to challenge these ideas and behaviours more, with even the adults questioning their relationship with technology and how children are acting because of it (again it's being used to bully children wtf?). However, I do think they do a good job in incorporating technology based toys in order to show how they can integrate into playtime, and be part of the fun too. It's a strength of the film and adds some fun characters to the mix. The main strength of this film is ultimately Jessie, and her story, which is great as she is a very fun and compelling character, with all her history and characteristics brought into full effect. But by making this film so much about her, and also having so many characters to juggle now, the movie does shortchange and skip over a lot of great characters, which now feel sidelined after being vital to previous editions. Even Woody and Buzz are quite inconsequential, for better or for worse. What doesn't help is that the film's brisk pace and tendency to jump from one element to another, accelerates this feeling we're not spending enough time in this world. Ultimately this film still has some decent jokes, some beautiful animation, and great voice acting. Plus the story does have an important lesson all about friendship, something these films have not touched on before, which proves to be a great element to push against the depressing technology. But is it the best in the series? Far from it. And I'm someone who really liked 4. Toy Story 5 is fun, engaging, and reflective, but also struggles with the weight of it's predecessors.

review: Let me start by saying that Toy Story 5 is by far the worst Toy Story film. I generally don't like writing long reviews, but in this case I feel like I need to make an exception. I went into this movie with low expectations, and it didn't even meet them. Pixar has set a high set of standards for Toy Story films, and when they don't meet them, it really doesn't work. So, why is Toy Story 5 the worst Toy Story movie? There are multiple reasons why. The first reason is the writing was horrible. It wasn't nearly as witty as the first four films. I don't know what happened to Andrew Stanton. He's a great writer, but he just didn't do a good job with this movie. I thought that if Toy Story 5 was a let down, it would at least have been funny. But it wasn't. The reason for that was because all of the characters we now and love were barely in it. Rex, the potato heads, Ham, Slinky, even Forky was barely in it. The only funny thing about it was Conan O'Brien as Smarty Pants. Rex had one funny line at the very beginning and that was it. And when Tim Allen described all of the Buzz Lightyear's on the island, he made it sound like it was going to be really funny, but again, it wasn't. It felt weird and unnecessary and I really didn't understand what was going on at times and why they even bothered to do that. Another complaint is the ending was unsatisfactory. I won't say what it was for spoilers, but the cut to credits was bad. Like almost all Toy Story fans, I had a problem with the ending of the fourth movie, but the forth movie's ending at least tied it up with the final pull away shot and Randy Newman's fantastic score playing in the background. This ending didn't tie anything up. I thought it couldn't get worse than Toy Story 4, that they would fix the ending, but they did not. Another thing I want to address quickly is that I don't understand what the big hype over the Taylor Swift song was. It was the credits song. It wasn't even in the movie. I am really disappointed that Randy Newman's didn't give us a new song. But my biggest complaint and the thing that totally ruined the movie was how little Woody and Buzz were in it. Woody is Toy Story the same way that Luke Skywalker is Star Wars. You could make a Star Wars movie without Luke Skywalker, but it's not going to be nearly as good as The Empire Strikes Back. That's exactly what we have here. It would have been better if it wasn't an official Toy Story movie and was instead a spin off about Jessie. That would have made a lot more sense. Andrew Stanton has already talked about how he wants to make a sixth film to end the "Bonnie Trilogy," and if Pixar does decide to do that, I really hope they have sense enough to make Woody the main character again. Toy Story has always been about Woody and Buzz's friendship, even before Jessie was introduced, and it worked so well. Jessie is an important character, but Woody is Toy Story, and that's what we need in a Toy Story 6, Woody and Buzz. Toy Story 3 is one of the greatest movies of all time and one of my personal top five favorite movies of all time, and it deserves so much better than Toy Story 5. Toy Story 4 was so much better that five, because although the ending was a downgrade from the third movie, it was a funny film, it was well made, and the ending brought tears to your eyes. Toy Story 5 does not bring you tears. It leaves you feeling let down and praying for a sixth installment. I'm sorry Pixar, but you let me down. 6 stars.

review_title: the most relevantly heartbreaking and brilliant installment yet
review: I'll admit, when Pixar announced a fifth Toy Story, I was deeply skeptical. How could they top the perfect emotional arcs of the previous films? But Toy Story 5 isn't just a cash grab-it is a deeply profound, incredibly relevant masterpiece that holds up a mirror to our modern world. The premise is pure genius: Woody, Buzz, and the gang face their ultimate existential threat-not a bully like Sid, and not growing up like Andy, but the terrifying allure of an iPad. Watching our beloved classic toys try to compete with "Lilypad" (the smart tablet beautifully voiced by Greta Lee) for Bonnie's attention is both hilariously witty and heartbreakingly real. What makes this movie a 10/10 is how it handles the conflict. It doesn't just lazily say "technology is bad." Instead, it crafts a deeply empathetic narrative about generational divides. The dynamic between Buzz Lightyear and Lilypad is spectacular, evolving from a bitter rivalry into a beautiful understanding of what it means to bring joy to a child in the 2020s. The introduction of other smart gadgets, like the hilarious "Smarty Pants," brings that classic Pixar humor we've all missed. Director Andrew Stanton has recaptured the absolute magic of the original trilogy while grounding it in a crisis every single parent and child today can relate to. The animation is top-tier, the emotional beats hit like a freight train, and the final 15 minutes left the entire theater in tears. Pixar proved us all wrong. Toy Story 5 is an instant classic and a necessary chapter in cinema's greatest animated saga.

review: Toy Story 5 may be the least great film in the franchise, but considering how consistently excellent the series has been, that's really not saying much. This is a film that feels very different from the previous installments. Firstly, it gives Jessie a well-deserved leading role, allowing her character to shine in a way we've never really seen before. Secondly, it tells a very timely story about the world we're living in today, where technology has completely taken over and children are growing up in a vastly different environment from the kids of the original Toy Story films. Toys simply aren't what they used to be, and many children are now completely absorbed by technology, for both better and worse, often acting like adults far too early instead of simply being kids. The film's exploration of this subject, its sharp commentary on modern childhood, and the powerful message it delivers are easily its greatest strengths. It's sad, emotional, and deeply resonant. Because of this, Toy Story 5 is quieter, more introspective, and more focused than its predecessors, while still featuring plenty of humor and exciting action sequences. The animation is once again at its absolute peak, looking breathtakingly beautiful, and the entire voice cast continues to bring these iconic characters to life with the same charm and heart as ever. It's wonderful to see a more character-driven story centered on someone who truly deserved it, as well as a cast of new characters who are instantly memorable and lovable. At the same time, I did find myself wishing for a little more time with the original gang, and for the next installment I'd love to see a story that brings everyone together equally. This is undoubtedly the most mature film in the franchise and arguably the one most geared toward adults, as it clearly aims to send a direct message to them. Gorgeous, funny, heartfelt, emotional, and surprisingly important, Toy Story 5 reminds us of one of the best things about such a long-running franchise: each film serves as a reflection of its era, allowing us to see just how dramatically the world continues to change from one generation to the next.

review: I went into Toy Story 5 with modest expectations after enjoying Toy Story 4 but feeling the franchise had already said its goodbyes. Surprisingly, this turned out to be the strongest sequel since Toy Story 2. Giving Jessie the spotlight was long overdue, and her emotional arc finally provides the closure she's deserved since Toy Story 2. The army of Buzz Lightyears is another inspired addition, delivering some of the film's biggest laughs. The story also deserves credit for tackling technology's growing influence on childhood. Rather than preaching about screens, it thoughtfully explores how digital devices can coexist with imagination and play, making the message feel natural instead of forced. Yes, many plot beats are predictable - but honestly, what great family film isn't? What matters is that the characters remain lovable, the humour consistently lands, and the emotional moments feel earned. 8/10: A warm, funny, and surprisingly meaningful return that proves there's still plenty of life left in Pixar's favourite toy box.

review: Toy Story 5 (2026) : Movie Review - Toy Story 1, 2, and 3 will always remain my favourite trilogy of all time-neck-and-neck with the original Star Wars trilogy and The Lord of the Rings. Toy Story 3 will forever stand as the greatest third instalment ever made in cinema history-not just because it is a masterpiece, but because of the way it concludes everything so beautifully. I still wonder how Pixar managed to make grown adults cry over toys. I was in my 20s, and I cried like a child during the ending of Toy Story 3. Neither LOTR, Star Wars, nor even The Dark Knight trilogy managed to do that to me. Then came Toy Story 4, which honestly wasn't needed after such a perfect finale, but it still worked well enough. The themes felt complete, yet Pixar chose to move forward with Toy Story 5. The only logical direction left was to explore digital gaming and modern play habits-and that's exactly what this film attempts. However, unlike its predecessors that delivered strong, universal messages, this one fails to land with the same impact. The fifth instalment remains honest to the franchise's legacy and values, but it lacks the emotional punch that defines Toy Story. For me, this series has always balanced toys and kids equally-50-50. This time, however, the focus shifts more toward kids and their friendships rather than the toys themselves, which feels like a significant intellectual misstep. Toy Story 5 begins with Bonnie struggling to befriend her neighbour's twins. She finds comfort in playing with her toys while the world around her rapidly evolves. Kids are no longer playing with toys-they're immersed in digital gaming devices. This is highly relatable and reflects a global shift over the past decade. The potential here was massive. Unfortunately, Pixar reduces this rich premise into a simplistic conflict-turning it into a mission where toys must help Bonnie find "real" friends. This feels overly specific and lacks the universal emotional appeal the series is known for. Jessie, Buzz, and Woody attempt to adapt by engaging with these digital devices to reconnect with Bonnie. Feeling embarrassed about playing with toys, Bonnie begins to reject them and gravitates toward her virtual world. Jessie believes Bonnie needs real friendships, not virtual ones, and the toys gang embarks on a mission to find her a true friend. While this setup has emotional potential, the execution feels limited and somewhat forced. There's a striking parallel I couldn't ignore. In My Man Godfrey (1936), William Powell says, "It's about time that I was moving on," which becomes an emotional turning point. That goodbye signifies a new beginning. Toy Story 3 embraced this philosophy perfectly. However, Toy Story 4 and now Toy Story 5 keep revisiting the same "moving on" theme repeatedly, and at this point, it feels redundant. It's as if the franchise is reluctant to truly evolve beyond its own emotional blueprint. The film focuses heavily on solving Bonnie's immediate problem, but what about the bigger picture? What about other children? What about Bonnie herself a few years down the line? Realistically, within five years, toy culture may diminish even further. The existential dilemma of toys-their acceptance, irrelevance, and emotional closure-is barely explored. This lack of depth becomes one of the film's biggest flaws. The second major issue is the absence of a powerful emotional climax. A Toy Story film without moist eyes at the end? That just doesn't feel like a Toy Story movie at all! The voice cast does a decent job. Tom Hanks, Tim Allen, Joan Cusack, Greta Lee, Conan O'Brien, Tony Hale, Craig Robinson, Shelby Rabara, Scarlett Spears, and the rest of the ensemble deliver competent performances. The animation quality remains consistently strong, as expected. The editing feels sluggish in the first hour but improves significantly in the final 30-35 minutes. The sound and art design are serviceable, though one might expect something more refined from a franchise of this stature. Andrew Stanton's script feels mediocre when weighed against the colossal legacy of Toy Story. That burden is immense-perhaps unfair-but unavoidable. In isolation, this script might have worked as a decent standalone film. However, as a Toy Story entry, it falls short. The film misses out on delivering an idealistic finale, meaningful sacrifices, a resonant message for both parents and children, and a deeper critique of digitalisation-all elements that could have elevated it into something truly memorable. Without these core emotional and philosophical layers, one has to question the purpose of continuing the franchise. Stanton's screenplay lacks the depth and sharpness expected, and that shortcoming reflects in his direction as well. Toy Story 5 is, at best, a good film-but "good" is simply not good enough for a Toy Story movie. Perhaps Stanton forgot what made these films timeless. What we get instead is a fairly entertaining experience, far removed from the profound emotional and intellectual world we've lived in with these characters since 1995. RATING - 6/10*

review: By Ian Chandler - June 22, 2026 Toy Story 5, directed and co-written by Andrew Stanton, is the latest entry in the now 30-year-old franchise. Like its predecessor, the film had to fight an uphill battle to justify its existence, as Toy Story 3 boasts one of the greatest conclusions in cinematic history. And while that will be debated for a long time, I would argue that this newest feature provides a strong case in its favor, thanks to treading new ground and evolving major character arcs. As the trailers suggest, Jessie is the star of the show, resulting in a fresh, distinguished tale that most will find investing. Wrapping that up in a gorgeous and endearing package, Pixar's latest offering is a must see. If there was one part of Toy Story 5 that was guaranteed to work, it is the legendary ensemble. Joan Cusack, like the toy she plays, Jessie, is noticeably older; but that does not in any way diminish her fierce, confident performance. The movie's focus on Jessie gives Cusack plenty of material to showcase her excellent voice work. Tim Allen is also noteworthy for his dedication to maintain Buzz Lightyear's energy and iconic vocals, despite his claim that it is now difficult to do so. Returning franchise stalwarts like Tom Hanks and Wallace Shawn are commendable and charming too but are not given much to be more than that. Finally, the newcomers in the cast are simply great, primarily Greta Lee as Lilypad and Conan O'Brien as another supporting character. Not only is the voice work charming, but the presentation is also as endearing as ever. The animation, per Pixar tradition, is immaculate. Though it is not as vibrant or as striking as its predecessor, Toy Story 5 is dazzling. I saw it in IMAX, and I am happy to say that, unlike Toy Story 4, it fills the massive screen with its 1.85:1 aspect ratio. Also complementing the stunning visuals is Randy Newman's easygoing, cordial score. Many fans may have to buy tissues once more thanks to Newman and the script. However, I did find some pieces to be distracting, as some were blatantly stolen from previous Pixar works, like Monsters, Inc. Nevertheless, the film is a pleasure to the eyes and the ears. The themes are more poignant than the already touching fourth installment. Though technology (particularly iPads) dominating and diminishing childhoods has been a significant issue for over 15 years, Toy Story 5 may have arrived at the right time, now that its topic may be at its severest point. But this movie smartly injects the consequences and misfortunes of screen addictions without drowning in gloomy, tiring cynicism. The point gets across even while the toys venture through silly shenanigans. I hope that the film will convince some children to consider a healthier balance of imagination and dopamine, even if the habit is hard to break. Alongside the material Toy Story 5 concerns itself with, it significantly develops a previous supporting character: Jessie. She is the feature's main character, and the writers take full advantage of that. I cannot say much, as they would spoil the movie, but what I will mention is that she has about as much substance as Woody by the time the credits roll. Buzz also is able to captivate and is granted to grow and contribute to the plot without relying on his pre-recorded voice-box for guidance. Like Toy Story 4, however, the other toys have next to nothing to offer. I believe Slinky, for example, has just one line in the entire film. But if they had to be pushed into the toy box in order to substantially grow Jessie and keep the plot focused, it is a compromise I can get behind. Toy Story 5, like the previous entry, has a burden of existing when Toy Story 3 seemingly closed the franchise perfectly. Where Toy Story 4, as delightful as it is, struggles to justify its existence, this picture plays with the toys in more meaningful ways. The situation it covers is more relevant, its central characters have a smoother arc, its ending is more satisfying, and it moves forward, embracing the bold decisions its forerunner pursued. The mildly inconsistent pacing, partially recycled score, and its negligence for most of the gang do hamper it a little, but its massive strengths counter it considerably. While the second and third films remain to be the pinnacle, Toy Story 5 maintains the franchise's reputation of being a prestigious, practically impeccable series. Score: 83/100 Summary (for quick reference): Though Toy Story 3 remains the perfect closure for the franchise, Toy Story 5 is a heartfelt adventure that pushes the franchise forward with its relevant commentary, sincerity, and additional depth given to Jessie's character.

review: For me, Toy Story will always be about Woody and Buzz. As a longtime fan especially of Buzz, I was excited to see this movie, particularly because of its central idea: what happens to toys in a world where children spend more time on tablets and screens than playing with them. I really liked the message. It's warm, relevant, and encourages children to make friends and spend more time together instead of letting technology take over their childhood. It's a thoughtful theme that feels very appropriate today. The movie also brought back some genuine nostalgia. Seeing Buzz and Woody together again was wonderful, and one of my favorite moments was the group of old Buzz Lightyears still believing they're Space Rangers. review: I went into this movie after hearing mixed reactions online. Some people said it was disappointing, yet everyone I personally knew who had seen it really enjoyed it. Since Toy Story 4 was a huge letdown for me compared to the first three films, I was hoping this installment would be a return to form and it absolutely was. In some ways, Toy Story 5 is unique from the rest of the series, but the way it embraces those differences is brilliant. Just as its core audience has grown up alongside the franchise, the toys have aged with them. It's rare for a film series to evolve in step with its audience, but this movie does it beautifully. Unlike previous entries, Woody isn't the central toy. This story very much belongs to Jessie. The filmmakers do an excellent job blending nostalgia with the realities of the world in 2026. Throughout the film, we see kids making friends online and relying more on technology, yet the story also emphasizes that there is still an important place for genuine, face-to-face human connection. The franchise continues its tradition of rewarding longtime fans with subtle Easter eggs and callbacks to earlier films. More importantly, it recaptures the original Toy Story charm that felt somewhat missing from the fourth installment. The humor is consistently funny while remaining family friendly, and the film introduces Smarty Pants who I expect most fans to enjoy. That said, some of the beloved supporting characters including Slinky, Mr./ Mrs. Potato Head, the Aliens, and Rex are unfortunately pushed into the background. While they're still present, their limited roles are noticeable and leave you wishing they had more to do. Overall, Toy Story 5 delivers exactly what I was hoping for. It provided laughs, nostalgia, and a heartfelt story centered on Jessie and Bonnie. Many viewers will likely connect with the emotions these characters experience throughout the film. For me, this was a welcome return to everything that made the Toy Story franchise so special.

review_title: toys still affect us even after we stop playing with them
review: This film beautifully explores the lasting impact toys can have on our lives. Unlike the previous installments, this time Jessie takes center stage. While the story satirizes today's digital society, it never portrays technology itself as the enemy. Instead, it offers a thoughtful and compassionate message about how we choose to use it. I especially appreciated that Lilypad wasn't written as a one-dimensional villain. My favorite part of the film was the revelation that Emily hadn't forgotten Jessie. Instead, she had grown up and given her own child Jessie's name. It was a beautiful way of showing that, even though Jessie believed she had been left behind, she had truly changed Emily's life. I can relate to that. There are toys I hardly ever touch anymore, but the memories I made with them are still precious to me. The same idea applies to Bonnie. As she grows older, she'll probably spend less time playing with toys. Even so, the film suggests that a toy's role is to be there when it's needed-to help a child make friends or provide comfort at important moments. I found that conclusion both convincing and beautiful. The comedy was excellent, with plenty of genuinely funny moments that make the film enjoyable and accessible for younger audiences. My biggest criticism is that I found it difficult to become emotionally invested. The pacing feels a little rushed, making some emotional beats harder to follow, and there are a few moments where the characters' motivations aren't entirely convincing. Woody's return also felt rather forced and will probably divide fans. That said, as someone who loves this series, I was still happy to see him again, and I really enjoyed the many callbacks and homages to the previous films.

review_title: different but in a good way
review: Toy Story 5 is a worthy entry in the franchise, primarily for its social commentary on the effects of screen time on family life and children's development. I appreciated the central emotional arcs of the characters Bonnie and Jessie. This develops nicely throughout the story and leads to a suitably heartfelt climax. Some of the new supporting characters are well used, particularly Smarty Pants and the updated Buzzes. As always, it does the exciting action spectacle exceptionally well. Are Woody and some of the original characters only there for nostalgia's sake? I think they are, particularly Woody, who you feel is written into certain moments to meet audience expectations. The filmmakers probably could have given other characters more time in his place, but I guess it wouldn't be Toy Story without him in some way. The writers use a major platform to tell some home truths about our relationship with technology, and I admire this aspect of the movie very much. Arguably, they could have been harsher in their critique and portrayed the character Lilypad as a more nefarious antagonist, akin to Lots'o/Prospector/Sid. I get the nuanced tale they wanted to tell with compromises, but in my opinion, children are better off without personal screens, and adults (who should know better) spend too much time as slaves to them. Although this theme is generally handled well, especially in certain visuals portraying people zoned out tapping/scrolling and the glow of screens in households like a spreading disease, I think an opportunity was missed to show a family choosing to put phones/tablets/laptops away permanently and spend quality time together. As you would expect from Pixar, the visuals are brilliant, and the voice performances are of a high standard.

Already in Toy Story 4 we saw how much Buzz had changed, and know it has gotten even worse. He now lacks inner security, maturity, wisedoms of experience and overall went from a leading character in charge to fumbling comically like a fool. They STOLE all the build-ups from past movies and the seasoning values he gained. And for what? Yes, the "new audience" narrative to raise a female character as the "better leader" and using the established male-hero as a living joke to accomplish that - as we have seen in SO MANY awful sequel attempts and remakes in recent years. As we left Toy Story 4, Woody LEFT the ol' gang to pursue new adventures with his long- lost love Bo Peep to help lost toys. Woody made this choise based on he was FINISHED being a child's toy. Having been for a longer time unwanted by new owner and Woody gradually realize his mission with Andy can't be repeated ever again. His time was complete- and done. This movie will forever leave a nasty stain on the franchise just like Disney's Star Wars sequels. No Respect - We Reject is a internet slogan that fits perfectly here, because respect is what this movie held NOTHING of.

review: Toy Story 5 takes the franchise in a surprisingly intimate direction, focusing less on big adventures and more on the emotional journey of finding genuine connection. Instead of the tech takeover story many expected, the film centers on Bonnie's struggle to understand what real friendship looks like and how easily kids can fall into relationships that feel forced or performative. The boldest choice is making Jessie the main character. Her history of being forgotten gives her a natural emotional link to Bonnie's arc, and the film uses that to deliver some of its strongest moments. While Woody, Buzz, and the classic crew are pushed to the sidelines more than longtime fans might prefer, their presence still matters. They become the quiet support system helping Bonnie navigate her feelings and discover what a true friend actually is. What really works is how the toys come together not to save the day in a traditional sense, but to guide Bonnie toward authenticity, without awkwardness, pressure, or pretending. It's a softer, more reflective Toy Story, but one that still lands with heart. Even with the shift in focus, the message hits hard: real connection is worth the effort, and sometimes the people (or toys) who step back are the ones who help you grow the most. 9 out of 10. A heartfelt, thoughtful chapter that earns its place in the series.

review_title: still has that toy story magic
review: Toy Story 5 is one of those movies that reminded me why I've always enjoyed this franchise. After so many years and several sequels, I wasn't sure if there was much left to say, but it still managed to be a fun and heartfelt adventure. It may not reach the emotional highs of some of the earlier films, but it definitely captures the same spirit that made the series so popular. The biggest strength is still the characters. Spending time with Woody, Buzz, and the rest of the gang feels familiar in the best way. Their chemistry hasn't gone anywhere, and the movie balances humor and emotion well enough to keep both longtime fans and newer audiences entertained. There are plenty of funny moments, but it also finds time for quieter scenes that remind you these characters have been growing for decades. Visually, it looks fantastic. Pixar continues to raise the bar with its animation, and every environment feels incredibly detailed. The action sequences are creative without becoming overwhelming, and the pacing stays steady throughout, making it an easy movie to sit back and enjoy. That said, I didn't feel like this installment was as impactful as the series at its best. Some story beats feel familiar, and I never had the same emotional connection I had with earlier entries. It's entertaining from beginning to end, but it doesn't leave quite the same lasting impression. Overall, Toy Story 5 is another enjoyable chapter in one of Pixar's most iconic franchises. It's funny, charming, and beautifully animated, even if it doesn't quite reach the heights of its predecessors. A solid 7/10 for me.

review_title: toy story 5 was a huge disappointment
review: As a longtime Toy Story fan, I was very disappointed with Toy Story 5. The biggest problem for me was the villain, Lilypad. Compared to memorable villains and emotional conflicts from previous movies, this character felt weak and uninteresting. What made the original Toy Story films special was the strong friendship between the characters, the emotional storytelling, and the feeling of adventure. In this movie, that magic was missing. The story felt more focused on introducing new ideas than building on what made the franchise great in the first place. Toy Story 1, 2, and 3 had heart, memorable moments, and characters that felt important. Toy Story 5 did not capture the same feeling for me. While the animation is impressive, good visuals alone cannot replace a strong story and compelling characters. I respect the effort that went into making this film, but as a fan of the classic Toy Story movies, I left the theater disappointed. I hope future entries return to the emotional depth and charm that made the series so beloved. Another major problem with this movie is how it treats the classic Toy Story characters. Slinky Dog, Hamm, Rex, Mr. Potato Head, Mrs. Potato Head, and the Aliens are not minor background characters. They are part of the heart and identity of Toy Story. review_title: it's surprising to see so many bad reviews when the movie is really good
review: Okay, okay... we all know that "Toy Story" ended with its third installment back in 2010, and everything that's come after only risks tarnishing the franchise's name in order to make money... we know that. However, before this movie, I felt like there was actually something to tell because of what I could glimpse of the plot, and luckily that feeling was rewarded! The kids who grew up in the '80s and '90s are very different from kids today. We don't play with toys anymore; video games and screens have taken over every space that used to be occupied. That's why the story told in this movie is so interesting. This time, Woody and Buzz are more in supporting roles, and the weight of the plot rests on Jessie and the old and new gadgets that technology has given us. The question arises: are these devices truly bad, cutting off and preventing us from dreaming, creativity, and making real, not just virtual, friends? The film's initial answer is yes, they are. They sever all contact between children (and adults too) and the reality that surrounds them. Looking each other in the eye, sharing pure, distraction-free moments, and creating those memories that stay with you long after childhood or adolescence are gone. But fortunately, this film isn't just about that. As we progress, we see that these devices are also very good, useful, and help us with things we couldn't even dream of before, not even in the most creative minds. They are capable of immortalizing moments, and while what remains in our minds shouldn't be permanent, we know very well that it is. This is why I liked "Toy Story 5" so much; it's a way of reconnecting with the purest part of our childhood and creating things that enhance the experience, not replace it, but complement it. Don't lose the essence that defines us and that we lose as adults. Children have their own pace; some things make them grow up too fast, causing them to miss out on other very important things. Special mention to the Lightyear squad, who are by far the funniest part of the movie, and some of the interactions with the other toys, who unfortunately have much less screen time. I really enjoyed the movie; I think it's a great addition to the franchise. However, please only exploit this when there are stories to tell... PLEASE!

review_title: pleasant reunion even if it's starting to wear a bit thin
review: I came to this installment of the long-running franchise with a good deal of skepticism. Hasn't Disney/Pixar gotten enough money out of us for this? Is this going to be nothing more than a pleasant couple of hours with old friends, telling the same old stories? I won't deny the last issue. Movies like this are expensive to make, and the ones that make money have to cover the ones that lose money. As well as paying the company's CEO a lot of money, as well as the compensations of the salary consultants and board of directors who are all basically hired by the CEO. But I digress. The story here is that the little girl of the previous episode has reached the age at which her parents buy her a tablet, which will let her make friends with other children her age. Naturally the toys, under the current leadership of Jessie, hate this. There's also a subplot of a carton of the latest version of the Buzz Lightyear figures getting loose on the docks and making their way towards the main plot. Very pleasant, if unremarkable. There is also a nice bit of subtext which the popular media ignored, going on about "Pixar hates technology!" It's in three parts: people grow in different ways even from their age groups; those in charge of making decisions don't always make the right decisions; and finally, that imagination and creativity are good things. Was it worth going to the theater to see this? For me, no. Pixar's CGI is great stuff, but there's nothing here that needs to be seen on a big screen. Had I waited a couple of years to see it free on TV, or a couple of months when it would be priced at $6 on On Demand would have been no hardship. Still, I was in a mood to see a movie, this is the one I saw, and it was pretty good to hear the usual Toy Story voice cast; Tom Hanks, Tim Allen, Joan Cusack, et al make it a familiar pleasure.

review: When Toy Story 5 was announced, I was very concerned. The first three films are easily one of the best trilogy out there with a beautiful and satisfying ending in the 3rd film. The 4th film, while not as good as the original three, it did still have a strong and emotional ending that felt like a nice wrap up for the whole series. Yet, here we are with a 5th entry that threatens to damage the whole poignant ending. Is this a necessary entry or is this a story not worth telling? What this new entry tackles is something incredibly relatable to our current times. What if kids stop believing in playing with toys and started being more interested in tech? It's an interesting dilemma and is something that the director, Andrew Stanton, takes a genuine deep dive into. The film doesn't just portray the new tech, Lilypad, as a straight-up villain and there is a layered exploration of toys and tech. At the heart of this new story is Jessie. She struggles with what feels like her losing Bonnie to tech. She is afraid of Bonnie abandoning her just like Emily did in the past. Jessie undergoes a wonderful character arc that feels like natural evolution of her character that would definitely bring a tear to people's eye. A big surprise is also Bonnie herself. There is a really meaningful journey for her as well, something that is a major motivator for Jessie, that leads to a genuinely heartfelt final act and ending. In terms of writing, there is a perfect balance between the serious, humour and even romance. For example, jokes never ruin emotional moments or romance isn't overshadowing the main plot. On that note, I do find the jokes to be well-executed and do mostly land. The voice cast also continue to do a great job. Special praise to Joan Cusack as Jessie who absolutely delivers some of her strongest voice performance yet. Randy Newton also returns to score the music for the Toy Story series and as usual, does a magnificent job. His music score elevates every moment and makes the story beats hit harder when it needs to. The animation is also easily the best the Toy Story franchise has ever been. This is especially noticeable when animals appear because they have never looked so close to real life than ever before! I really love how the art style changes during the "imagination" scenes which look gorgeous. There are also many fantastic looking shots within the film which is the result of great cinematography. Now Toy Story 5 is clearly Jessie's film but Woody and Buzz do return. Buzz was completely sidelined in Toy Story 4 but he is given a bit more to do in this new entry. However, it is mostly just to deal with the small arc between him and Jessie. Apart from that, he is still quite sidelined here. Woody's return is completely forced, especially considering his conclusive arc in the previous film. His return is just to be a joke and comedic relief which is kind of weird to see. Him and Buzz are basically the B-plot of the film but what they do isn't that interesting compared to Jessie's. There is also a really silly conflict between the two that feels very unnecessary. There is also another subplot concerning an army of Buzz Lightyears that is a bit distracting. The film will sometimes just cut from the main plot to them and it does take a long time for that plot line to have any payoff. While it does feel obvious that this was made to capitalise on Pixar's most iconic franchise. The story being told here is incredibly meaningful and relevant. Jessie gets to properly shine and even gets a satisfying character wrap up for her. Toy Story 5 is another phenomenal entry and is an absolute must-watch!

review_title: i guess they really meant infinity and beyond huh
review: There are only so many times you can rehash the same themes, and 'Toy Story 5 (2026)' is close to the limit. Although it focuses on a different primary character than before, it has her undergo the same arc she's been through at least once (if not twice) before, and centres around a relatively weak "tech is taking" over premise that doesn't also have a keen real-life counterpoint (other than exactly what it says on the tin) like the central conflicts of the previous pictures so cleverly did. For the first 45 minutes, the flick feels closer to something you'd expect to see on Disney+, an episode rather than a full-blown feature. It's rushed, it's unceremonious, it reeks of "cash grab". Then, Conan O'Brien enters the chat and things start to get a little more fun (and I don't think that's a coincidence). There are a handful of fun set-pieces, some really successful gags, and a fairly nuanced underlying message that dares to say "some kids, like their adult counterparts, are just jerks". The voicework is all as good as you'd expect, the animation is lively and well-rendered, there are a couple of emotionally potent moments, and everything comes together rather nicely (despite the finale paling in comparison to the heights of literally every other 'Toy Story' third act). It isn't a bad movie. In fact, it's pretty good on a moment-to-moment, or even comparative, basis.
