review_title: the only time i've ever been compelled to leave a review for any movie
review: For years, I was an advocate for Toy Story 1, 2 & 3 of being one of the true great trilogies in cinema history. Genuinely funny, warm and endlessly entertaining - worth multiple rewatches. Proper comfort viewing. I was apprehensive about 4 but that earned it's place in the franchise with the new charming characters it added. However, 5 is a completely different film. It doesn't gel with the rest of the franchise and merely exploits the existing characters as a vehicle to carry a very different message to the earlier films. Previously we've seen the links to the individual toy owners and the emotion of when they've outgrown the toys. We know the drill - kids grow up but the toys find new owners with the next generation. The cycle works, the movie ends on a happy note. In this outing we have a broader proposition foisted upon us - what happens when, not individuals but the whole of society falls out of love with toys. While the advent of cheap and widely available technology has definitely changed the face of kids growing up and is undoubtedly an issue that has to be addressed, I felt the manner in which it was handled was somewhat clunky. I also felt it did a disservice to the characters we've all come to love. The comedic buddy act of Woody and Buzz is reduced to little more than a footnote. A couple of call backs here and there but overall, the story left their friendship cold. Truth be told, it felt as though Woody had just been shoehorned in because he had to be in it but his role added little. Honestly, I can't imagine Tom Hanks being happy reading the script. That aside, the warm humour we've come to love was seriously lacking - I genuinely can't remember laughing at all during the film. To not come over too negative, I will say that visually it is very impressive. The quality of the animation is spectacular and credit to the production team, they are masters of their craft. Overall however, my feeling is - it is the right story being told in the wrong way. We absolutely have to address the amount of screen time our children have. And that cyber bullying is a real issue in society that needs to be addressed. To that end, I hope this can play a part is making children take heed of their online activity. I did feel though that the mesage was aimed at the parents rather than children. It was however done in a finger wagging "look what you've done to your kids" kind of way. It would also be a showing of real hypocrisy if a mobile game was released to coincide with the film without proper inbuilt mechanisms to reduce the harms that can come from excess screen time. So yes, we need to address the issue but as a movie - honestly this message could have been told in a completely different film and not by borrowing the Toy Story universe to tell it. I don't feel this fitted with the franchise at all and has little appeal for rewatchability like the previous installments.

review_title: better than it has any right to be but the formula is starting to show its age
review: I'll admit, when Disney announced Toy Story 5, I groaned. Toy Story 3 was the perfect, tear-jerking trilogy closer. Toy Story 4 felt a bit unnecessary but gave Woody a beautiful send-off. So why do a fifth one? We all know the answer is "money," but I went into the theater today hoping Pixar would at least give us a story worth telling. And honestly? They mostly did. It's a solid, incredibly well-made movie, even if it feels a bit like a "greatest hits" compilation at times. The central conflict of "Toys vs. Tech" provides a fantastic existential crisis for the gang. Since Woody left, Jessie is the leader of the room, and Joan Cusack absolutely steals the show here. The emotional weight of the movie lands squarely on her shoulders, especially during a deeply moving sequence where she rediscovers her own history with her old kid, Emily. The comedy is great, too. Tim Allen pulling double duty voicing an entire army of 50 defective, internet-connected Buzz Lightyears stuck in demo mode is peak chaotic Pixar humor. The animation is predictably stunning-the way the animators contrast the matte, scuffed plastic of the classic toys with the sleek, cold glass of modern tablets is a masterclass in visual storytelling. So why only a 7? Because despite the high-tech makeover, the skeletal structure of the plot is identical to every other *Toy Story* movie. A toy gets separated from the group. The toys have to venture out into the dangerous human world on a rescue mission. They encounter a flashy new toy who seems nice but turns out to be an antagonist. They have a realization about what it means to be outgrown by a child. Andrew Stanton's direction keeps things moving at a brisk, entertaining pace, and Randy Newman's score will definitely make you well-up in the final act. But it's hard to shake the feeling of deja vu. If you have kids, they will love it, and if you grew up with these characters, you'll definitely get hit with a massive wave of nostalgia. It's a very good movie. I just really hope Pixar finally lets these characters rest in the toy box now.

review: Pixar's gang returns for round five and this time the villain isn't a tyrannical teddy bear or a vindictive ventriloquist dummy - it's a tablet. Bonnie's toys find themselves face-to-face with Lilypad, a tablet that arrives with her own ideas about what's best for their kid and the film wastes no time turning that into its central anxiety: What happens to a child's inner world when a screen does the imagining for her? It's a sharp premise and for a while the film commits to it with real bite. Watching Woody and Jessie get demoted from "beloved playthings" to "legacy hardware" is the most cutting Pixar has been about modern parenting since Inside Out made us cry about a console glitching. There's a genuinely bleak image early on - a doll in a sort of backyard cemetery of abandoned playthings intoning that the age of toys is over and for a beat, Toy Story 5 feels like it might actually let that idea sit and sting. But true to franchise form, the satire gets the training wheels back on. The film can't quite bring itself to indict the tablet outright - instead it pivots Lilypad into a sympathetic device just trying to help her kid make friends, which softens the commentary right when it should be sharpening. The result is a movie that raises real questions about screens replacing imaginative, hands-on play, then resolves them a little too neatly, as if Pixar got nervous about offending the very iPads its own movies get watched on. Performances carry a lot of the weight - Hanks and Cusack still find new notes in characters they've voiced for three decades and the new 'Buzz battalion' subplot is good comic relief, even if it is mostly filler. Visually it's gorgeous, particularly the chalk-pastel imagination sequences. Solid, handsome, occasionally brave - but it doesn't have the emotional ruthlessness or thematic nerve of Toy Story 3, which remains the franchise's high-water mark and what should have been a perfect finale to a groundbreaking part of cinematic history. That was of course, before Disney decided that none of the other Pixar movies seem to be able to keep putting pennies in the electricity meter quite like Woody and his 'Round-Up'. I fear 6, 7 and 8 are already in the works.

review_title: a soulless sequel that forgot its characters
review: So disappointed with this totally soulless and unnecessary entry into a beloved series. I rewatched all of the previous Toy Story films before seeing this one, and the difference was impossible to ignore. The biggest problem is that this movie doesn't seem to understand its own characters. Woody, Jessie and Buzz all behave in ways that feel completely at odds with who they've been and become across four previous films. Their decisions, dialogue and relationships all completely lack continuity, and the personality, bravery, comeraderie and sincerity that made these characters so enduring. Buzz, in particular, has been stripped of the confidence, charm and competence that defined him. Instead of writing Jessie as a strong character in her own right, the film weakens her love interest to make her appear more capable. It's awfully lazy character writing, so out of touch and does a disservice to both characters. The humour is also a shadow of what came before. The original films were packed with clever visual gags, inventive escapes and intricate plans that only these characters could pull off. Here, that ingenuity is gone, replaced by action that feels predictable, uninspired, rushed and completely unrealistic (I mean, I know we're talking about a film about talking toys here, but previous films managed to pull off some serious plot believability!) Even the central message never quite lands. The film *seems* to be exploring the idea that children's imaginative play is being overtaken by technology, while also suggesting that technology itself isn't the enemy if it's used with good intentions and balance... It's a potentially thoughtful theme, but the storytelling is so muddled that the message gets lost. The animation is undeniably gorgeous, but technical excellence can't replace heart. The earlier films delighted in the tiny details of the toys' world and made it feel alive. This one looks beautiful but feels empty. The emotional depth that made the earlier films so special is almost entirely absent. Previous Toy Story films have had me in floods of tears, but the emotional climax in this one feels forced and manufactured, and instead of feeling moved, I found myself rolling my eyes. I also couldn't have cared less about the Buzz Lightyear army subplot! Ironically, for a film commenting on technology replacing creativity, it feels like a product of exactly that: polished on the surface, but lacking the heart and soul that made the original Toy Story films timeless. SO disappointed.

review: This film was always going to be a hard sell, especially after the gorgeous-looking but underwhelming story of Toy Story 4, but I can pleasantly report that Toy Story 5 is a sweet and fun film, that feels like a true continuation of the story from Toy Story 3. I went into this film with low expectations, after all, how often does the 5th film in the franchise managed to truly justify its existence. But from the opening scene, my interest piqued and my engagement never waned once throughout the runtime. Essentially focusing on Jessie as the main character (a lovely change of pace after she was severely sidelined in the previous film), the story focuses on the very real world issues of kids relying too much on tech devices. This plot focus, a joke and meme made numerous times after the release of Toy Story 3 about the future validity of the franchise, is tackled in a decent enough way and with a hope that parents/kids will take the right message away from the film (although the sad reality is probably not). But what really elevated the story for me was Jessie's journey throughout the film, which starts off in typical fashion but slowly evolves into a very heartfelt reconciliation on her own past, culminating beautifully with a scene that had my eyes welling up at its genuine emotional sincerity and call back to her original owner. All the returning voice talents are naturally great, including franchise favourites Tom Hanks, Tim Allen and Joan Cusack, but it's new additions to the story that I really enjoyed, especially Greta Lee as the antagonistic LilyPad and Conan O'Brien as a forgotten and outdated device called Smarty Pants. There's also a fun subplot involving a whole fleet of new and improved Buzz Lightyear toys on their own little journey, and while it's a little contrived how they connect to the main story, I ultimately didn't mind it. Plus some of the imagery in these scenes is some of the most beautiful and distinct I've seen from the franchise. Overall, this is a film greatly surprised me with how much I enjoyed the story and characters 5th time around, and I think that is a true testament that Pixar can still make the right creative choices despite the cloud of cynicism that hangs over the studio these days. Is this film better than Toy Story 3? Probably not, but at the moment this is definitely feeling like a story continuation that I'm super glad exists.

review: There were some nice moments, but this installment felt a little disorganized and messy. It's definitely not Pixar's best film of the year, with Hoppers taking that title, and it falls short of many of the previous entries in the franchise. The toy versus tech premise was intriguing, but the writers seemed too distracted by several minor storylines and never fully capitalized on the central conflict. I liked Lilypad as the film's new toy antagonist (or is she really a toy?), but the character felt underdeveloped. She has very little backstory, doesn't get enough direct conflict with the other characters, and her character arc lacks the emotional weight it needed. Clearly, she's intended to function more as a thematic presence than a traditional villain, but that leaves her as a middling Pixar antagonist when she had the potential to be a great one. Part of the issue is that the film repeatedly circles back to the original characters for sequences that don't meaningfully advance the plot. After enduring a barrage of boomer-style complaints throughout the first half, however, the movie finds its footing in the second. It begins to recapture the spirit of Toy Story by thoughtfully exploring how to build authentic relationships and maintain a sense of self in a digitally connected world where failing to conform can come with significant social costs. The animation is excellent, as expected from Pixar, and perhaps even more photorealistic than usual. I especially enjoyed the "playtime" sequences, which feature a softer, hand-drawn pastel aesthetic that helps them stand out visually. While the film never reaches the heights of the franchise's best installments, it offers enough fresh ideas and worthwhile themes to give longtime fans something to enjoy.

He lacks the irreplaceable central role he once had, which is a bit disappointing for longtime fans. In addition, the film touches on the very real issue of children becoming absorbed in tablets and video games, but it handles the topic rather gently. Bonnie is shy and lacks friends, and she eventually finds new companions with the help of the toys. There is nothing wrong with that ending, but it feels a little shallow. In reality, excessive gaming can do more than affect social skills-it can also take time away from studying, eating, talking with parents, exercising, and developing other interests. If the film had explored how children can balance online entertainment with real life more deeply, the story would have felt more meaningful and relevant. So my overall view of the film is this: the emotions are still touching, but there is still room for improvement in character development and in how it addresses contemporary issues.

review_title: a lovely fifth addition to the beloved series that manages to hit all the right emotional notes once again
review: "Toy Story 5" is the fifth installment in the "Toy Story" film franchise. Directed and co-written by Andrew Stanton and featuring the voices of Tom Hanks, Tim Allen, and Joan Cusack, it is a lovely fifth addition to the beloved series that manages to hit all the right emotional notes once again. Sometime after the events of "Toy Story 4", Bonnie Anderson is now eight-years-old and hopes to make friends with the other kids who all happen to be focused on their smart devices. Bonnie's parents soon gift her with a frog-themed tablet named Lilypad (voiced by Greta Lee), who causes the young girl to become addicted to the technological aspects and neglect playing with her toys. As the new leader of the toys since the departure of Woody (voiced by Tom Hanks), Jessie (voiced by Joan Cusack) takes it upon herself to inform Lilypad of the damage she is causing to Bonnie's social life, but the device ignores her and continues to prevent Bonnie from interacting properly with others. Realising that this new modern technology can't be reasoned with, Jessie reconnects with Woody to ask him to assist her with this issue, as Bonnie becomes even more dependent on using Lilypad. After making his way back to Bonnie's house, Woody reunites with Buzz (voiced by Tim Allen) and the rest of the toys but quickly discovers that Jessie has not yet returned with Bonnie after a sleepover with one of her online friends. Though the two of them can't agree on who should be leading the charge, Woody and Buzz set off to find Jessie and rescue her from the increasing electronic threat. The "Toy Story" franchise has always held a special place in my heart due to the original film being the very first movie I remember seeing in theatres. Ever since then, I have credited that film with what helped kick off my lifelong love of cinema as a whole, as well as my appreciation for animation as a medium rather than something aimed exclusively at children. Though many consider the third movie to be the perfect conclusion to the series, a fourth film was made years later that remains polarising to fans, whereas I remain in the camp of those who nonetheless enjoyed it for what it was. Now in 2026, we have a fifth mainline film in "Toy Story 5", which continues the saga of the toys in a movie that thankfully proves Pixar still has what it takes to be as emotionally investing with one of their best known IPs as they were decades ago. Starting things off in the Anderson household, we watch as Bonnie happily plays with her toys in her room, with Jessie being the clear favourite of the bunch. As she puts all of the toys through some creative scenarios, Bonnie soon notices some kids around her age next door outside on their lawn and longs to become friends with them. Grabbing Jessie, Bonnie heads out to interact with the pair, but becomes frightened when it comes time to approach them up close. Barely acknowledging her at all, the two kids walk off to sit down on their front steps to resume playing with their smart tablets, of which Bonnie does not currently own. Amidst this awkwardness, Jessie also notices what is happening and comes to the shocking realisation that today's kids are more preoccupied with technology rather than playing with actual physical toys. To make matters worse for the toys, Bonnie herself soon comes into possession of her own smart device; a frog-looking "Lilypad" tablet that connects to virtually every electrical item in her house. With this new gadget, Bonnie quickly becomes heavily invested in playing online games, which causes Jessie and the rest of the toys to become neglected in the process. Even after Jessie attempts to persuade Lilypad to help Bonnie with making friends in real life, the smart device disregards her polite request and instead chooses to set her young owner up with people online. Once the severity of this sinks in, Jessie's post-traumatic stress disorder is triggered, as this whole thing reminds her of back when her original owner Emily abandoned her on the side of the road. Anyone who watched the second film in the series will remember how hard hitting this was to watch the first time around, and the way the film brings back that old memory for us is handled in a believable way without feeling contrived or tacky. Much like with the previous four entries, this one deals with some adult-oriented problems that are easily relatable to both young kids and their parents. In this case, we have the very understandable fear of convenient technology consuming every aspect of our day-to-day lives and the ways it has caused problems with how we interact with others. For instance, Bonnie feels pressured to use her Lilypad tablet to fit in with the other kids, who all tease her for still playing with physical toys. Likewise, many of those kids in question are shown to lack real social skills due to them constantly using their touchscreens to talk to one another instead of face-to-face. As someone who grew up before the advent of the internet, it's sad to see today's generation of children languish away like that, but this film should hopefully bring awareness to this issue for both the young and old audiences watching. Deeply provocative themes aside, the film still has all of that signature charm that only Pixar could ever deliver. There are several clever jokes and references to the other four movies that fans of the series are sure to enjoy pointing out, including ones that might go over the heads of even the most seasoned of Pixar viewers. One of my favourites was this scene where the toys are sneaking through a house trying to be quiet so as not to alert the humans, only to realise that all of the people are so glued to their devices that they don't notice them right in front of their own faces. There's also some funny banter between Woody and Buzz that feels like an amusing throwback to how the two of them initially hated each other in the original movie, except here it feels more in jest rather than outright hostility. Like I said about "Hoppers", it's looking as though Pixar are on their way to returning to what made them great in the first place. The one major criticism that comes to mind about this movie is the large cast of characters that have since accumulated over the past three decades. While just about everyone who has a reason to still be around appears in this movie, it also regrettably forces many of the fan favourites to being relegated into forgettable supporting roles. This means that the likes of Rex, Slinky Dog, Mr. Potato Head, and Hamm sadly only end up having about one or two lines if they are lucky. While we still have some great new faces here, like a talking potty-training toy named Smarty Pants (voiced by Conan O'Brien), I can't help but feel sad to see the older characters being sidelined into irrelevance as a result. The main cast of voice actors all did a fantastic job once again, with Joan Cusack being a particular standout as Jessie. I've always found Jessie to be a very emotionally deep character, especially considering the abandonment issues she developed as a result of losing her original owner, Emily. This film calls back to Jessie's insecurities, showing how they still haunt her even after so many years. Without giving away spoilers, there is this one part near the end where I felt so much emotion towards what Jessie was going through that it actually brought back memories of when I watched the infamously sad "When She Loved Me" scene in "Toy Story 2" for the first time. Tom Hanks and Tim Allen also return as Woody and Buzz, which are easily the two actors' best voiceover roles. It is shown that Woody still remained in contact with Jessie and the other toys over the years via a walkie-talkie, proving that his supposed exit in the fourth movie was never going to be a permanent thing. I enjoyed this recurring joke involving the back of Woody's head becoming so worn out that it makes him look like he's going bald, prompting many of the newer toys to label him as an "old man's toy". As well as this, Buzz has been made second-in-command by Jessie, giving him a bit of a superiority complex in the process. This leads to some disagreements arising between these longtime friends, and anyone who has been with this series since the very beginning will remember that their bickering has always been fun to watch over the course of these thirty plus years. In the antagonistic role, Greta Lee has some pretty memorable moments as the smart tablet Lilypad, otherwise known as "Lily". The reason I refer to Lily as "antagonistic" and not as an outright villain is because she isn't maliciously evil but is rather acting what she is programmed to do as a technological device. This means that like the other toys, Lily only really wants to make her owner Bonnie happy, even if that means shafting aside any competition in the process. While some might complain that this film doesn't have a proper villain, I think that it instead allowed an opportunity for the movie to examine the ethics of technical advancement without disregarding the good and bad aspects of its implementation in our lives. After all, I don't think Pixar will ever be able to top a darkly twisted "Toy Story" villain like Lotso from the third movie. Though many still believe the series should have concluded as a trilogy, "Toy Story 5" nevertheless proves that this saga of sentient toys has plenty of life left in it for generations to come. Many people within my age bracket who grew up with these movies now have kids of their own, and it is clear that the creatives at Pixar have taken this into account. As a longtime fan, I'm just happy to see that these characters who have entertained me since I was a small child are equally as enjoyable to watch today as they were all the way back in the 90s. With that said, does this mean that we could get a "Toy Story 6" in the future? At this point, only time will tell. I rate it a solid 9/10.

review: The original Disney Pixar film was the fantastic breakthrough for computer animation, the brilliant sequel surpassed it, and the terrific third was presumed to be the emotional conclusion, but then the fourth film came along and just about fit in nicely, but I had mixed thoughts of this fifth entry in the franchise. Basically, a cargo ship filled with several high-tech edition Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen) toys crash-lands on a deserted island. With nowhere to go and stuck in demo mode, the shipwrecked Buzzes build a raft to escape the island and follow the North Star, seeking to find "Star Command". Eight-year-old Bonnie (Scarlett Spears) is finding it difficult to socialise with other children her age in the neighbourhood and at school; unlike her, they have abandoned playing with their toys and are playing with tablets. Jessie (Joan Cusack), Bonnie's favourite, has become the new leader of her toys, with Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen) as her deputy. Hoping she can make friends, her Mom (Lori Alan) and Dad (Jay Hernandez) buy her the latest frog-themed tablet named Lilypad "Lily" (Past Lives' Greta Lee). As with so many other children, Bonnie soon becomes addicted to Lily and neglects her toys. Jessie tries to reason with Lily and explains that she needs a real friend. Lily sees technology as the way forward for all kids and tries to solve the problem by sending a friend request to Chelsea (Sailor Mae Money), one of Bonnie's classmates, on social media. Jessie's friend Woody (Tom Hanks) has remained a lost toy, alongside his love interest Bo Peep (Annie Potts), to help find homes for abandoned toys. Fearful of losing Bonnie's affection, Jessie contacts Woody using a walkie-talkie for advice. Mishearing the message, Woody assumes that Jessie is calling for help and plans to return to Bonnie's room. When Chelsea invites Bonnie over for a sleepover, Jessie and Bullseye stow away in her suitcase while Bonnie takes Lily with her. Though she is initially happy to have them, Bonnie has her father take Jessie and Bullseye home after Chelsea, alongside her friends Heidi and Kara, questions Bonnie for still playing with toys. Jessie and Bullseye escape but are found by an elderly couple, who assume they are forgotten. Finding an old address written under Jessie's chaps, the elderly couple take them back to the farmhouse of Jessie's original owner, Emily. Jessie ends up in the shed, along with several other forgotten toys, including a potty-training device named Smarty Pants (Conan O'Brien). Bullseye was picked up by a young girl named Blaze (Mykal-Michelle Harris), who lives in the farmhouse, and Jessie and Smarty go looking for him. As they enter the house, Jessie changes Smarty's batteries and is introduced to his fellow device friends, GPS receiver Atlas (Craig Robinson) and camera Snappy (Shelby Rabara). They inform Jessie about the new family, the Manoukians, living in the farmhouse. After experiencing a joyful playtime with an imaginative Blaze, Jessie thinks she is perfect to become a friend for Bonnie and wants them to meet each other. When Woody reunites with Bonnie's toys, he and Buzz confront Lily about Jessie's whereabouts. Believing the toys are hindering Bonnie's social life, Lily tricks Bonnie's father into putting them in storage while Woody and Buzz escape. At the farmhouse, Jessie works with the device toys to send a picture of herself to Bonnie in Blaze's name. Discovering that Lily's weakness is her speech recognition function, Woody and Buzz call out her name and force her to show the picture to Bonnie so that she can retrieve Jessie. Bonnie and her mother go to the Manoukians', and Woody and Buzz secretly hitch a ride. However, upon arriving, Bonnie rejects Blaze returning Jessie and Bullseye after reading messages in a group chat where Chelsea and her friends continue to ridicule her for playing with toys. Upset, Jessie feels despondent and goes to the tree and swing where she played with Emily. Lily realises she has hurt Bonnie's feelings and is riddled with guilt, so she throws herself out of the car and ends up aboard a donation truck. Jessie and Bullseye unearth a lunchbox buried beneath the tree with late-20th-century objects alongside photos of an adult Emily and her daughter, who is named after Jessie. Realising she still had an impact on Emily's life over the years, Jessie regains her faith in Bonnie. Meanwhile, Woody and Buzz are captured by the Buzzes, believing they are in league with Emperor Zurg. Buzz helps and convinces the other Buzzes that they are toys and that their "mission" is to make children happy. With the help of the Buzzes' drone propellers, along with the device toys, Jessie tracks down Lily on the truck. Jessie and the others catch up and convince Lily to help Bonnie befriend Blaze. Buzz professes his love for Jessie, and they share a kiss. The toys and devices arrange a new meeting between Bonnie and Blaze. After some hesitation, they bond over their mutual silliness and love of toys. They play together and pretend to marry Jessie and Buzz, with Mr. Pricklepants (John Hopkins) as the priest, and Hamm (John Ratzenberger), Slinky Dog (Blake Clark), Rex (Wallace Shawn), Mr. Potato Head (Jeff Bergman) and Mrs. Potato Head (Anna Vocino, replacing Estelle Harris), Forky (Tony Hale) and his new wife Karen Beverly aka "Knifey" (Melissa Villaseñor), Dolly (Bonnie Hunt), and Trixie (Kristen Schaal) in attendance. Woody happily watches from the window before departing with Bo. Bonnie and Blaze's friendship blossoms, and their playing attracts the attention of other children in the neighbourhood. At a school playground, the many Buzz Lightyears land to be taken by various children, and one enters the playground with an Emperor Zurg figure. Also starring Krys Marshall as Blaze's Mom, Ernie Hudson as Combat Carl, Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio aka Bad Bunny as Pizza with Sunglasses, Matty Matheson as Dr. Nutcase, Keanu Reeves as Duke Caboom, and Alan Cumming as Evil Bullseye, with additional voices by Ashley Bell, Michael Bell, Bob Bergen, Terri Douglas, Barbara Goodson, Mona Marshall, Anndi McAfee, Scott Menville, Andrew Stanton, Tara Strong, and Fred Tatasciore. The characters we have grown to love for three decades all remain appealing, the new characters are likeable, especially the toilet-based device, and the voice cast bringing them to life are great. There is nothing wrong with the fantastically colourful animation, and most of the story works, but I will agree there is perhaps too much going on, which makes the pace and tone uneven at times. However, you would have to be a psycho not to be moved by the themes of friendship and bonding, Jessie's past experiences give her character more depth, and there is enough to laugh at, and the whole family will still have fun, so it is a worthwhile computer-animated adventure comedy-drama. Good!

review_title: this is how to make a sequel to the perfect original trilogy
review: In the annals of animated feature films, there may never be a better trilogy than Toy Story 1-2-3. Judging any further sequel by those standards would be foolhardy. Toy Story 4 had some decent ideas, but ended up a mishmash of new flavors with the old gang. An okay film---but not compelling. Toy Story 5 is a much better approach to complementing that original trilogy by focusing in on a core character and keeping the toys' owner front-and-center. For a very basic overview, TS5 tells the story of Bonnie (Scarlett Spears) now becoming a pre-teen. With that change comes less of a reliance on physical toys and more a need-to-fit-in dependance on technology. So, when a Lilypad (Greta Lee) tablet device finds her hands and eyes, it becomes all-encompassing for friendship and play. The one toy who has seen this before: Jessie (Joan Cusack)---who starts a quest to unite Bonnie with a potential new real-life friend Blaze (Mykal-Michelle Harris). Centering TS5 on Jessie is perhaps the masterstroke here. TS4 really lacked input from those original toys, but that isn't a problem with the cowgirl and her trusty steed Bullseye front and center. Due to this structure, it organically brings Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen) & Woody (Tom Hanks) back into the proceedings too. Sure, they aren't necessarily the starring roles like in the '95 original, but they felt like those characters just in supporting roles. Having the real-world story revolve around Bonnie is another step in the right direction. As fun as it is to see the humor/adventure of the toy hijinks, the emotional core of these films is always in the relationship between toy and owner. As such, the "Bonnie turns away from toys and to tech" really is a genius angle, mirroring the society it is released into in many ways. A very relatable topic/concern, in other words, especially in a world that is just beginning to understand the limits and downfalls of social media & device consumption. Is Toy Story 5 a perfect film? Not quite. It sort of waffles on---if perhaps simply not addresses at all---the potential solution to the "tech problem" other than "get out the old physical toys". Though, it perhaps mirrors society in that regard. It also does not nail the very specific "Jessie returning to her roots" angle (to say more would be spoiler-y) of the narrative, even if the other Jessie material is largely compelling. Overall, I really enjoyed this 5th Toy Story installment. It had me excited, laughing, and feeling at the right moments all the way through. Like I said, nothing that will put it in the rarified stratosphere of the original three---but strong enough on its own merits to be a really enjoyable (and sometimes meaningful) romp with the old gang.

review_title: toys vs tech perfect film no storyline morally sound yes
review: Having viewed all of the Toy Story films from 1995 to the present as a little kid back then to when I was in college in 2010, I assert that the fifth installment effectively captures contemporary societal customs and trends in the integration of technology. The initial three films primarily focused on the toys and their owner, Andy Davis. However, following Andy's departure for college at the conclusion of the third film, the narrative now centers on Bonnie, the current owner, as she navigates life after being gifted a tablet named LilyPad. While the toys express apprehension about being supplanted by technology, it is up to cowgirl Jessie along with the assistance of Buzz Lightyear and Woody (having parted ways with the toys to be with Bo Peep in the fourth film) to assist Bonnie in demonstrating that the essence of "playtime" remains significant for actual toys. Under the direction of Andrew Stanton (Finding Nemo, Wall-E), returning voice actors Tom Hanks, Tim Allen, and Joan Cusack delivered exceptional performances as Woody, Buzz, and Jessie, respectively. New cast members Conan O'Brien as the learning toy Smarty Pants and Tron: Ares star Greta Lee as tablet LilyPad also contribute to the narrative. You might think Toy Story's sequels after the third movie didn't quite live up to the original, or that the brand has already "worn out its welcome" and "sequel fatigue." But Toy Story 5 actually shines brighter than the fourth film in my opinion. The first four films focused on Woody and how he navigates through life as a child's toy. So now he takes a backseat in order for the focus shifting towards Jessie taking center stage and getting a deeper dive into her backstory. Feels like a hidden gem from Toy Story 2. Jessie was definitely impactful in her original owner Emily's life. The callbacks to the first two movies are spread about as to remind us how important they are when tying them to the storyline. It also suggests that it doesn't necessarily replace toys as obsolete with the rise of tablets and smartphones. Instead, it highlights the shared experiences between toys and tech. Finding common ground. Andy's story was wrapped up with the first three movies, so something tells me this implies the start of a new trilogy surrounding Bonnie. One thing's for sure, there were more stories to tell for these toys. Although the movie may not be as flawless as the first three Toy Story films, the underlying moral lesson remains quite sound.

review_title: it still has a friend in me
review: I was 3 years old when the first TOY STORY came out. Now, while some people my age now have kids of their own, TOY STORY 5 has just been released. This one shifts the main focus away from Woody (Tom Hanks) and Buzz (Tim Allen) and onto Jessie (Joan Cusack). Still struggling with her PTSD, she is the new leader of the toys owned by 8-year-old Bonnie (Scarlett Spears). Bonnie is in that awkward phase where every kid around her has been brainwashed by technology, leaving her behind. When Bonnie's parents get her a Lilypad tablet (Greta Lee), Jessie takes it upon herself to prove that making friends online is not the same thing as in person. I can imagine this aspect hits a very relatable nerve with most people, especially these days. Yet again, this franchise keeps finding ways to justify its existence. Many people, myself included, hoped the 3rd installment would be the final one. It ended on a very emotional high, having an adult message about growing up and letting go. Despite this, this franchise continues to surprise me with their awareness and heartfelt care towards these beloved characters. Randy Newman is back doing great music. It's nostalgic, yet the storytelling still finds ways to evolve and grow with its audience. It captures the anxiety of an older generation looking at an increasingly lost younger generation. It touches on the draining of imagination, on cyberbullying, and addiction to technology. There are actually 3 distinct storylines that eventually mesh together very nicely. There's a lot of laughs, especially with a new toy voiced by Conan O'Brian. I feel like Woody's character arc was sufficiently finished in the last one, but I understand why he had to be included. Despite the fact that this is one of the most expensive animated movies out there, it has already blown past breaking even. Frankly, my biggest issue with the movie is there's no blooper reel at the end. Bring them back, Disney! That's some core memory poop right there. Overall, TOY STORY 5 is yet another amazing adventure full of characters I've loved my whole life, with a message that's for kids and adults alike. Be brave enough to show who you really are, and don't let technology change that. This might be the 5th installment, but they've still got a friend in me.

It gives hope that technology and imagination can coexist, as long as we don't let one replace the other. Every child, teenager, parent, and teacher should watch this movie. Honestly, it should be shown in schools. A beautiful reminder of what childhood is supposed to feel like. 10/10!

review_title: old toys new tricks mixed results
review: Toy Story 5 is a film that starts weaker than it finishes, earns more than it initially promises, and lands in a place of genuine emotional warmth that partially justifies its existence without quite escaping the shadow of the franchise's best work. It is charming, occasionally moving, and consistently well intentioned - which for a fifth installment in a beloved series is a more complicated achievement than it sounds. The film's opening gambit is its weakest. The toys versus technology conflict introduced through Lilypad, a tablet device threatening to displace traditional play, arrives with a preachiness that feels forced and heavy handed. The film announces its themes too loudly before it has done any of the character work that would make those themes resonate, and the early sequences have the quality of a message being delivered rather than a story being told. What saves it is a gradual and genuine shift toward Bonnie. As the film centers itself on her struggle to make friends and the role the toys play in her emotional development, the technology conflict stops feeling like a concept and starts feeling like something real. The toys serving Bonnie's growth is the natural and meaningful extension of everything the franchise has always been about - what it means to be there for someone, to help them navigate a world that doesn't always make room for them. When the film remembers this is its true subject, it finds its footing completely. Jessie's arc is the right choice for a central focus, and her backstory gives the technology conflict the emotional grounding it needed from the beginning. The ending resolves the film's central tensions with genuine warmth and earns the feeling it reaches for. The film's most significant structural weakness is its ensemble. A franchise this long has accumulated a cast of beloved characters, and Toy Story 5 struggles to honor them while keeping its focus where it belongs. Woody, Buzz, and the supporting toys too frequently feel like reduced versions of themselves, their personalities compressed into familiar gestures rather than fully inhabited. The film cannot give everyone sufficient room and pays the price in characters who feel like caricatures of their former selves. Toy Story 5 works well enough as a standalone film and considerably better in its second half than its first. It cannot match the emotional ambition and execution of the original trilogy, but it finds something genuine to say about childhood, connection, and what imagination does for a lonely kid. That is enough, even if it is not everything.

review: This review comes from a 90s kid, now a mom to a tween girl. This was especially relevant to us and I LOVED it. I think this has to be viewed as a separate Toy Story story. It showed the importance of friendship and social connection in real life and how that will always be more genuine than social media. It showed screen addiction, showed how the parents first had good intentions and meant to help her connect, meant to set limits on its usage...but failed to do so. They also failed to keep up on what she was doing on the tablet even when subtle changes in her attitude showed and she became more down...even before the big blow up. It showed how involved people of all ages are on screens, even while with each other. The only exaggeration was the glow of them, to make them stand out, but the amount of people on them is accurate. It showed how us parents can be just as guilty. As a family who is very light on tech and works hard to allow our tween the space to remain a kid and play with her toys in a world that's changing too fast and going online too soon, this really related. I'm starting to see more parents my age realize their kids need the simpler childhood we enjoyed and I really hope to continue to see a change towards less electronics for kids...and for the parents who are vital to connect with them face to face. But even with all of the points made, it was so much fun and I found myself smiling nearly the whole movie start to finish. I'm looking forward to seeing it again when it's on streaming. But 4...I've never watched again. I love that the girls formed a friendship in the end...and even found an appropriate use of the tablet for a quick pic before getting back to playing in real life with real toys.

review: Toy Story 5, while seemingly a critique of technology, is also a societal perspective. We all try to conform and co-opt the creative people around us, and this conformist culture, like a pair of scissors, tries to cut the individual, to make everyone the same. The topics it touches upon are heartwarming, and its comprehensive treatment of the lack of control over children due to new technology and cyberbullying is truly remarkable. This fifth film was a good one after the fourth. Definitely check out this movie in theaters.

review_title: very preachy and sad for a 'toy story'
review: This movie spends way too much time preaching at the audience about devices. I get it, the old people in Hollywood feel exactly the same way the toys do in this movie, afraid of being replaced by skibidi toilet. It's ridiculous and made me laugh out loud at the multitude of 'dramatic' scenes where the toys go to some rooftop vantage point and manage to see EVERY kid in the block conveniently sitting in front of their window with the curtains fully open so you can see them and their screens fully for 'dramatic effect' but it also just makes me realize the people that are making this, and most of the people who will be watching this, are from completely different generations and it shows in the extreme level of preachiness this movie exudes for no reason other than 'you should buy more Toy Story toys instead of playing video games or having fun online with friends' because this movie tries so hard to definitively draw the line between playing a game and 'play' that happens with toys which once again just makes my eyes roll how much they're trying to diminish this modern age in favour of 'turns out the old ways are better' which feels like such a hollow and empty message in this day and age. Now that I've finished being angry at the crappiness of the first half of the movie, I must say i really enjoyed getting a deeper dive into Jessie's lore and character and backstory. She really provides the perfect emotional centre for this film, considering it feels like Buzz and Woody's character arcs had already finished by the last entry in the series and they feel somewhat tacked on near the beginning and end of the film compared to the newer 'tech" characters and bullseye and Jessie. I appreciate how they spend time acknowledging once they find out the truth about Jessie's original owner that they've done their part as toys and now it's time to find someone else to help along, that was nice but it's also weird because all the characters are sitting with unsettlingly wide eyes and big smiles which makes the scene feel weirdly cheesy. It felt like such a waste of time to preach at us about how tech is ruining everything only for them to work alongside the tech at the end, it just felt like they needed the tech storyline to come back around, but considering how dismal and depressing the first chunk of the movie with the main characters lamenting the existence of technology was, it just didn't feel totally earned for us to just suddenly love this iPad because 'oh she got self conscious' it feels lazy. Overall I really liked the deeper exploration of the main characters Jessie and Bullseye, I also like the reject toys thing coming back i also enjoyed the 'island of buzz' subplot that was fun. Toy Story 5 has a lot of deep emotional moments for the main characters and a lot of shallow technology bashing for the writers involved, I enjoyed the parts I enjoyed but I found the preachiness and depth of the sadness of this movie to be overwhelming at times for a kids movie about toys. 6/10.

review_title: heartwarming reflection on technology and childhood
review: Toy story franchise never disappoints me. This was another typical heart warming installment in the series. There are 3 things I like about it. First of all, the story plot is intense and never suffers from any dull moments. The imaginary world created by the kids in the story are incredibly creative and filled with many twists and turns that left the theatre echoing with laughter. It reminds me of the imaginative stories I used to invent when I was a child. It made me wonder where my childhood creativity had gone. The film transitions smoothly between nervous and funny scenes, making me glued to the story from the start to finish. Secondly, the film brilliantly integrates the modern technology into the toy universe. From introducing new devices from toy camera to tablet, the film walks us through the evolution of technology. These different toys observe a kid in distinct ways and serve different purposes. While physical toys accompany kids and foster their creativity, new technology feeds them with knowledges and connects them with people from afar, yet it lacks the emotional "child-toy friendship". I am impressed by how each new tech devices play their roles seamlessly in helping the main characters build their relationships. Thirdly, I like the visual style that depicts the imaginary world of the kids. The film introduces a distinct, childlike visual style to represent the kid's inner world. I suppose this is a first for the franchise. These new visual elements brings a new dimension to the series' animation style. Ultimately, the film provokes reflection on whether physical toys can be replaced by digital devices. As an early gen Z, I grew up playing with physical toys, inventing all kinds of imaginary scenarios. I remember crying when my mum threw away my teddy bear when I grew older. That kind of pure love between a toy and a kid can never truly be replicated in adult world. This is absolutely precious and can never be replaced by modern technology.

review_title: a sequel that actually had something to say
review: *Toy Story 5* was one of my most anticipated animated films in recent years. I actually found myself connecting more with the new child introduced in this installment, whose innocence and enthusiasm reminded me of Andy and even of my own childhood. Visually, Pixar once again delivers stunning animation, and the score fits the emotional moments well, although I did miss hearing "You've Got a Friend in Me." Overall, *Toy Story 5* isn't among the franchise's best, but it's far from being a cynical cash grab. review: Greetings again from the darkness. It's been thirty-one years since I sat stunned in the movie theater after being first introduced to Woody, Buzz, and the entire gang of Pixar toys. It was the year BRAVEHEART won five Oscars and TOY STORY, which marked a shift in filmmaking, won none. That was Pixar's first feature film and since there was no Animated Feature Film category at the time, the Academy didn't really know what to do with it. Fortunately, John Lasseter (since fired) and Andrew Stanton certainly knew what to do, as this is the fifth film of the franchise, and they've managed to create cinematic magic with each one. We've established that I'm a raving fan for the franchise. Yet with each entry, I still go in concerned that this will be the first dud. I'm relieved and happy to report that the fifth film is funny, colorful, filled with great characters, and maintains the emotional charge we've come to expect. Pixar's Andrew Stanton has been involved with each of the TS films and he's joined this time by co-director and co-writer McKenna Harris (her first feature). They have managed to uphold tradition, while making the film entirely contemporary and introducing the beloved characters to a new generation (it's been seven years since TOY STORY 4). The familiar characters are back, which means most of the familiar voices are as well: Tom Hanks as Woody, Tim Allen as Buzz Lightyear, Joan Cusack as Jessie, Wallace Shawn as Rex, Annie Potts as Bo Peep, Tony Hale as Forky, and Keanu Reeves as Duke Caboon. New to the scene are Scarlett Spears as Bonnie (she's the third to voice the character), and of course, with the passing of Don Rickles, Estelle Harris, and Jim Varney, there have been new voices for Mr and Mrs Potato Head and Slinky Dog. And yes, Pixar's good luck charm John Ratzenberger returns as Hamm. Among the others making their first Toy Story credits are the voices of global sensation Bad Bunny as 'Pizza with sunglasses', Greta Lee as Lilypad the smart tablet, Conan O'Brien as a 'specialized' device, and Mykal-Michelle Harris as Blaze. This is definitely a female-centric story as Jessie takes the lead role. Woody and Buzz are featured prominently, but Jessie is the one focused on ensuring young Bonnie makes friends. The emphasis on technology is one all parents will recognize. Kids don't "play" the way they once did, and the story emphasizes how that adds complexity to not just making friends, but also in defining what friendship actually is in this modern world. Smart devices, screens, and tablets have pushed toys to the background - or the garage, or even worse. It's heartwarming, and sometimes nerve-wracking, watching Jessie and this crew of toys do what they can to help kids hold onto childhood as long as possible. There are some subplots included regarding Buzz and Jessie, Jessie's background with previous kids, and the ongoing challenges faced by parents. The animation is as stunning as you'd expect, and Randy Newman returned to compose the film's score. By now it's no secret that Taylor Swift, with a writing boost from Jack Antonoff, performs her new song, "I Knew it, I Knew You", over the closing credits (and stay for the stingers). DISNEY & PIXAR'S TOY STORY 5 releases exclusively in theaters June 19, 2026. Run time: 1hr 42min.

review_title: a worthy successor that understands what made the series timeless
review: When Toy Story premiered in 1995, it didn't simply introduce audiences to Woody and Buzz Lightyear-it changed animation forever. As the first fully computer-animated feature film, it established Pixar Animation Studios as a creative force and raised the bar for animated storytelling. Over four films, the franchise has explored friendship, loyalty, loss and growing up. Woody learned that loving someone sometimes means letting them go. Buzz Lightyear discovered who he truly was beyond the identity he believed in. Jessie carried the emotional scars of abandonment, while Rex, Hamm, Slinky, Bullseye and the rest of the gang reminded us that every toy has a purpose. Like any long-running series, the previous four films had remarkable highs and a few moments that didn't resonate with me as strongly. With Toy Story 5, directors Andrew Stanton and McKenna Harris have crafted what I consider the strongest entry in the franchise. The film successfully captures the spirit of the original films while embracing a modern world shaped by technology. Rather than portraying tablets and screens as the enemy, it takes a more balanced approach, highlighting what children may lose when digital entertainment replaces imagination, shared adventures and genuine interaction. It also touches on how unkind children can sometimes be without becoming overly sentimental or preachy. Most importantly, the toys remain the emotional centre of the story. Their relationships, humour and unwavering loyalty continue to carry the film, reminding us why these characters have endured for more than three decades. For longtime fans who grew up with Pixar in the 1990s and early 2000s, Toy Story 5 feels both nostalgic and refreshingly relevant. It honours the legacy of the franchise while confidently telling a story for a new generation. Rating: 10/10.

review: Making Toy Story 5 was not necessary. Making it that good wasn't either. As all good Pixar does, this film entertains you, makes you laugh, and even tugs at your heartstrings, all with stunning animation to boot. It's even surprisingly relevant, with the social commentary about technology driving the plot while also making you think. Greta Lee's Lilypad provides both satire and suspense while telling a chillingly accurate tale about tech replacing play. Joan Cusack's Jessie, who takes the spotlight in this film gives an emotional performance, making the character much more than just "girl Woody". Although, the first forty-five minutes are messy. On one hand, we have the conflict between tech and toys, the heart of the movie. On the other, a story about a league of alternate Buzz Lightyear toys on a mission to rehash the original's arc from the first movie. Eventually, even the Toys v. Tech storyline branches off, making the viewer question where the whole plot is going. Also, Woody's presence in the film feels more like the writers checking a box rather than them actually trying to do anything meaningful. The animation, sadly doesn't reach the heights of the fourth one, which at times felt more stop-motion than computer-generated. This isn't a huge gripe, just something I noticed. But, it all comes together in the third act. By the end, the messages of the film shine through, with a few solid emotional beats that may even make you tear up. Overall, while not on the level of the first three, Toy Story 5 is a must-watch for families and all fans of animation. Good job, Pixar!

review: Having been against the grain in thinking Toy Story 4 was a worthy follow-up to 3 and a very pleasant surprise, I can really feel the rot setting in with part 5. It's by no means a bad film, and has some great messages about how too much technology is stunting the minds of our kids and inhibiting their ability to socialise, whilst also highlighting the off-neglected positive side of it. But there's just too many characters, not enough laughs. Woody is entirely irrelevant to the story; he's only in it for (what else) corporate reasons. The climax, involving LOADS of Buzz Lightyears on horseback, is dumb . Lilypad (as the villain) shows promise, but is given far too little to do. On the plus side, it's nice to see Jessie as the main character. Her character arc is handled well enough, and there's a really nice ending for her. I just wish I could say the same for those annoying 'imaginative' moments when the children play, the animation style changes and we see what's going on in their heads in the most bizarrely off-putting way, though I'm sure some people thought they were cute. Overall, Toy Story 5 is what I feared Toy Story 4 would be... an aimless cash -in with no real reason to exist other than to rake in the big bucks. With the talent behind the movie, there were always bound to be amusing and charming interludes, but for a franchise which started off with one of the greatest animated films of all time... it's just not good enough, I'm afraid. No Toy Story 6. Ta. 6/10.

review_title: what if growing up means forgetting how to play
review: Toy Story 5 feels like a quiet ache hidden inside a colourful world. It does not scream nostalgia. Instead, it slowly lets nostalgia hurt in a very gentle way. This time, the conflict is not between toys and humans in the usual sense, but between imagination and replacement. Between presence and distraction. The film's emotional core works best when it focuses on Jessie stepping into leadership and Woody returning with a more reflective silence. These characters feel older, not in age, but in emotional weight. They are no longer just toys fighting for attention. They are symbols of something children are slowly losing without realizing it. The introduction of modern technology as a "new kind of toy" is not handled as a simple villain concept. It feels more like an uncomfortable mirror. The film quietly asks what happens when love, imagination, and physical play are replaced by glowing screens that never look away. Visually and emotionally, it stays strong in Pixar's familiar language. However, at times the message becomes slightly too direct, reducing some of the subtlety that earlier entries carried more naturally. Still, the emotional resonance remains intact, especially in moments of silence where the toys simply observe the world they can no longer fully belong to. Toy Story 5 is not really about toys. It is about what childhood becomes when attention is no longer given, but consumed.

review: I don't shy away from admitting that I'm still salty about 'Toy Story 4'. I still consider 'Toy Story 3' one of the greatest animated films ever made, and more importantly, a perfect ending to what should have remained a trilogy. While the fourth film wasn't bad by any means, it always felt like a passable add-on that never quite justified its own existence beyond the obvious financial incentive. So naturally, I walked into 'Toy Story 5' with zero excitement, having avoided every trailer and knowing absolutely nothing about what it was about. Maybe that complete lack of expectations is what worked in the film's favour. To my surprise, 'Toy Story 5' turns out to be a thoughtful and surprisingly timely story about childhood, technology, and growing up. It explores themes that feel relevant today without ever becoming heavy-handed or preachy, and it does so with a level of restraint that's become increasingly rare in family entertainment. More importantly, it tackles these ideas in a way that feels like it'll still resonate another decade from now. One of the smartest decisions the film makes is shifting Woody and Buzz into supporting roles and allowing Jessie to lead the story. It's a gamble that pays off. Jessie has always had an infectious energy, and here she proves more than capable of carrying the emotional weight of the film. Better still, the movie gives her a meaningful and satisfying character arc that genuinely feels complete. And yes, I'm using the word "complete" very carefully when discussing anything related to Toy Story. Y'ALL COULDN'T LET 'TOY STORY 3' BE! I'm sorry. Overall, I found 'Toy Story 5' far more enjoyable than I ever expected it to be. It doesn't suddenly make me forgive Pixar for refusing to let Toy Story remain a perfect trilogy, but once you accept that the past can't be changed, this feels like a much better direction for the franchise than I anticipated. It's not essential in the way the original three films were, but it's a worthwhile chapter that earns its place far more convincingly than its predecessor.

review_title: finding balance in a digital age
review: My favorite Pixar franchise is still going strong with this fifth installment. The fear of being abandoned and forgotten by children has always been the emotional backbone of the series. In the earlier films, however, this fear stemmed from children growing up and entering adolescence, whereas in this new film, it arises from children becoming captive to technological devices such as computers, tablets, and smartphones. Another strength of the series is its ability to introduce memorable new toy characters in each installment. This time, the cast gains Lilypad, a tablet, and through her, the film explores themes such as technology addiction, peer approval, exclusion, and bullying. At the same time, the film does not adopt a simplistic, entirely technophobic perspective that views everything in black and white. Instead, it acknowledges that change is inevitable and that technology cannot be completely excluded from childhood, seeking a more balanced approach. I felt that the subplot involving a large army of Buzz Lightyears seemed somewhat detached from the rest of the film and slowed the pace, but in the end, the film succeeds in integrating that subplot into the main story. I also enjoyed the sequences depicting the imaginative scenarios children create while playing with their toys: Presented in a different animation style, these scenes add visual variety to the film. In this installment, Jessie becomes the main character, and her complex relationships with her former owner Emily and her current owner Bonnie are quite moving. Ultimately, while I do not think it is as good as the first three films, I found it better than the fourth one.

review_title: pushing the limits somewhat but still a worthy addition
review: STAR RATING: ***** Brilliant **** Very Good *** Okay ** Poor * Awful In this fifth instalment of the wildly successful Toy Story franchise, the toys are feeling a growing sense of isolation, with their new owner, Bonnie (Scarlett Spears) spending more time with her portable online device, Lilypad (Greta Lee) and being neglected in the process. However, new technology is leaving even older technology behind, in the form of discarded older ipad 'Smarty Pants' (Conan O' Brien), who joins the gang as they try and forge a real life friendship between Bonnie and fellow tech loving pre-teen Blaze (Mykal-Michelle Harris.) The old saying used to be 'leave it at three', but during the last few decades 'four' has become the new normal, and here, Toy Story 5 has rolled around, reaching a point where even the most ardent devotee might say is pushing it. No one can argue it's a franchise with reliable, consistent box office potential, with four sequels that drew in crowds a decade apart from each other, and now this latest instalment arriving nearly seven years after the last one. But does the premise still sustain itself? Arguably the biggest positive going in its favour is a doubtlessly relevant and inspired plotline, highlighting the growing schism between traditional kids toys (that even I as an older millennial remember having in my youth) and the digital, online devices kids possess today, which I can certainly observe with my younger nephews. However, it seems this may have come at the expense of a structured, coherent plot that really threads one event logically to the next, as well as a lack of any established villain, aside from some mean girls who don't include Bonnie in their play. It's curious just how far this series has the potential to stretch, but by sticking to it's established themes, characters and their personalities, and never forgetting the heart at its core, it's delivered a fifth entry with limited but still worthy success. ***

review: Forget the critics over-analyzing the "message." Toy Story 5 works because it stops trying to be a philosophical treatise and starts being a movie for kids again. While the press fixated on whether the film was "anti-tech," they missed the forest for the tablets: this isn't a Luddite rant; it's a validation of the kid who just wants to play with a doll while everyone else is scrolling. The film's genius lies in its simplicity. By shifting the spotlight to Jessie, the story grounds itself in a tangible fear of obsolescence that resonates with any child who's felt left behind by trends. The villain isn't technology itself-Lilypad actually helps Bonnie make a friend-but the disconnection it causes when it replaces active imagination. The movie argues that screens are fine as tools, but they fail as companions. It's a nuance that adult reviewers called "muddy" but that any parent watching their child light up over a shared make-believe game understands instantly. Critics complained about "IP exhaustion" and "heavy-handed themes," yet the audience score hit a franchise-high 95%. Why the disconnect? Because adults look for subtext, while kids feel the text. The film doesn't need to deconstruct the digital age; it just needs to show that a plastic horse and a tablet can coexist if the human element remains central. It acknowledges that not every kid has the latest gadget, and more importantly, that not every kid wants one. In the end, Toy Story 5 succeeds where recent Pixar entries stumbled by respecting its audience. It doesn't talk down to kids with complex metaphors about anxiety or consumerism; it tells them their way of playing still matters. The toys aren't fighting to destroy the future; they're fighting to ensure that "play" survives it. And for a franchise built on the idea that you've got a friend in them, that's enough.

review: Pixar returns to its flagship franchise with a warm, technically polished continuation built around a genuinely timely premise - the toys losing ground to a new screen-based device that monopolizes Bonnie's attention. The commentary on modern childhood and screen time lands with real relevance, and the film's moral core, prioritizing human connection over consumption, comes through as coherent and heartfelt rather than preachy for most of the runtime. Jessie emerges as the clear standout here, carrying the most emotionally compelling arc in the film and giving the story a genuine center of gravity. Tom Hanks and Tim Allen slip back into Woody and Buzz with the same warmth as ever, and their vocal work still anchors the quieter moments effectively. The animation remains genuinely impeccable - meticulous character design, lighting, and environmental detail, paired with smooth, dynamic action sequences that showcase Pixar's continued technical mastery. The farewell sequences in particular resonate strongly with longtime fans, tapping into the franchise's ongoing themes of memory and purpose, and the humor throughout stays consistent and family-friendly, with a few genuinely memorable comic set pieces along the way. Where the film falls short is originality - the "toys replaced" conflict treads awfully close to ground already covered in "Toy Story 4," and the toys-versus-technology framing occasionally flattens into an overly binary moral argument that doesn't quite capture the complexity of the issue it's raising. The three-act structure is clear and accessible but leans episodic, with recurring cycles of separation and reunion that dilute tension over time, and a few mid-film stretches feel more like filler than essential story beats. Woody and Buzz largely reiterate roles we've already seen rather than evolving further, and some emotional beats feel engineered for maximum impact rather than fully earned through the narrative. Visually and musically, the film is accomplished but not groundbreaking - there's no standout new theme or visual innovation to distinguish it from its predecessor, and a handful of jokes about technology feel a bit over-familiar at this point. Verdict: A heartfelt, beautifully crafted continuation that honors the franchise's legacy without quite matching the emotional or narrative ambition of its best entries - enjoyable, but not essential.

review_title: you got a friend in me too again
review: Toy story 5 is another awkwardly unwelcome addition to the iconic animated franchise, and yet it is also a highly enjoyable experience in entertaining families and offering some insight on the wonders and the dangers of technology. This time around, the plot is given equal attention to the toys as well as Bonnie, their owner. She was ignorantly neglected in the previous entry, and here she finds herself given much more emotional depth and eventuates with a relatable arc. It is anxiety inducing to watch as Bonnie is subjected to the difficulties of making friends whilst also being the outcast who prioritises creativity and is feeling the terrifying pull of conformity to fit in. It is heart-wrenching stuff that has a continual bitter sweetness to it. All of this is maturely complemented with Jessie taking centre stage as Bonnie's favourite toy as well as the movie's lead, as her feelings of abandonment start to unravel with the arrival of technology, and more specifically Lilypad, whose purpose is simply to help Bonnie, only with more 'modern' methods that does not require Jessie and the rest of the gang. Speaking of, although not many of them have large roles and some spend the movie literally boxed away, the toys all still feel fun to have around. The newcomers played by Conan O'Brien, Craig Robinson, and Shelby Rabara are all individually funny welcome additions that also bridge the gap between tech and toys in interesting ways. Thematically, the movie highlights the importance of creativity best through the imagination sequences as well as the shift in animation paired with it, and it is an immaculate demonstration of visual talent. And with that said, the default animation just barely shy of looking vibrantly real; from the textures, to the shadows, and the character movements, if it weren't for the human characters you'd be forgiven for thinking it was live action mixed with digital effects. But as aforementioned, tech is centre stage as it is actually treated fairly and as an inevitable necessity, making its plot feel necessary and justified better than its immediate predecessor. The messaging of how much sooner technology is being integrated within the childhoods of the next generation fearlessly breaks down the effect it can have on kids' mental wellbeing, their overexposure to social media, and the lasting effect of social embarrassment within the existence of group chats, and it's all carried through the character of Lilypad. Initially established as purely antagonistic, she is similarly viewed as an inevitability that can be just as necessary as toys, which is a really powerful and mature viewpoint that never comes across as too preachy. However, the problem with discussing the dangers of technology is that parents play a major role in kids' discovery and ownership of such devices, and this film does not take much of an interest in exploring that and portray parents as emotionally distant and downright incompetent, leaving the audience to be forced to believe there would be no attempt at intervention from Bonnie's parents throughout the runtime; it is recklessly lazy storytelling to treat such a fundamental aspect so apathetically. And beyond that, the plot structure is messily jumbled, as the first half and especially the cold open are really weird in dividing the movie into three jarring plot threads that go in wildly different directions. There's the central story of Jessie helping Bonnie to the best of her ability which thrives as the heart and soul of the movie, then there is Woody and Buzz's b-plot that sees them bickering over a plan on how to overcome Lilypad that wastes more time than it spends, and then there is the weirdly out of place c-plot following a group of defective Buzz Lightyear's on a desert island journeying to the mainland that may have been better off acting as a fun short film instead. All of these threads eventually come together in the third act, but it remains a jarring experience nonetheless to the point where a majority of it could have been trimmed down or cut out. And as a minor nitpick, there are some tech moments that stretch the suspension of disbelief incredibly thin, even by the franchise's standards. And onto the franchise overall, obviously audiences are well aware that Toy Story 3 acted as the perfect conclusion, but after the fourth entry already crossed the threshold of breaking the promise of leaving the story at that satisfying conclusion, this entry does a much better job in providing a story that feels relevant as well as worth telling. But now, there is seriously no more ground left for more to be told with these characters, and it would be ideal to have this movie be the last addition with these characters; Woody already feels unnecessarily crammed in for nostalgia sake, and the rest of the cast get maybe two lines each due to there being such a bloat in the pre established ensemble as well as all the new editions. But regardless of its imperfections, Toy Story 5 still manages to be very funny, very moving, and very compelling, all things considered. It is thematically mature, relevant, relatable, and sure to give audiences of all ages a fun enough time to be had.
