review: Cons: My first complaint about this movie might be superficial, but the absence of the song "You Got a Friend in Me" was deeply felt. I'm sorry, but Taylor Swift's original song for this movie "I Knew It, I Knew You" was forgettable, and if you didn't tell me that she wrote a song for this movie, then I would not have really paid attention to it at all. I also didn't like that a majority of the side characters (Ham, Rex, Mr. Potato Head, Slinky, etc.) were once again heavily sidelined in this movie, maybe even more so than usual. They literally sat in a box in the garage for practically the whole movie. Their absence was definitely felt and made this movie feel smaller in scale compared to the previous movies. I also really just couldn't stand the Smarty Pants device. He was so annoying. Since Toy Story 4 the franchise seems to be obsessed with putting a very annoying character in the forefront forcing other, more loved characters to be sidelined (ahem Buzz Lightyear deserved more screentime). With regards to the end of this movie, I have mixed feelings about it. I understand that if Lilypad had not had a redemption arc then it would have been hard to justify that the toys would be happy coexisting with her after everything that she did to them. But boy would it have been fun to see the toys go up against a truly nefarious device who gets sick joy from consuming all of humanity's attention. Up to this point, it seems like the Toy Story movies have done a good job navigating the life cycles of toys in the most realistic way possible, but this was the only movie where the ending felt a bit naive. In the real world, most children won't go back to playing with toys after being introduced to a device which they touched on a bit in this movie. This is why giving Lilypad a redemption arc felt off to me. Sure she might have good intentions, but is that supposed to make me feel better about Bonnie's life slowly being consumed by her? It honestly felt like a slap to the face from the tech industry, like you're subtly telling me, "hey, devices are here to stay, and you're just going to have to deal with it. We just want what's best for you after all." Yeah, sure totally, Toy Story 5. Finally, my last issue with this movie is the weird dynamic between Jessie and Buzz. Don't get me wrong. I have always shipped Buzz and Jessie. But their dynamic in this movie felt forced and not earned. Buzz practically spent the entire movie trying to propose to Jessie, and yet they hardly said a word to each other throughout the entire movie. How do you go from not talking at all to suddenly getting married at the end? Where was the build up? Pros: I love that this movie focused on Buzz and Jessie's romance even if the execution of it was kinda disappointing. It was nice though that a Toy Story movie finally at least acknowledged the tension between the two and did something with it. As usual while watching a Toy Story movie, this one made me cry once again. The scene where Jessie realizes that Emily named her daughter after her was one of the most emotional beats that I felt while watching a movie in a while. And don't even get me started when Jessie realized that while she can't be someone's beloved toy forever, the least she can do is be there when she is needed and make an impact for as long as she can. I thought Jessie's mission to help Bonnie find a friend who understands her was just so sweet and reminded me how it was making my own friends when I was younger. I also thought the way this movie showed cyber bullying and just bullying in general was just so real and hit close to home. I'm sure most kids can relate to Bonnie's struggles in making friends. Finally, this movie did a great job showing how devices can take over a child's life and make them act older ahead of time. It was honestly such a wake up call of how serious this issue has gotten to the point where it almost disturbed me. However, just like the toys in the movie, I'm not sure how we can solve this issue without taking the devices out of the equation altogether.

review: The battle for playtime begins in "Toy Story 5". The sequel that only got green lit because of the box office failure of "Lightyear" in 2022. The toys are back for a fifth adventure and this time, they have some unwelcome company. "Jessie" (Joan Cusack), "Buzz Lightyear" (Tim Allen) with romance on his mind, Woody (Tom Hanks) and the rest of the gang's jobs as toys are challenged when they come face-to-face with technology. "Lilypad" (Greta Lee voicing a spoof of Leap Frog) a brand-new tablet device arrives with her own disruptive ideas about what is best for "Bonnie" (Scarlett Spears). Will playtime ever be the same? In this "Toy Story" there's a new gang in town, "The double A team"...all old superseded battery powered devices led by TV show host Conan O'Brien as toilet trainer "Smarty Pants" who can only count ones and twos. Plus "The Office" Craig Robinson as "Atlas" a highly inaccurate GPS. "Toy Story 5" best quote is, "Don't be dumping us something you can't flush!" and the poop jokes keep coming. Watch out for: a tribute to the Tom Hanks movie "Big" where "Jessie" is dancing on "Smarty Pants". Listen out for: "I Knew It, I Knew You" by Taylor Swift she wrote in just 8 hours. Turns out Tay Tay has been a huge fan of the franchise since childhood. Coincidence or not 2026 is the Chinese "Year of The Horse", so expect to see more of "Bullseye" and other horses featured in this animation. "Toy Story 5" is an original story from a series that I thought had drunk the well dry by the 4th edition, but this gives it new batteries to power up for possibly a sixth instalment under new directors Andrew Stanton and McKenna Harris. The "Buzz Lightyear" subplot is hilarious. The main fable is about limiting screen time on devices and how, if used properly, can be beneficial and not necessarily the end of human creativity and interaction. It's truly glorious to watch the photo realistic animation and all your favourite characters come back to life on the big screen, when humans aren't around of course. Come see "Toy Story 5", and you'll be in a world of pure imagination.

review_title: toys fight back against technology's grip
review: The fifth Toy Story installment in this now-iconic franchise has a lot to unpack regarding how much childhood has changed since the Toy Story franchise and its characters first came to life in 1995. This time around, Woody, Buzz, Jessie, and all their toy companions find themselves facing a new rival for their kid's attention, a digital tablet called the LillyPad designed for children. These toys suddenly find themselves out of their element because this device can seemingly do everything - or so it appears at first. The film might not tackle head-on some of the more complex issues surrounding children growing up too fast with too much technology. In fact, it is often quite willing to dance around these issues. Nevertheless, it provides a thoughtful starting point in a fairly benign and optimistic setting from which to explore these pressing questions. Does a child connect less with his or her peers because of technology? Are children's friendships more superficial, less wholesome, and perhaps less rewarding as a result? Or does technology enhance friendships by putting them quite literally at a child's fingertips? These are the questions the film is willing to explore, but it never pushes us too strongly in one direction or the other. In all fairness, the new allies are not only other toys but also some of those technological devices. Incidentally, unlike previous Toy Story installments, it is Jessie, not Woody, who carries the story this time around. That break from tradition is another feather in the film's cap. Whether you're a longtime fan or a newcomer, this film is well worth seeing. Enthusiastically recommended.

review: It's not the freshest take to say that I felt that "Toy Story 4" was an unnecessary continuation of a story that had reached an almost perfect conclusion. Therefore, it's perhaps not unexpected that I felt that "Toy Story 5" was a largely unnecessary continuation of that story too. Bonnie (Scarlett Spears) receives a Lilypad Tablet (Greta Lee) which replaces Jessie (Joan Cusack) and the rest of her toys as the focal point of her playtime. Whilst tech offers Bonnie a chance to connect and make friends, it also opens her up to bullying and judgement for still wanting to play with toys at her age. Elsewhere, a shipping container of Buzz Lightyears (Tim Allen) wash up on a desert island and, unsure of what to do, follow the North Start towards "Star Command". I mean, I don't want to go overboard with my criticism, the film is fine. It looks great, as Pixar films all do and particularly as this one was so expensive. The vocal performances are never less than brilliant - whether that's returning established stars like you rarely see now in anything else, like Tim Allen, Joan Cusack or Annie Potts, or the new ones like Greta Lee and Conan O'Brien. It's just that I felt the plot was covering ground that had been covered before. It's a Jessie focused movie and we revisit the traumas that have appeared in two and three, we're again using Buzz as a character who doesn't believe he's a toy, though this time not in the case of the original Buzz. Original Buzz still hasn't declared his love for Jessie, which I though had to have happened already, but apparently not. It quickly undoes the ending of "Toy Story 4" by bringing Woody and Bo back. It's not quite willing to commit to it's "Tech is Bad" storyline all the way, which feels like pressure from Disney corporate offices not to risk all the tech equipment that they want to sell. The quality is too strong to actively dislike the film, but it does feel unnecessary and, whilst I'm clearly in the minority, given the box office, I'd prefer Disney made less sequels and more original stories.

review: Toy Story 5 is a wonderful continuation of the franchise that understands exactly what has always made Toy Story special. While the earlier films were largely driven by Woody and Buzz, this installment makes the bold decision to place Jessie at the center of the story, and it ends up being one of the film's greatest strengths. After years of being an important supporting character, Jessie finally receives the emotional focus she deserves, allowing audiences to see her vulnerabilities, heartbreak, fears, and growth in a much deeper way than ever before. What impressed me most is that the movie is not just another adventure for the sake of having an adventure. It actually has something meaningful to say. One of the central themes revolves around how technology affects friendships and relationships. The film explores how people can be physically together while being emotionally disconnected because everyone is staring at a screen. Rather than presenting technology as the enemy, the movie takes a more balanced approach by showing that technology has its place, but genuine human interaction, friendship, and shared experiences are still irreplaceable. It is a surprisingly mature message that feels relevant to modern audiences without becoming preachy. Jessie's storyline carries much of the emotional weight of the film. The writers take the time to explore her past experiences, her lingering insecurities, and the sadness she has carried for years. There are several moments throughout the movie that give her character a level of depth that rivals some of the best emotional scenes in the entire franchise. Watching her confront those feelings while continuing to care for others makes her journey incredibly rewarding. I also appreciated how the film handled the returning cast. Woody is present, but he wisely takes a supporting role for much of the story. After four films centered heavily around him, it was refreshing to allow other characters room to shine. Buzz remains fun and likable, receiving a smaller side story that complements the main narrative without distracting from it. Meanwhile, characters such as Bunny, Ducky, and Bo Peep take a step back, which feels appropriate given how much focus they received previously. The new characters are another highlight. Toy Story films have always excelled at creating memorable toys with distinct personalities, and this movie continues that tradition. The introduction of Lilypad and the other new characters helps keep the world feeling fresh while still fitting naturally into the established universe. The villains are also handled well. Like the best Toy Story antagonists, they are given understandable motivations rather than being evil simply for the sake of being evil. That added complexity makes the conflict more engaging and emotionally effective. Visually, the film is stunning. The animation continues to push the boundaries of what audiences expect from animated storytelling. Every environment feels alive, every character movement feels natural, and the emotional expressions are so detailed that entire scenes communicate feelings without needing much dialogue. Pixar once again proves why they remain one of the industry's strongest animation studios. What ultimately makes Toy Story 5 work is its balance. It delivers adventure, comedy, emotional moments, new characters, returning favorites, and an important message without feeling overcrowded. The movie respects the legacy of the franchise while still finding new stories to tell. Instead of relying solely on nostalgia, it expands the world and gives audiences a fresh perspective through Jessie's eyes. Overall, Toy Story 5 is a heartfelt, emotional, and surprisingly thoughtful addition to the series. By allowing Jessie to take center stage, exploring themes of technology and human connection, and introducing compelling new characters, the film successfully proves that there are still meaningful stories left to tell in this universe. It captures the heart, imagination, and emotional depth that have defined Toy Story from the very beginning, making it a must-watch for fans of the franchise.

review_title: not quite to infinity and beyond
review: Toy Story 5 follows the original gang as they navigate the modern era of "kid tech" and try to discover where they fit in. Having just seen the film, I have mixed feelings. It begins shortly after the previous installment-my personal favorite-and sets up its premise relatively quickly. What I loved about the movie can be split into three aspects: its heart, its moments of relevance, and its high production value. I also appreciated the bits of humor sprinkled throughout and the deeper focus on characters who usually take a backseat. While there were moments that truly felt like the original Toy Story, the overall narrative ultimately lacked purpose. For fans of the franchise, this film is still a worthwhile watch, even if it doesn't quite hit the highs of previous installments. My main caveat is that the premise lacks a satisfying and purposeful resolution. It felt like there were one too many subplots that either lacked relevance to the main arc or simply retold events we've already seen in earlier films. Consequently, many original characters felt underutilized. From a production standpoint, however, the film is great. Pixar's grounded animation and cinematography really anchor the movie, even if the score leaves a little to be desired. The cast is another highlight, despite being underused. Tom Hanks (Woody) and Tim Allen (Buzz) are iconic as always. Joan Cusack (Jessie) delivers a memorable performance, Greta Lee is excellent as Lilypad, and Conan O'Brien is a pleasant surprise. The rest of the supporting cast all do a great job as well. Overall, Toy Story 5 delivers on a relevant story with heartfelt moments, humor, and high production value, though it doesn't nearly reach the heights of previous films. A worthwhile watch for fans! Also, don't forget to stay for the mid & end credit scenes. _ For Content Sensitive viewers, like myself: the film contains brief (partial) profanity, crude humor, and a semi-brief LGTBQ+ scene.

review: Toy Story 5 - Review: PIXAR HAVE DONE IT AGAIN! So much better than the 3rd & 4th instalments by FAR! So much more heart and depth to this story and it really pays off! The Story: Woody, Buzz, Jessie and the rest of the gang's jobs are challenged when they're introduced to electronics, a new threat to playtime. Honestly the story is just incredible, very beautifully well made, the heart and the emotions play a vital park throughout the story and had me well gripped for the whole 1 hour & 42 minute runtime. The Story is mainly focused around Jessie and well I'm very please they did this, her character arc was just crafted so delicately, the way they developed her character was perfect. And you know it works if you feel the emotions which I did and there were quite a few moments that had me on the edge of tears. The story goes back to the original Toy Story made the film even more emotional but when you watch the film you will understand why! But I loved that focused on her character, I loved how they wanted to give her character the backstory that is very well deserved. (Woody & buzz + the gang play 2nd fiddle in this film) Outstanding Story writing and couldn't have wished for a better story then what they gave us. As I say you can see the love for the film from everyone involved working on it, the depth and heart is exactly what the franchise needed. Before going into this film I wasn't sure about it, the trailer for me had me thinking it was going to be another poor attempt at adding to the franchise but boy I was wrong. I'm also wasn't sure of Taylor Swift making a song for it, I thought it was just Pixar jumping on the bandwagon but again I was proved wrong and the song is written wonderfully for the film. The soundtrack was crafted by the legend of the franchise that is Randy Newman, who I was pleased to see attached to the film when I was looking before release, the soundtrack helps to create the atmosphere that was just what the film needed, it made the emotional scenes more emotional which is exactly what it wanted to do. For me this is going back to the basics of what a Toy Story film is meant to be and brings back all those amazing memories from the original, which brings me so much happiness. Overall it is just a wonderful film so much love and passion for it (unlike the 3rd & 4th films), I'm so happy that this was the end result and everyone's hard work involved. For me 10 out of 10 just a fantastic addition to the franchise.

review: The 5th entry in the Toy Story franchise. It's creative, carries the same tone/intent of previous movies and tackles the theme of technology in today's world. However, it lacks in key aspects and feels repetitive. The iconic lineup of Tom Hanks, Tim Allen, and others return and are just as incredible and convincing as ever. Two new villains are introduced: Lilypad and technology in the modern world. The theme of technology and how its applied in this story is great. It creates an underlying message, a conflict between the main characters and Lilypad, and sets up an internal struggle for Bonnie as she's mocked for still playing with toys. Jessie for some reason is the prominent main character. While the tiebacks to Toy Story 2 and emotional beats are great, she takes up far too much screentime, leaving other characters (in particular, Woody) as an afterthought. The story takes you on an adventure, throws you for loops here and there, but at the same time is predictable, and ends the same way every movie has. Character beats aren't any different from previous movies; the emotional highs are there but cut off quickly by a cheap joke or gag. Lilypad, just like Gabby from Toy Story 4 serves as an antagonist for half the movie. She's fun, has great scenes of with the main characters, but was just another copy and paste. By no means a bad entry nor an easy cash grab but has become played out and lacks the character balance/depth, charm, and storytelling of entries 1-3.

review_title: jessie shines the brightest in a stellar continuation of the toy story saga
review: "Now this is flying. With style." Toy Story 5 proves once again that this franchise ain't ever running out of steam. It meticulously maintains the spark of the previous films and might even shine the brightest of them all. The essence of Jessie, Buzz, Woody, and the rest of the toys is still there and soaring high. While the film primarily focuses on Jessie, Woody, and Buzz, it still gives the side characters some action. One of the numerous aspects of the film I enjoyed was the continuing hijinks of Buzz, Woody, and the other toys, along with their very "inconspicuous" hiding places. The villain of the film is technology. While most technology is inanimate in real life-it's humans who bring it to life-the film showcases a device inspired by Apple's iPad that is designed in a whimsical manner. The device, named "Lilypad," initially seems conniving and malicious, constantly cooking up schemes to keep Bonnie away from her toys. Later on, however, she becomes more human, empathizing with both Bonnie and the toys. We all know how difficult it can be to make friends during childhood, adolescence, and especially adulthood. Bonnie represents people who have always had a tough time making friends. I imagine many people who grew up with Toy Story will find themselves in a similar boat to Bonnie as adults. Adult friendships are much harder to maintain and nurture. Bonnie may only be eight years old, but she reflects what countless people experience every day. The end credits featured Taylor Swift's return to country music with her hit song "I Knew It, I Knew You." The song hits differently when interwoven with Jessie's arc throughout the film. I don't usually love country music, but this song is a banger and will be a certified classic for years-nay, decades-to come. The post-credits scene featured the newly enhanced Buzz Lightyears parachuting into a playground in the hope of finding responsible and loving owners. It serves as a heartfelt reminder that technology can never replicate the warmth, comfort, and joy of a real toy. Much like Inside Out, this franchise holds a very special place in my heart. I don't think anyone expected the series to continue after Toy Story 3, but I'm really glad it did. The creatives at Pixar have done a spectacular job crafting this vivid and exuberant universe filled with multifaceted characters and exceptional storytelling. I have so much nostalgia for this franchise. Toy Story 2 remains my uncontested favourite, but Toy Story 5 is a close second. That said, every Toy Story film is remarkably consistent in quality. I loved everything about the fifth instalment. The playful animation of Buzz and Jessie's wedding was wonderful to see and made my childhood dream a reality. Woody being asked to be Buzz's best man is deeply meaningful and brings their friendship full circle. There was never any doubt in my mind that the latest entry in the Toy Story universe would stick the landing and tug at my heartstrings. My eyes watered during multiple scenes between Bonnie and Jessie. The emotional moments hit incredibly hard. When Jessie discovers the time capsule that the daughter of her previous owner, Emily, left behind, I felt the emotions most strongly. It was so fitting that Emily named her daughter after her favourite cowgirl growing up. I can't help but think she would have kept Jessie if circumstances had been different. Toy Story 3 concluded Andy's story, Toy Story 4 capped off Woody's story, and Toy Story 5 beautifully focused on Jessie with sincerity, sensitivity, and pathos, wrapping her story up with a nice bow. Yeehaw! Final verdict: 10/10 (no notes)

Toy Story 5 is a good movie that delivers a thrilling adventure, great comedy and animation, and a semi-emotional message about friendship.

review: Toy Story 5 is a heartfelt reminder of why this franchise has remained one of animation's finest for decades. Rather than relying solely on nostalgia, the film finds fresh emotional ground while staying true to the characters that audiences have grown up with. It balances humor, adventure, and genuine sentiment with remarkable confidence, delivering a story that feels both meaningful and thoroughly entertaining from beginning to end. The returning cast slips effortlessly back into their iconic roles, making every reunion feel natural rather than manufactured. The relationships between the toys remain the emotional backbone of the film, and the screenplay gives each major character a purpose without allowing anyone to overshadow the others. At its core, the film continues to explore themes of friendship, change, and finding purpose, proving that these characters still have stories worth telling. Visually, the film is stunning. The animation is among the finest ever produced, with every environment filled with extraordinary detail and every character animated with incredible personality and expression. The action sequences are inventive and energetic, but they never come at the expense of the quieter emotional moments that have always defined the series. The score complements every scene beautifully, blending familiar musical motifs with new compositions that reinforce the film's emotional impact. What makes Toy Story 5 so successful is its ability to evolve without losing sight of its identity. It embraces new ideas while respecting the legacy of the previous films, creating an adventure that feels both fresh and comfortingly familiar. The humor lands consistently, the emotional beats feel earned, and the film trusts its audience enough to tackle themes that resonate with both children and adults. If there's one criticism to make, it's that a few new supporting characters could have benefited from more development, as some of them leave a stronger visual impression than an emotional one. A handful of story beats also follow familiar franchise rhythms, making certain developments easier to anticipate than expected. These are relatively minor shortcomings in a film that succeeds so confidently in nearly every other area. Ultimately, Toy Story 5 stands as another excellent chapter in one of cinema's greatest animated franchises. It captures the heart, imagination, and emotional sincerity that have always made these films so beloved while offering an adventure that feels worthy of the characters' legacy. Funny, moving, beautifully animated, and filled with genuine warmth, it's the kind of sequel that reminds audiences why they fell in love with these toys in the first place. While it may not surpass every previous installment, it comes remarkably close, delivering an experience that is both emotionally rewarding and immensely satisfying.

review_title: technological evolution and the silence of imagination
review: For those who saw the franchise being born and grew up side by side with Andy, Woody, and Buzz, there are still flashes of that original charm on screen. However, as we dive into this new iteration, the inescapable feeling is that we, the 90s generation, were the forgotten toys under the bed. The film clearly redirects its gaze, seeking to communicate with newer generations and focusing on delivering ultra-modern messages. Although the work invites reflection on subjects that undeniably need to be debated with the youth, the script is heavy-handed in directing the plot so incisively toward these agendas. The attempt to avoid repeating formulas is understandable, since seeing more of the same after the first three films would sound redundant. The cost of this choice, however, takes a high toll. Characters who were once so captivating and masters of their own narratives are gradually becoming supporting actors in their own story. The narrative focus has been absorbed by the theme itself and what it intends to teach. This discursive priority takes away a bit of that purer, magical element the saga has always offered. That delightful invitation to imagine, that feeling of coming home and peeking to see if the toys are going to move, loses ground to a structure that prioritizes the moral lesson over fantasy. The direction bets on a safe execution and relies on very accurate elements used previously. This ensures that the film provides emotion and entertainment smoothly, but it leaves the lingering doubt whether this is, in fact, a good path for the franchise's future. In the graphic and technological aspect, the feature is an unquestionable spectacle. It is impossible to deny that, release after release, we see visual evolutions that make the eyes shine. However, all this aesthetic perfection ends up falling short in delivering that playful warmth that the well-crafted universe of the first three films built. The shine of the plastic is real, but the invitation to innocence seems to have been left in the past.

review: Such a shame what this beloved franchise has come to. Such a shame that this franchise is owned by a greedy, money hungry company. I remember watching the first 3 Toy Story movies when I was a kid and how I couldn't stop watching them because they gave me a sense of who I was and how my toys were "alive". Not just the feeling they gave me but the story behind those movies too. This movie lacks in every aspect of what made the first 3 movies so great. There isn't a story being told in my opinion, even though the movie is literally called Toy Story. What I mean by this statement is that it's messy and continues to flip from POV's which is disorienting. It also fails in making the viewer feel interested, for me at least. Some directors can nail this narrative, Disney just failed in it with this movie. It overdoes the comedy so much that it gets old pretty fast. The first 3 movies had funny moments too, but they didn't overdue it which made it funny and not another: "Oh, here we go again..". Just explain a story that the viewer, no matter child or adult, can follow and relate to, like the first 3 movies did which led to them being so good. Stop using Toy Story's good name to get a quick payday. Stop insulting the fans that grew up with this franchise. Yes, I get the message of what they're trying to say with how technology lives everywhere which leads to people, kids but also adults, to not bond with each other anymore. But make it an interesting movie to watch. You have an idea of a plot, you just fail in nailing it for the viewer. For me at least. In my heart the Toy Story franchise ended with the 3rd one. review_title: a movie i didn't want but now glad it's here
review: Written and directed by longtime contributor to the franchise Andrew Stanton, Toy Story 5 is the latest installment into this series that was probably the least requested of the entire saga. I don't think it's hard to argue that many fans were hoping that the third film was going to be the end of it, but here we are welcoming the fifth. I generally don't try to give too many spoilers on the plot with new movies like this, but the entirety of the plot was essentially given away in the first full-lengthened trailer that released. It sees Bonnie getting a new tablet, and becoming obsessed with the new digital toy. The obsession becomes so bad, that it affects her growth socially, and the other toys have to try to rescue her from this new toy, while helping the new device who is guilt ridden for what she has done to Bonnie. I'm not gonna lie, I went into theaters expecting something that was very manufactured and cliché. It was a feeling that was very hard not to have because this was a film that no one really requested. It was obviously going to make money, but that doesn't mean that the end product was going to really justify its overall existence. The revealing of the subject matter also didn't help. It gave me and many others the inclination that this was going to be yet another attempt by Disney to use one of their more popular established franchises to deliver a social commentary Andrew Stanton takes a subject matter that is very prevalent in today's world with children that is a touchy subject for most parents, and delivers a story that is so rich emotionally, that it is hard to turn away from it. The third act alone is probably the best writing I've seen from Pixar since the third film. It thankfully doesn't go in the traditional villain direction that was, very deceivingly, hinted at in the trailer with the tablet (Lily), and actually went in a completely different direction, which was so much better. That's not to say that everything is perfect, the fifth film does suffer from the same issue as the fourth, where it does feel like the first act drags. The film is surprisingly long at just a shade under two hours, which is primarily thanks to that first act because it has to build the plot gradually. It's also not helped by the fact that it does have to reunite Woody with the other toys, which was clearly a challenge for them to quickly resolve when writing the film. I do love the animation. Pixar didn't really go out of their way to make too many advancements from the animation that the fourth film presented, which I'm extremely grateful for because it already looked perfect. There's a few minor advancements with the clothing on the characters, but other than that, everything is largely the same, which is definitely a positive. The cast is also magnificent, the returning cast delivers as always, and I absolutely love Greta Lee in the role of Lily. So overall, I was very pleasantly surprised, and judging by the reaction from the audience that was in the theater I was in, so were a lot of other people. Is it as emotional as the third film? No, but I don't think anyone was really expecting it to be. With that said, it delivers a message that is not only great for kids, but wonderful for parents as well, without being heavy-handed about it, which is a common problem with Disney. It is a fun movie, but also emotionally satisfying, which makes it a great addition to this long running franchise.

review: Toy Story 5 had all the makings of the kind of comeback that makes us raise an eyebrow and think, "Pixar, again?" But, to everyone's surprise, the franchise finds a very strong reason to exist once more. The nostalgia is still there, of course-all it takes is for Woody, Buzz, and Jessie to show up for our hearts to melt a little. But the movie doesn't rely solely on that. The real stroke of genius is turning the tablet into the new "villain" of childhood. And the most interesting part is that it doesn't even have to be exactly evil. The threat is now more subtle: the child is in the room, the toys are there, but their attention has been hijacked by a screen. Heavy stuff, right? Having Jessie take center stage also makes a lot of sense, especially given her history of abandonment. Not everything works perfectly-some characters feel a bit left out-but the strength of the theme holds it all together. In the end, Toy Story 5 proves that it's still possible to have fun with these characters without coming across as just a nostalgic cash grab.

review: The toys are back in town. Honestly, I still can't believe it. Toy Story 4 seems like it came out just yesterday, not seven years ago. Truly, the pandemic shaved so many years off of our lives. At this late date, Pixar is once again gambling with its most beloved franchise. With every sequel comes the risk of that one really bad one breaking through. Almost no film franchise has been spared from that curse. If the day ever comes that that happens to Toy Story, I will feel a big piece of my heart break. The first Toy Story is one of my all-time favorite films. 2 and 3 round out what to me is the perfect film trilogy. That is, if it stopped there. Toy Story 4 has not stood the test of time for me. By no means was it bad, but it couldn't be further from what made the first three so unforgettable. Now, you can really feel the cracks in the foundation. This series is now running the risk of becoming 30 years out of date. For all of our sakes, we should hope that doesn't happen. So, with all that being said, I'm happy to report that Toy Story 5 is a wonderful film. In fact, it feels more in line with the amazing first three films than the 4th film did at any point of it. The balance of humor, heart, imagination and play just comes so naturally to this one. With the rise of tech taking over the lives of children, the fear of abandonment that the toys once again find themselves in feels more urgent and existential than the simple fear of being replaced with a new toy. Toy Story 5 wearily asks if the age of playtime and old-fashioned make-believe is over, now that magical screens can show anything and everything to young minds. God help them when they find out what A. I. is. New characters come to focus, this time with their own footprint on the digital age. The standout being a flamboyant talking potty-training toy, played by Conan O'Brien. The former king of late-night brings his A-game big time here. I laughed hard and often, which is what any good comic relief should make you do. Meanwhile, Jessie takes the reins from Woody as leader of the pack. For much of this film, it's her story, and it's about time she's gotten one. Toy Story 2 introduced us to her, not simply as a female counterpart to Woody, but as someone who has lived through prolonged abandonment and has the emotional scars to prove it. Jessie faces this painful history again here, and while it doesn't reach the tear-jerking heights of Toy Story 2, it gives us something that is, in the end, so tender and sweet. Toy Story 5 is a joy to see in a theater and worth your time as a fan. Do I recognize its flaws? Sure. But I can see this film, in the long run, aging much better with time than a lot of people might think it will right now.

review: Meeting our old friends from the Toy Story universe, Toy Story 5 puts Jessie and her friends Buzz and Woody at the center of the story. We find Bonnie playing wedding with her toys in the garden when she overhears the neighbor kids returning home from a trip. To her surprise, they show no interest in playing with her - or with toys at all. Bonnie struggles to make friends, and most children her age seem completely absorbed by their screen devices, known as LillyPads. Recognizing her difficulties, Bonnie's parents eventually give in and buy her a LillyPad as well. Jessie and the other toys soon realize that these devices have spread everywhere, leaving toys abandoned and forgotten by children all over the world. Bonnie and her favorite toys, Jessie and Bullseye, quickly discover that playing with toys is no longer considered "cool" and is often seen as childish by her peers. Before long, Bonnie leaves her beloved toys behind to attend a LillyPad sleepover with her new friends. This sets off an unexpected adventure for Jessie, one that forces her to confront long-lost memories while embarking on exciting new experiences. Toy Story 5 is perhaps the most timely entry in the series. It explores how toys shape creativity while offering an honest look at both the benefits and the drawbacks of modern technology. Most importantly, the film shows a hopeful path forward, demonstrating how traditional toys and high-tech entertainment can coexist to create richer experiences, stronger relationships, and more joy for children. A movie for the whole family. I highly recommend it.

review: Five movies (and 31 years) in, "Toy Story" remains a truly great franchise. While not quite reaching the highs of the first three movies, "Toy Story 5" is an improvement from the (still very good) fourth movie, and even more importantly, it feels truly relevant to today's kids and parents in fresh and creative ways. This time around, the film centers on now-8-year-old Bonnie getting a "Lillypad" tablet. The "toys vs. Tech" plot is done in very clever and incisive ways that can be understood thoroughly and engagingly by both kids and adults. It's also a lot more nuanced than you'd think. Just like in the other "Toy Story" films, there's plenty of humor and emotionally endearing moments here. The charm still feels genuine and organic rather than forced, and always playing into the hands of a compelling and entertaining story. The screenplay is able to effectively develop and properly use all the characters, and kind of like in "Toy Story 2," Jessie is the most important character here for much of the story. The animation is beautifully done and improved over earlier films in the franchise, including a few scenes done incredibly well in a different style of animation from the rest of the movie. The film manages to be consistently charming throughout, although the charm arguably isn't quite as unique as in the first three films, when the toys' relationship with Andy was uniquely special to their respective narratives. A sub-plot about her works very well, but what doesn't work quite as well comparatively is another sub-plot involving multiple Buzz Lightyears. But this is still an undoubtedly great film that narratively justifies its existence and relevance to today's children and families. Gladly recommended. 8.5/10 Note: I saw the film in "The Big Show," Alamo Drafthouse's premium large format screen. The picture and sound quality were very good, although the film does not really need to be seen a premium format.

I wouldn't go as far as to say it's a great movie. But it does have a lot of great stuff in it. A recurring theme I've been seeing in a lot of modern Pixar movies, is accurately portrayed depression. Characters are forced to confront obstacles beyond their understanding. And even when things do get better, they've become so conditioned to pain that they can't bring themselves to smile anymore. While Lilypad is definitely the main antagonist of this movie, I'm really glad they didn't make her the villain. I really didn't another "Technology is Bad" message like in "Ready Player One". Though this film does do a really good job of visually showing the negative impact smart devices can have on young children. All of those scenes showing kids in dark rooms completely entranced by their screens, is pretty unsettling to watch. Now I know why my parents set screen time limits when I was younger. It is really easy to ignore the rest of the world when you're in the zone. Let this be a reminder to all parents, make sure your kids are playing outside regularly.

review: After the announcement of Toy Story 5, I really didn't think we needed another Toy Story flick. Toy Story 4 ended things on an emotional note so a follow-up didn't made much sense, but after watching the fifth installment of the franchise, I admit I was terribly wrong. Pixar's Toy Story 5 is a thoughtful continuation of one of the most beloved franchises. Rather than simply repeating the formula of previous installments, the film explores a contemporary conflict: the changing nature of childhood in an era dominated by digital entertainment. The film's strongest aspect is its emotional maturity. While earlier Toy Story films focused on abandonment, friendship, and moving on, this chapter examines what happens when the very idea of play begins to evolve. The introduction of technology as a rival to traditional toys gives the story a surprisingly relevant foundation, allowing Pixar to explore questions about imagination, connection, and nostalgia. The character work remains one of the film's biggest strengths. Woody and Buzz Lightyear remain the hilarious duo but the film gives greater narrative importance to Jessie, whose struggles with change and belonging provide much of the movie's emotional weight. Visually, the film looks beautiful, with expressive animation, detailed environments, and a strong sense of visual storytelling. The humor is effective, though the movie occasionally relies on familiar franchise patterns rather than fully reinventing the formula. However, the movie is not without its flaws. It does not reach the emotional heights of the previous installments, particularly Toy Story 3, and some story beats feel familiar. The film's message, while meaningful, is not entirely new. Overall, Toy Story 5 is a well-crafted and emotionally intelligent sequel that justifies its existence through a timely theme and strong character exploration. It may not surpass the heights of Pixar's greatest work, but it proves that the world of Toy Story still has something valuable to say.

review: I genuinely enjoyed the movie. I love that they're being a bit more "daring" by addressing the obvious elephant in the room... the iPad kids. The animation was stunning at some points and lacking at others. There's a long scene on a barge and the character (security guard?) has no discernible texture, I wonder if it was a miss. Speaking of skin, it's odd that there are hardly any white people in the movie. I half-expected Jessie's long-lost to have changed. When will Disney stop pandering to the mob? The "they/them" cult. The "anything but white" race hustle... it's tired. Real people aren't obsessed with race... just the online trolls virtue signaling. The plot was jammed with side-quests that could have been cut. I'm disappointed that the first time Bonnie received any boundary with the LilyPad was the most unrealistic part of the whole movie. Bonnie didn't have any issue giving it up to Mom. No meltdowns. No talk about mom and dad's screentime. Just oblivious parents sleepwalking through life as their daughter's toys show more concern for her wellbeing. Dropping a little girl off to a sleepover having not communicated with the parents or met them... ignoring huge red flags that something was amiss with their daughter... in some ways it felt daring, but ultimately it pandered. No room for Woody in this one. We already swapped Andy for Bonnie. Where are the boys and men? Another character has an absent father on zoom all the time. Perhaps it's a commentary on weak men, but we should have seen more of our favorite two. One tender moment and I think twice we laughed out loud. I'll still take this over Toy Story 4. Even still. Big strides are left to be made. Critics and iPad moms alike, would do well to remember that constant screens are not healthy for any child. Whether disabled or not. Get outside. People offended at its about-face from tech should perhaps examine why they feel so defensive. Swift's inclusion feels like a cash grab. I don't want a pop star. Nobody wants that for Toy Story. We want an original Randy Newman song. I was definitely disappointed to see the torch handed to Swift.

review: To celebrate my son's eighth birthday, I rented out a local cinema for him and twenty-nine of his mates to watch Andrew Stanton's 2026 release Toy Story 5. When you're dealing with a room full of hyperactive eight-year-olds, the stakes are incredibly high, but I can happily report that the film held them in absolute full attention. Not a single complaint from the kids, and frankly, the parents in the room were equally won over. There was genuine, infectious laughter throughout, and I'll admit, a few sniffles from the adults during the more emotional beats. It is, without a doubt, a massive crowd-pleaser. However, once the birthday sugar rush wore off and I had time to properly reflect, a narrative issue emerged. While the animation and visuals are, as expected from Pixar, absolutely top-tier and gorgeous to behold, the character focus is bafflingly lopsided. This is a franchise that has spent decades meticulously building a sprawling, beloved ensemble, yet here, most of them are reduced to mere background furniture. Woody and Buzz Lightyear feel like absolute afterthoughts in their own movie. Beloved staples like Rex, Hamm the piggy bank, and the Potato Heads are relegated to such tiny, blink-and-you'll-miss-them roles that it feels like a massive waste of established character equity. The bulk of the runtime is instead dedicated to Jessie and a deep dive into her specific backstory. Now, Jessie is a brilliant character, and giving her the spotlight is a fine creative choice on paper. But let's be real: this isn't a Jessie spin-off. It's Toy Story 5. By narrowing the lens so aggressively onto her singular arc, the film loses that essential, chaotic ensemble magic that made the earlier entries feel so rich, dynamic, and lived-in. It feels a bit like a missed opportunity to properly reunite the gang for one last, truly collaborative hurrah, opting instead for a narrower, more solitary character study. So, where does that leave us? It's certainly not a genre-defining masterpiece on the level of the original Toy Story or Toy Story 2, but it is also a long way from being the worst entry in the series. It's a highly polished, visually stunning, and undeniably entertaining film that does exactly what it needs to do for a family audience. Stanton has delivered a perfectly serviceable, emotionally resonant ride, even if it feels a bit too much like a solo vehicle masquerading as an ensemble piece. It's a cracking good time for the kids, and a decent enough watch for the rest of us.

Since this is supposed to be the final chapter, I would have loved more closure, especially regarding Andy and what became of him. Despite never liking Bonnie because of how she neglected her toys, I unexpectedly found myself sympathizing with her in this film. Jessie completely stole the show for me. I loved every scene she was in and genuinely felt her emotions. Lily Pad also surprised me by not being nearly as villainous as the trailers made her seem. The ending was satisfying, but I still walked away wanting answers to a few lingering questions, particularly about Andy. Overall, I enjoyed Toy Story 5 more than Toy Story 4, but it still couldn't reach the emotional and narrative greatness of Toy Story 3.

review_title: a heartfelt return that proves toy story still has something to say
review: After four beloved films, I went into Toy Story 5 wondering whether this franchise still had a reason to exist. To my surprise, it doesn't just justify its return-it delivers one of the most relevant and emotionally engaging stories in the series. This time, the conflict isn't another toy or a new owner. Instead, the film tackles a challenge that feels incredibly modern: technology. As children become increasingly attached to screens and digital devices, Woody, Buzz, Jessie, and the rest of the gang find themselves questioning their place in a changing world. It's a clever premise that feels both fresh and meaningful without losing the heart that has always defined the franchise. One of the movie's greatest strengths is its emotional maturity. Rather than portraying technology as purely good or bad, the story explores how it changes the way children interact, imagine, and play. The film asks difficult questions about connection, attention, and growing up while remaining accessible to younger audiences. That balance is something Pixar has always done exceptionally well. The animation is stunning. Every frame is packed with detail, vibrant colors, and impressive visual storytelling. Pixar continues to push the boundaries of animation, and several sequences are among the most visually creative moments the studio has produced in recent years. The voice cast remains fantastic. Tom Hanks and Tim Allen effortlessly step back into their iconic roles, while Jessie receives some well-deserved attention and character development. The newer characters bring fresh energy to the story and help keep the franchise from feeling repetitive. What impressed me most was how the film understands the emotional connection audiences have with these characters. Rather than relying solely on nostalgia, it builds on the themes that have always made Toy Story special: friendship, purpose, loyalty, and the fear of being left behind. Those themes feel just as powerful today as they did in 1995. The movie isn't perfect. Some supporting characters don't get as much screen time as longtime fans might hope, and a few plot points feel familiar. However, the emotional core is strong enough that these issues never significantly detract from the experience. Ultimately, Toy Story 5 succeeds because it evolves with its audience. It respects the legacy of the previous films while introducing a timely message for a new generation. It's funny, emotional, visually spectacular, and surprisingly thoughtful. Many franchises struggle to stay relevant after so many installments, but Toy Story 5 proves that these characters still have meaningful stories left to tell.

review_title: i'm falling for you more and more
review: I was surprised by the decision to focus on Jessie at this point in the story. While her response to her disappointment brought me to tears, it also made me wonder, "Why?" That question would be a spoiler, but this film was plagued by many other questions as well. Why did they base Woody's return on a misunderstanding on his part? Why were Woody and Buzz made to fight over something so unrelated to the main story? Why is Buzz constantly thinking about proposing? Why did they introduce so many Buzz figures? Why is the Device portrayed as such a villain? Why aren't the kids' parents monitoring the Device? Why is the Tech Trio so advanced? And why does a potty-training toy have network capabilities? All of these feel like convenient plot devices to move the story forward. This film really has a lot of scene changes. It's structured around three main storylines-the battle between the toys and the Devices, the story surrounding Jessie's past, and the adventures of the mass-produced Buzz-and on top of that, it delves into Bonnie's inner conflict and even explores the new character, the girl Blaze, in greater depth. I think this level of cramming is unusual even by Pixar standards. Perhaps because of this, the editing is fast-paced, with time frequently skipping ahead, and each adventure is inevitably condensed, making the sense of distance between locations feel off. The "why?" questions I mentioned earlier might actually have been necessary elements to cram the script full and rush the plot along. I don't dislike the answer presented regarding the "Toys vs. Devices" conflict. It's a very satisfying resolution that even reminds me of *Inside Out 2*. However, there simply isn't enough time. It's all too crammed in. I wish they had devoted more time to Lily Pad, who could be considered the film's second protagonist-rather than focusing on the grand adventure of the mass-produced Buzz. Just as they did with Gabby Gabby in *Toy Story 4*, I wanted them to delve deeper into Lily's inner world. I wanted a more satisfying catharsis in her rescue. As for Bonnie's story... it all worked out in the end, but it was a bit of a stroke of luck that a god-like new character happened to be there. It'll be fine if this serves as a catalyst for her further growth. The fact that the other kids' device addiction remains completely unresolved is just like *Pinocchio*. There were many points in this film that left me with some reservations, but I'm still grateful that they depicted these characters' new adventures. This series always presents new perspectives, new situations, and new problems. I'm really looking forward to seeing what kind of world they'll show us next. --------------------------- It's common for your understanding to deepen and your appreciation to grow as you read various online reactions, and this work is no exception-I find myself having more and more things to say about it, haha. I was wondering why they were repeating the message from the second installment-"Toys should be there for their owners when they need them"-but this time, they took it a step further: even if humans stop playing with their toys, the feelings they once had for them might not change. Toys don't grow up, so they don't forget. Humans, as they grow, forget. That might be cruel, but forgetting isn't the end. Because humans have the power to pass on their feelings. This might be the same thing depicted in *Coco*. While it appears to be depicting the lives of toys, it's actually depicting the connections between us humans. After all, living humans can't depict that. That's why it's portrayed through ghosts and toys. It's interesting when you think about it that way.

review_title: it's good for what it is
review: For the record, I'm in the "Toy Story 3 was the perfect ending" camp. There didn't need to be another Toy Story movie but I saw movies four and five anyway. The words "unnecessary sequel" come to mind when I think of those last two Toy Stories, but I want to say right now that the artists at Pixar at least tried to tell stories that matter, and I think they've had some measure of success. So what is Toy Story 5? Assuming you saw the trailers, you already know of the conflict between conventional toys and tech. When eight-year-old Bonnie gets a tablet computer, named Lilypad, she's immediately absorbed in the mindless games and Web chats the device offers. Naturally, the toys feel threatened, fearing they've become obsolete. There are several plot threads running through this movie, but the strongest by far is Jessie's. In an effort to find a real friend for the timid Bonnie, instead of Internet "friends," Jessie winds up at her old house; the house where her original owner, Emily lived. It reminded me of seeing my childhood home long after I grew up. Different, but somehow the same. Jessie learns to get over her technophobia, eventually befriending a trio of abandoned techie toys and she goes through her own soul searching journey that's similar to Woody's arc in Toy Story 2. And speaking of Woody, he reunites with Buzz and the rest of the gang, but he and the rest of the gang are shunted off to the side, much like the supporting cast of Dragon Ball Z. Yes, Rex is Pixar's answer to Yamcha and Slinky Dog is Krillin, I guess? Joking aside, I think they made the right call focusing on Jessie, though I didn't like the way Woody and Buzz quarreled. I mean, didn't they mature past that after the first movie? As usual for Pixar, the animation is brilliant, and the painterly visuals of Bonnie's imagination sequences are a nice touch. The writing is OK, but not Pixar's best. I'm glad I saw Toy Story 5, though I won't be revisiting it nearly as much as the first three movies. On one final note, am I out of touch? I found it really weird that the other kids made fun of Bonnie for still playing with toys. Their bullying felt more like what I would expect from a middle schooler than a second grader. Either way, cyberbullying is messed up!

Tom Hanks did not need to return as Woody but like the characters themselves state, it's undeniably nice to see him reunited and fighting with Tim Allen's Buzz, who gets to have a lot of fun thanks to Lightyear's inability to pop the big question. Out of all the new characters, Conan O'Brien's Smarty Pants is easily the strongest and his winning humour is used just the right amount. Andrew Stanton's direction only slows down when needed to let the most emotional moments unfold in the most engaging fashion and generally keeps things moving forward with ease. The animation is faultless as the overall level of fidelity only continues to improve even when it feels like it's already peaked and it's nice to see experimentation thanks to the play time sequences. Randy Newman's score never fails to match the film's emotions and Taylor Swift's impactful end credits song really works.

review: The rule of thumb for me, as an audience member, for the majority of films across a variety of genres is simple: is this a story worth telling? Do we really need another Toy Story? Does it have a point beyond mindless entertainment? And above all, never, under any circumstances, should you go beyond a trilogy... or, indeed, to infinity and beyond! Somewhat satisfyingly, Toy Story 5 has evolved with the times and the world we currently live in, making it one of the strongest fifth instalments in movie history. Don't get me wrong, there have been other odd gems. One of notable significance would, of course, be Rocky V. Toy Story 5 is up there with the best of them. It even suggests my trilogy theory might be less solid than a globe chasing Woody into extinction. My theory comes from years of disappointment with watered-down sequels to films that were once great, as well as my belief that every story should have a beginning, middle, and end-making a trilogy the perfect recipe. Andy gave away his toys, goddamnit! So let's continue with Bonnie, though admittedly I can't remember too much about her or Toy Story 4, for that matter. Luckily for me, this time round I don't need to. The film has a relatable point close to home in the present, which gives this Toy Story more credibility and helps it stand the test of time. As I currently write this review on a device of my own, I can't help but see the irony in it all. Edging back to the original story with references to Star Wars, Indiana Jones and, dare I say, Child's Play's Andy Barclay, who also has his fair share of moving toys-or dolls. "So, do you wanna play?" Chucky would say. Yet the kids no longer wanna play, and it's not down to Chucky; it's down to devices. With our Andy all grown up now and a distant memory, it seems somewhat inevitable the sequels to this popular CGI animation would continue. Toy Story was the pioneer of three-dimensional computer-generated animation, and it isn't surprising to see it evolve. However, what is surprising is how its quality of narrative has been maintained. As the film comes to its epic conclusion, you slowly cast your eyes across the cinema to see flashing lights materialise, only to think the point being conveyed went way over people's heads. Or had the addiction to devices already become far too prominent to be eased off slowly now? Visually, Pixar continues to set the standard. While audiences have come to expect technical brilliance from the studio, it never overshadows the story. The animation serves the emotion rather than distracting from it. With a subplot involving an army of Buzz Lightyears on a mission to find their Star Commander tying in nicely, and the main themes of loneliness and isolation for Bonnie, Toy Story 5 has just about the right mixture of adventure and emotional empathy. It appears Bonnie, a playful child using her imagination and creating her own adventures through the magic of toys, is now the oddball, and the new 'norm' is for kids to maintain their screen time on whatever happens to be the most popular app of the day. Perhaps the most heartfelt emotional scene comes through the vehicle of Jessie's character, as a past rejection becomes a delightful discovery. To conclude, Toy Story 5 doesn't just justify its existence-it earns it. It captures the hearts and imaginations of children while reminding adults what has quietly been lost along the way. Against all odds, it proves that sometimes a fifth film really does have a story worth telling.

review_title: a fun entry in the toy story franchise
review: It's always fun to get back to the characters and world of Toy Story so I was happy to see another instalment on the way, and although it probably is the worst of the five Toy Story films it's still a fun time. The story is a bit of a mixed bag. I thought overall it lacked a bit of focus, with multiple story threads that took a bit too long to all converge and come together. That being said, I thought the overall themes of technology and its impact on children, their friendships, and imaginations were well done and highly relevant. It carried emotional heft when it needed too, and provided light relief as well. I don't think it hit the emotional of comedy highs of any of the previous Toy Story films, but it was all well done nonetheless. If i'm being nitpicky, I would have liked to have seen more from some of the original characters. The likes of Rex, Slinky, Ham etc were all relegated to walk on parts, and even Woody felt somewhat sidelined. This was very much a Jessie and Buzz movie, not that that's a bad thing necessarily, but I like the other characters so much it's a shame not to see more of them. What can't be faulted with a Pixar movie is the design, sound, music and just the overall production quality. The whole thing feels and looks clean and imaginative and engaging. Overall this is another fun and entertaining Toy Story movie. It doesn't quite hit the highs of any of its predecessors, and the story maybe feels a bit muddled at times, but the overall themes are fitting for these times and it has its emotional and funny moments.

review_title: a worthwhile film to the toy story series
review: For the fifth film in the Toy Story series, I'm more than happily surprised at how the magic is still there. This film was a great, fun experience to see, and personally for me, better than Toy Story 4. Surprisingly, I don't have much complaints with this film. The one nitpick I would say is that the structure of the film, which for most of it has three separate plots, did feel a bit weird. However, it didn't take away from the experience and I was still able to enjoy it. The Plot- I felt like the story this movie had was a fun and interesting one for the series. The toys vs tech hook worked very well for me, and I found the plot fresh for this series. Even though the three separate plots were a bit weird at first, I didn't mind each one of them. The multiple Buzz Lightyear and the Woody/Buzz plots were fun; while the Jessie plot was a heartfelt one: None of them dragged the movie down for me, and by the ending, I was satisfied with the resolution. The Characters- I really appreciated how unlike in Toy Story 4, the majority of the characters weren't sidelined for the new ones. While supporting characters like Rex, Mr. Potato Head, and even Forky were in the background, I still didn't mind much. I did enjoy how the film gave focus to Woody, Buzz, and especially Jessie. I'm glad Woody isn't the main character in this, as his arc was complete in TS4, and Buzz has some great banter with him. As for Jessie though, I love how the film gave her more development, and really let her shine this time, also by giving her an arc of learning that technology isn't all bad, which ties into the message of the film. I also enjoyed how the film gave some depth to Bonnie, as in TS3 and TS4, she was mostly in the background. Her struggle of socializing and wanting to make a friend was deeply relatable to me, and probably lots of other people out there. Additionally, the new characters like Smarty Pants(Conan O'Brien) were fun new additions, but out of the new cast of characters, I enjoyed Lilypad. I liked how Lilypad wasn't just a standard evil villain, but someone who thought they were helping out. The Animation- The animation in this film is breathtaking, and I can understand why it cost 250 million dollars to make this. The characters move smoothly, the environments look real, the film just looks beautiful and some shots even looked real to me. Additionally, I also enjoyed the stylized sequences whenever there was a "playtime" scene, as the animation style would change to resemble a pastel drawing. The Message- I really enjoyed how the message of the film was handled. It was handled in a smart, mature, and engaging way. I loved how it wasn't a "technology is bad and should be destroyed" message, but instead a "technology can be useful, but it shouldn't replace human connection". I enjoyed how throughout the film, the toys(mainly Jessie) learned to accept and coexist to technology(like Smarty Pants, or even Lilypad) instead of just destroying technology. The Music- I don't have much to say about it despite that it's just fine. Good, but not memorable. Overall, Toy Story 5 is a surprisingly good entry in the Toy Story series. Even though I still believe this franchise should have ended after the third film, I don't mind this film at all. I would definitely recommend to see this film in theaters, it's worth it! 8/10.

review_title: a charming and surprisingly necessary sequel that finds new meaning in a digital world
review: 88/100 Against all odds, Toy Story 5 proves that Pixar still has meaningful stories to tell with these beloved characters. What could have been an unnecessary sequel instead becomes a surprisingly thoughtful and emotional exploration of childhood in the digital age. This time, Woody, Buzz, Jessie, and the gang face a new challenge: technology, ipads to be exact. As Bonnie becomes increasingly attached to a tablet called Lilypad, the toys begin to question whether traditional play still has a place in a world dominated by screens. It's a timely premise that could have felt outdated or heavy-handed, but the film handles it with remarkable balance, acknowledging both the benefits and drawbacks of technology without turning into a lecture. The film's greatest strength is its focus on Jessie, who finally receives the spotlight she has long deserved. Her emotional journey gives the story fresh energy while Woody and Buzz continue to provide the heart and humor fans expect. The animation is stunning, with Pixar once again setting a benchmark for visual storytelling. Several sequences rank among the most beautiful in the franchise. While the plot occasionally retreads familiar themes of change and growing up, the emotional beats still land effectively. It's final act delivers genuine laughs, heartfelt moments, and a conclusion that feels earned rather than manufactured. Although not everyone will agree that a fifth installment was necessary, but Toy Story 5 justifies its existence with charm, intelligence, and emotional sincerity. It may not surpass the original trilogy (especially 3), but it comfortably stands among the series' strongest entries.

review_title: the weakest toy story but still has pixar's heart
review: I have always believed that Toy Story 3 was the perfect ending for this franchise. It closed the story so beautifully that the first three films could have stood forever as one of the greatest animated trilogies ever made. Even Toy Story 4 worked as a decent epilogue, giving Woody a new purpose and a new life outside the bedroom. So when Toy Story 5 arrived, my biggest question was simple: what else is there left to say? Apparently, the answer is: kids have iPads now. The movie finally tackles the decline of traditional toys in the age of smartphones, tablets, and online social life. It is a strong and very relevant idea. Children today are often more interested in screens than toys, and I was genuinely curious to see how Pixar would handle such a complicated issue. Unfortunately, the film takes the easiest route. It suggests that kids are hooked on the online world mainly because of social pressure, and the solution is basically to find another kid who also likes toys. That feels too simple for such a big subject. I understand why Pixar avoids going too deep. A serious look at screen addiction, social media, and childhood loneliness could easily become too heavy for a family movie. Still, the theme feels underdeveloped. The film brings up a fascinating modern problem, then quickly backs away from it. My bigger disappointment is how many beloved characters are pushed aside. Mr. Potato Head, Slinky Dog, Rex, and several other classic toys are almost background extras here. Forky, who was so important in Toy Story 4, barely matters. But the most painful part is Woody. His story felt complete in the fourth film, yet he is brought back with almost no real purpose. He does not drive the plot, and the movie too often treats him like a washed-up joke. If there is nothing meaningful left to do with Woody, I would rather Pixar let him remain a beautiful memory. Buzz Lightyear works better, mostly as a romantic fool chasing love, but he also feels more like a plot device than a fully developed character. Jessie becomes the real lead, and I actually do not mind that. She has always deserved more focus, and the film gives her one of its strongest emotional moments. The new electronic toy characters are cute, especially the weird little gadget with disgusting functions but a sweet personality. However, the idea of abandoned electronics could have been explored much more deeply. Toys can become collectibles and memories; electronics are usually replaced and thrown away. That contrast had real emotional potential, but the movie only scratches the surface. That said, Pixar's magic is not gone. The final rescue mission is exciting, creative, and full of energy. The flying Buzz Lightyear sequence is genuinely fun, and Buzz's romantic moment with Jessie, complete with music from the tablet, is silly in the best Pixar way. Even better is Jessie discovering a time capsule from her first owner and realizing she was never truly forgotten. It is a small scene, but it hits hard. That is why, despite all my complaints, I cannot call this a bad movie. It is probably the weakest Toy Story, but it still has warmth, imagination, and a few emotional moments that remind you why this series matters. If Pixar continues the franchise, I hope the next film explores how toys have become more meaningful to adults than children: collectibles, blind boxes, Labubu figures, Gundam models, and all the things grown-ups buy to comfort their inner child. That would be a more interesting direction. For now, Toy Story 5 is unnecessary, uneven, and sometimes frustrating - but still charming enough to work.

review_title: a worthy sequel that knows it's standing in the shadow of greatness
review: I'll be honest, I went in skeptical, because Toy Story 3 already gave this franchise one of the most perfect endings in animation history, and every sequel since has had to live with that comparison. Toy Story 5 doesn't quite reach those heights, but it earns its place anyway by handing the spotlight to Jessie for the first time, and it's genuinely refreshing to see the story through her eyes instead of Woody's after four movies of him carrying the emotional weight. The film tackles its central theme of kids drifting away from toys toward screens with more nuance than I expected going in, never fully painting technology as the villain, which is a smarter choice than the marketing led me to believe. The animation is gorgeous as always, the new characters add some genuine laughs, and there are a couple of scenes in the back half that hit harder than I was prepared for. My main gripe is that the film juggles a few too many storylines at once, so some of them feel a little undercooked by the time everything ties together, and longtime fans might miss spending more time with the classic side characters who mostly get sidelined this time around. It's not a new classic, but it's a thoughtful, well-crafted continuation that justifies its own existence, which honestly is all I was hoping for.

review_title: beautiful but emotionally heavier than expected
review: Beautiful, but emotionally too heavy for what is supposed to be a family movie I walked into this movie expecting a touching Pixar story, but I left feeling emotionally unsettled in a way I did not expect. What affected me most was how strongly the movie focused on loneliness, abandonment, and the fear of being left behind. These themes have always existed in Toy Story, but here they felt much heavier and more direct. At times, it no longer felt like a children's movie. It felt like a movie speaking to adults who still carry wounds from childhood. Some scenes made me tear up because they reminded me of what it feels like to be lonely as a child: shy, insecure, unable to connect easily, and afraid of being forgotten. That emotional honesty is powerful, but it also made me question whether the movie may be too intense for younger kids. I do not think this makes the movie bad. In fact, the emotional depth is one of its strongest parts. But I also felt that the sadness sometimes became overwhelming. Toy Story has always balanced heartbreak with warmth and adventure, and here the abandonment theme felt so strong that it stayed with me even after leaving the theater. It is a beautiful movie, but not an easy one emotionally. For adults, it may hit very deeply. For children, I am not sure all of it will feel light or comforting.
