review_title: a sequel with something to say
review: Toy Story 5, man, I can't believe we've gotten to this number of sequels for a movie most of the general public would tell you should've ended with Toy Story 3 in 2010. Now I don't need to give any background on the Toy Story franchise; it is one of the most iconic and well-regarded animated series of all time. It jump-started Pixar into becoming the powerhouse it is today; it is a staple of animated movies for 90s kids, and now, with parents raising their kids on it. So I have nothing but positive things to say. That being said, when I saw Toy Story 4 back in 2019, I had just started to review movies on Twitter, and I enjoyed it quite a bit. It's more of a good, not great movie in the Toy Story saga, rather than an ABSOLUTELY necessary sequel. Most fans agreed ending the series on 3 was the right move, and while 4 introduced us to ideas like what is a toy to kids, and had a concluding arc for Woody's character, it feels very unnecessary. It's still good, just didn't need to be made other than, well, you know, MONEY. So, 7 years later, we have Toy Story 5, a movie that wants to deal with the problem of smart devices being the toys kids play with nowadays, and an interesting arc for Jessie and Buzz. So, does this feel like another cash-grab sequel to a beloved franchise? Yes, it is a cash grab, but I think this brings a lot to the table in terms of a sequel than I expected. Toy Story 5 follows the same toys we know and love in the hands of Bonnie now, but this time without Woody, who has joined Bo Peep and the other toys on the run in the last movie. Jessie (Joan Cusack) now runs the show as the main sheriff, and Buzz (Tim Allen) is struggling to reveal his feelings to her. When Bonnie starts to have trouble fitting in with the neighborhood kids, her parents decide to get her a Lilypad (Greta Lee) to help her make friends online. Unfortunately, this leaves a lot of screentime for Bonnie, but less playtime for the toys. Running out of options, Jessie radios Woody (Tom Hanks) for help to bring back playtime. With the gang back together, it's up to our returning toys to bring back the age of toys and ensure Bonnie makes a friend along the way. Now I think this idea for a story fits VERY well with our current climate. As a 5th-grade teacher, I can tell you that screentime is a major issue with kids nowadays. Most kids would rather play on an iPad or use their parents' phone than actually do playtime outside or with their toys, so I think relating this to the Toy Story universe is a great idea. I also love how they incorporate it into Jessie's backstory, where 2 other times now, she has lost her owner to something else, and she ultimately feels like she is the problem, not the kid themselves. She's in danger of losing another kid to this device, and she feels responsible; that makes a lot of sense. While Buzz mostly serves as support to Jessie and fights with Woody like the good old days, he's mostly there to confess his feelings, and that's about it. Which brings me to my biggest issue with this movie: Woody should not be in this movie. Now I've heard arguments from others that it wouldn't be a Toy Story movie without him, but honestly, he doesn't add much here at all; his story concluded in 4, and he's really just brought in to support Buzz of all the toys. I think this easily could've worked without him being there, and that's my major issue with the story. The animation is obviously gorgeous, and it truly is a spectacle to watch the progression of Toy Story 1 in 1995 (one of the first major motion pictures that was fully computer-animated by the way) to this in 2026, which shows realistic humans, environments, and characters. The emotions are also very well done, because my issue with Toy Story 4 was the ending, with Woody feeling like it was TRYING so hard to make you cry, but with this, everything that Jessie goes through and her character arc are really well crafted. When it gets to the emotional gut punch at the end, it feels worthwhile and ties in extremely well with what this movie is trying to say. review: After a fourth installment that divided audiences, Toy Story 5 brings the franchise much closer to what made it so special in the first place. The story feels fresh, even if it relies on a familiar formula that has always been part of the series: the toys setting out to rescue one of their own. Fortunately, it never feels repetitive. Jessie finally gets the spotlight she has deserved since Toy Story 2, while Buzz Lightyear once again feels like an essential part of the story after taking a back seat in the previous film. Where Toy Story 5 truly succeeds is in capturing the spirit of the original trilogy. It is filled with nostalgic moments and clever callbacks without relying solely on fan service. At the same time, it offers a thoughtful reflection on how childhood has changed in an age dominated by screens, while never losing sight of what made these characters so timeless. Perhaps the film's greatest strength is its message about growing older. Time has passed, even for Woody, yet he never stops being Woody. In the same way, many of us are no longer the kids who watched these movies on VHS, but Toy Story 5 somehow makes us feel exactly the way we did back then. That's what makes this sequel so successful: it recaptures the heart, warmth, and emotional honesty of the original trilogy, reminding us why Toy Story remains one of animation's greatest franchises.

review: I can say for a fact that i was one of the many that thought the story should have ended at 3. I dont recall ever going to see the 1st one since i was so young, but i remember seeing the 2nd at 5, and the 3rd one at 17. Age now? 33. The plans for a sequel shouldve stopped once Don Rickles (voice of Mr Potato Head) died in 2017. As a close to a wonderful franchise. Right? Well WRONG! I guess Disney / Pixar needed some of that big money to give them something to fund future projects, so it happened and while it was good, it just felt so unnecessary. The only thing it closed was Woody being the focus of the story. All and all, it wouldve made sense to end it right there, right?? Well..... Disney has had a few misses since then, so once the announcement came that would be another sequel in the making, I wasnt surprised. I see it as their "saving grace" to get out of the hole. Naturally I still wanted to go see it, just to see what the hub bubs about and well.... THIS shouldve been our Toy Story 4! The tackle of our favorite characters that we have all come to love trying to come to grips with technology that have fully taken over our lives. And the main character to drive the plot? Not Buzz, but Jesse! Her backstory from Toy Story 5 set up perfect motion for the movie. She knew exactly what it was like to see a kid basically grow up and eventually drop old hobbies for new ones, and living in almost a fully automated world with tablets and phones was different, but not an unfamiliar feeling to her. I expected Buzz to kind of pick up where Woody right off, but I wasn't too mad at how they utilized his character as well. Wasnt too much of a fan with his glaring incompetence sometimes, you know the stupid male lead / strong female lead dynamics. But it also just me realize that he was always the perfect 2, or the robin i would say. I also wasn't mad about Woody's lack of presence in this movie, 4 was supposed to be a close for him, so bringing back a beloved character for a supporting role was a nice touch in this instance. Our supporting characters? Did their job, no more, no less. As far as the message goes, yes the message is great. Of course we have gotten the whole "Cant stop a kid from growing up but we're gonna make it the best childhood they have" trope, but opening eyes to how much technology has so much control in our daily living and social dynamics has so much weight to it. As a milennial, i was raised in the era of going outside and playing, being a kid, and as I got older, social media started to come about, cellphones started to get smarter by the year, everyone stopped having a braincell to keep in their head, and with tech spearheading everything, now with that basterdly A. I., you dont find too many people that you could still hold a logical conversation with, or just normal activities because everyone has a phone or a tablet shoved in their hand. Noticed how in one scene where the toys had to cut through a house to get to the donation truck, and NO ONE in the house ever noticed because they were too busy screen gazing. The only member to notice was the dog lol. The toys had fell onto a trampoline and bounced right in view of the window but the man of the house was too in a trance to see it. Technology has taken our abilities to be aware. How many times have there been an accident, and it was maily due to someone being on their phone. Im glad im one of the few that even though I loved what technology has done, and Im glad to be alive to see it, I can still have some type of know how that seems either very foreign or very "ancient" as time marches on. It's some things that I have to keep from that "child" me that made me into the adult I am today. All and all, it was a great movie. But the only question is will there be any more future sequels? Im not too keen on the idea but I'm not opposed to it either. I can kind of seeing it be like Toy Story 3, but with an older Bonnie plot. When they do announce another one, ill gripe a little, but I'll be there. To infinity and beyond.

review_title: they did again for the 5th time
review: Well, stunning animation, heartwarming storyline (as usual), fun new characters. Toy Story 5 feels incredibly cinematic. The framing, color grading, and lighting are all absolutely gorgeous. Every shot feels carefully crafted, and honestly, I loved it. One of my favorite parts was the make-believe sequences. They looked so beautiful that it made me wish Pixar would stop chasing hyper-realistic 3D perfection and lean more into this kind of artistic visual style. It has so much more personality. I also love how the film handles the "toys vs. Technology" theme. It never feels preachy. Instead, it quietly reminds us that traditional toys and modern technology don't have to compete, they can coexist. We can embrace new technology without letting go of the simple joy that toys have always brought us. That said, I was a little confused by Lilypad's decision to leave in the donation truck. I wasn't entirely sure why she ended up feeling so guilty, especially when it led to Bonnie deciding not to bring Jessie back home. That emotional beat didn't completely land for me. Another thing I noticed is that the bond between Bonnie and her toys doesn't feel nearly as intimate as the relationship Andy had with Woody and the others. With Andy, every goodbye carried so much emotional weight. Here, it feels a little more distant. I hope Pixar explores that relationship more deeply if there's another sequel. On a personal level, this movie really resonated with me. I've been bullied before, so I could relate to Bonnie's struggle to find people who truly understand her after being labeled as "weird." Thankfully, she eventually finds Blaze, a friend who accepts her for who she is. And as much as people often criticize technology, it's also technology that helps many of us connect with people we never would have met otherwise. This movie feels surprisingly relatable. If there's one message I took away from it, it's this: don't give up on finding people who are on the same wavelength as you, and cherish the friendships that truly matter. By the end of the film, I couldn't stop wondering about the toys I had as a kid. Did they look at me the way Woody and Jessie look at Bonnie? Did they feel lonely when I slowly stopped playing with them and they were eventually left in a box somewhere? Because that's what growing up is, isn't it? We move forward with our lives... while quietly leaving their world behind.

review_title: a worthy and touching entry to this phenomenal franchise
review: It happened again: Pixar went and made another Toy Story movie after already "ending" the franchise, causing severe backlash, only for people to realize that the movie is pretty good. A very familiar cycle that happened first with Toy Story 4, and now with Toy Story 5, and we'll probably see it again when they do Toy Story 6. Once everyone got their eyes on this movie, the talk around it was VERY positive, I've seen a few claim that this is potentially the best Toy Story movie which is obviously a very bold statement. I'm a huge fan of this franchise, I grew up on the first three. My first ever Halloween costume when I was like 2 years old was Buzz Lightyear and Toy Story 3 is one of my favorite animated movies, I unironically think it's a cinematic masterpiece. But I wasn't very fond of 4, so like everyone else, I was skeptical for this. But I'm happy to say that it is pretty dang good, although a tad overrated. First and foremost I think this beats Toy Story 4 quite easily, and that's all I could've asked for tbh. It's a really good film but I had more issues with it than I thought I would, the biggest being the pacing. The pacing is prettyyy awful ngl. The entire first half of this movie is genuinely confusing because it is so chaotic and so fast-paced. The second half's pacing was much better but still wonky. This movie just feels overstimulating sometimes; the soundtrack never lets up, everyone is always talking over each other, and the dialogue is loud. Thankfully this issue is almost entirely resolved by the halfway point, but it's still a big issue nonetheless. I think the narrative shouldn't have been as hard to follow as it was, the pacing really killed the setup. Luckily, my complaints end there. The pacing was bad enough for me to take several points off, but I liked basically everything else about Toy Story 5. Having this installment revolve around technology and the decreasing time kids spend with their toys just makes sense, there really wasn't any other direction this movie should've gone. Even better, it's not a cliché "kids and those darn phones" movie, it's way more nuanced than that. It's more of a criticism of how tech has made kids grow up too fast rather than kids using tech itself, which is a GREAT theme imo. This is something I found 11 year old me thinking when I was getting bullied online by kids from my school. It's so so much better than simply making Facebook boomer jokes about kids trying to swipe books and using internet slang irl. Kudos to Pixar for the theme. The plot is great too, I didn't mind Jessie being the lead in the slightest. Woody stole the show in Toy Story 4, and Buzz's main story has technically been over for quite some time. Jessie learning to resolve her trauma and anxious attachment was really touching. This movie also places a bigger emphasis on their kid. I will always prefer Andy over Bonnie, but this movie makes you care about her in many ways that the original trilogy didn't do for Andy. Lastly, I LOVED seeing Woody and Buzz goof off again, I was smiling like an idiot every time they were on screen. Overall this was an excellent and worthy addition to one of the best franchises of all time. If it had better pacing, I would consider this on the same level as Toy Story 2 and 3. It's that good. Strongly recommend! 8/10.

I was on board with the story concept based on the trailers but just really hoped that it wouldn't be just an episodic adventure that had nothing to say. While it did take some time to really come into focus for me I'm glad to say that by the time it concluded I really felt like this was a more than worthy entry into the franchise. I would say for the first 2 acts I was entertained enough and was enjoying the experience but it wasn't feeling very consequential to me. I don't want a Toy Story movie that doesn't have any substance and I was worried that's where 5 was going for the longest time. But by the time we get a certain reveal about Jessie's character the film totally won me over and actually got me a bit choked up. Making her the protagonist was absolutely the right choice and the film as a whole feels like a character study for her and gives her the closure I didn't actually know that she needed. Woody and Buzz continue to be a perfect duo and even if it feels like they do take a bit of a back seat in this movie it still felt right to me and I was very happy with the material they were given. It's the first instalment since the 90's that doesn't feel like a definitive end but that would bother me more if I hadn't basically loved the ending we did get and it left me so fulfilled. I think the final third did this movie a lot of favours because the journey getting to that point was definitely a bit messy. There's a lot of plot threads that don't even feel remotely connected and it can feel a bit plodding as the film attempts to bring them together. The whole army of Buzz Lightyear's never totally meshed all that well for me and while I liked where it ultimately went I did feel that the commentary on tech could've gone a bit deeper. It's almost a certainty that Pixar are going to make more of these movies at this point and I'll always be a bit nervous about it but they've more than earned the benefit of the doubt from me at this point. It's far from the best in the franchise but I was just so happy that it had a story with something to say and executed it in a mostly satisfying way. While these movies always tug at your heart strings the actually ending here left me uplifted more than anything and when we inevitably get a sixth film I'll be excited to see how they continue it.

review: I came into this with pretty much zero expectations, but wow, this was such a charming and heartwarming watch. It's amazing how this franchise has stayed relevant for so many years, and honestly, it's no secret why. At its core, it still just wants to tell a good story. I really liked how the film tackled technology and the whole rise of "iPad babies". It's such a timely topic, especially with all the debate around whether parents should raise their kids with tablets and screens. For a family film to take that on feels quite courageous, and I thought it was handled really well. That's also what makes the film feel like it's not just for kids. It's very much for parents too. Beneath all the cute, funny and sentimental moments, there's something genuinely meaningful about childhood, imagination and what kids choose to connect with. And honestly, if I had a kid right now, I'd probably buy them a toy from this franchise after watching this. That's how much the film made me feel. It somehow reminded me why owning a toy can feel so cool, special and full of life.

review: Rating - 8.8: Overall, while I still feel like the franchise should have ended after 'Toy Story 3', 'Toy Story 5' is a well-executed Pixar movie that continues the legacy of the franchise by continuing to break ground with their animation, storytelling, and voice acting while also staying relevant and fresh as they shift the story from Woody and Buzz to Jessie's perspective and address more pertinent topics like iPad kids and abandonment, making this movie feel more profound than 'Toy Story 4'. Direction - Very Good: The direction on a macroscale is very strong, following the classic Pixar Toy Story template, especially considering they know the world they are building with this being the fifth installment in the franchise; The direction on a microscale is also very strong as they know what they are doing, maintaining strong chemistry with the returning characters while integrating the new voice actors very well; The storytelling is very strong and keeps you fully engaged as the Pixar story team shows why they are the best in the business, keeping it somewhat fresh by telling the story through Jessie's perspective; The tension is good as it helps keep you emotionally engaged with the characters and what they are going through, but it definitely does not feel as strong as the rest of the franchise because it doesn't feel like there are any stakes anymore Story - Very Good: The concept is very relevant and fresh, focusing on the toys navigating a new world of technology as Bonnie becomes an iPad kid, which feels like a much better story than Toy Story 4; While this movie is still not needed after the franchise ended with Toy Story 3, they were able to find a way to continue the franchise and leave the door open for possible sequels instead of making it "the last Toy Story" like the previous two movies; The plot structure is pretty sound as it follows the Pixar Story template, but even though I enjoyed the Buzz Lightyear army side plot and thought it converged well with the main story in the end, it kind of just felt thrown in; The character writing is strong as they successfully make Jessie the emotional center and the main character, though Bonnie's character writing just makes her the absolute worst kid compared to Andy Screenplay - Great: The dialogue is very well-written, tight, and profound, showing why the Pixar creative team is the best in the business; The humor is good and quite funny, especially with the Buzz Lightyear side plot; The symbolism is very strong, dealing heavily with themes of feeling left out as a kid, feeling forgotten and no longer useful as a toy, and feeling abandoned; The foreshadowing is standard for what you expect from a Pixar family movie, so you can kind of expect what will happen because they are never going to go as dark as they did for Toy Story 3 Acting - Very Good: Tom Hanks - Great (Continues where he left off as Woody as he can performance this character in his sleep at this point; while he is more of a side character this time around, which makes me very sad, his voice acting acting is still top tier and adapts well to the new role; still has great chemistry with the rest of the cast, especially Tim Allen and Joan Cusack), Tim Allen - Very Good (Gives a strong performance as always, especially in the funny Buzz Lightyear army side plot, as he can basically do this character in his sleep; has strong chemistry with the rest of the cast, especially Tom Hanks and Joan Cusack), Joan Cusack - Great (Really adapts to Jessie becoming the main character of the story as she really is the emotional core of the story as it it is told from her perspective, as it shows her doubt as a leader and her abandonment from her previous owners; has strong chemistry with the rest of the cast, especially Tom Hanks and Tim Allen), Conan O'Brien - Good to Very Good (Feels like a great fit as he really is a dynamically funny character and his charisma really transfer well to the character, especially in a comedic way), Greta Lee - Good (Plays a very standard Pixar character, but does a good job with it and has good chemistry with the cast), Rest of the cast - Good (The voice acting is strong as always, though it was kinda sad how the originally cast almost felt like cameos in this movie (but when you keep adding new members the gang, this was bound to happen); the cast has incredibly strong chemistry, and they did a great job of integrating the new voice actors alongside the returning cast.) Score - Good to Very Good: The score is very strong and continues the work Newman did on the past four movies; Since the movie is told from Jessie's perspective, it interpolates her main theme from Toy Story 2 a lot throughout the movie, and does so very well Soundtrack - Good: The soundtrack is minimal but features a Taylor Swift song during the credits, which feels like a very obvious push by her and Pixar to get her an Oscar Editing - Very Good: This is very standard for a Pixar movie, as they know what they are doing and are not going to slip up on their bell cow Sound - Very Good: Well-executed and very standard for a Pixar movie, as they know what they are doing and are not going to slip up on their bell cow; It uses a lot of the same sound effects as the other Toy Story movies to help continue building this shared world Animation - Great to Incredible: The animation is top-tier Pixar, featuring incredible detail, especially in the animal animation; I really liked the mixture of traditional Pixar 3D CGI with hand-drawn elements in the playtime moments, resembling the style of Puss in Boots: The Last Wish, which shows Pixar trying to innovate and remaining willing to adapt to the industry's shift toward hand-drawn styles Pacing - The pacing is strong and does not move too fast or too slow; I really did not feel like anything could have been cut, and I actually would have loved even more time with these characters because I just love them so much Climax - The climax is well-executed, though it is your typical high-speed action chase climax that almost all of the Toy Story movies have at this point, so it ends up being exactly what you expect from a Toy Story climax Tone - Tonally, it is what you would expect from a Pixar and Toy Story movie, continuing to build and tell more stories in this iconic world while helping to balance family humor with deep emotional resonance to leave a profound effect on you as you leave the theater and reminisce about your childhood toys stored in your mom's basement.

review_title: an emotional and thematically rich triumph for pixar's crown jewel
review: When a franchise reaches its fifth installment, skepticism is not just expected; it is practically mandatory. Yet, under the seasoned direction of Andrew Stanton, Toy Story 5 masterfully dismantles any cynical preconceptions, delivering a profoundly moving chapter that feels both necessary and remarkably fresh. This time around, Woody, Buzz, and the beloved ensemble find their very existence threatened not by a malicious child or a dusty antique store, but by the relentless, glowing allure of modern technology. By pitting classic playthings against the inescapable tide of electronic devices, Stanton brilliantly grounds the narrative in a deeply relatable contemporary anxiety, asking poignant questions about obsolescence, loyalty, and the enduring power of imagination. The film's greatest strength lies in its impeccable balancing act between sweeping visual spectacle and intimate character beats. The animation, as to be expected from Pixar, is breathtakingly detailed-capturing the subtle scuffs on plastic and the warm textures of fabric with photorealistic precision. However, it is the emotional weight of the vocal performances that truly anchors the film. Tom Hanks and Tim Allen slip back into their iconic roles with effortless grace, bringing a mature, lived-in gravity to Woody and Buzz that reflects their decades-long journey. The pacing is razor-sharp, allowing for sequences of thrilling, inventive action-particularly a clever confrontation involving an army of rogue Buzz Lightyear toys-without ever sacrificing the quiet, tender moments that have always been the heartbeat of the series. Ultimately, Toy Story 5 succeeds because it refuses to coast on mere nostalgia. It is a visually sumptuous, thematically mature exploration of what it means to be left behind in an ever-accelerating world, wrapped in a genuinely hilarious and heartwarming adventure. While it honors the legacy of its predecessors, it confidently charts new emotional territory, resulting in a rare sequel that enriches the overarching mythology rather than diluting it. A masterful achievement in storytelling that will leave both children and adults misty-eyed long after the credits roll. Essential viewing.

review: So toy story is a multi generational franchise the first film came out 31 years ago that means people who were kids when the first one came out now probably have their own kids or parents when the first film came out have grandkids now like this franchise is not only one of the most famous animated and just in general franchises ever and every film has delivered. The first film though the animation is a little outdated now it still hits and I've watched time and time again toy story 2 however I've had a mixed relationship its probably my least watched toy story and I haven't watched it in years due to the fact I always remember as a kid watching and just finding it a little cringey at times toy story 3 however won best animated film at the Oscars and is one of the only animated films to get nominated for best motion picture too at the Oscars and it is a billion times deserved like you know that homelander perfect down to every detail meme that represents toy story 3 perfectly and I think it could very well be the best animated film ever definitely pixars best and my favourite pixar film but it could also be one of the best animated abd just in general films ever. And despite toy story 3 having a perfect ending and people saying we don't need a 4th we got one and I really liked it I feel like I'm in the minority but I really liked it even the ending I didn't mind yes it did go against the ending of toy story 3 a little but overall I really enjoyed it and the franchise overall. Though pixar isn't where it used to be since 2020 pixar has been on abit of a dip with only a few shining films here and there and there most recent films Elio and hoppers have both been alright not great or bad just fine but unlike other people I was hyped for toy story and I knew this would another pixar high despite the last toy story related film being lightyear and we'll that didn't go so well. So did the film live up to my excitement...yes absolutely yes this reminds me of the old pixar days and I was laughing,feeling emotional and overall just had a amazing time with the film. The positives Just to get it out the way we've had 30 years of them now so we all know the cast is amazing with Tom hanks and Tim Allen being the stars and while you can definitely tell the recasted roles like slinky or mr potato head the cast is still great overall with the dynamics,chemistry and line delivery. Also the characters are great and yes if you've heard it its true woody and buzz are side characters here which for buzz isn't that much of a shock but for woody it is a little though we still get alot of buzz and woody and their just great here. I'll admit woody doesn't really get any development or anything like that but he's still here and hillarious and then buzz he was really good here in the last film I don't really know what they were doing with him but this is definitely a step up and the best he's been since 3 but also as a long time fan of this franchise the fact that buzz's entire story in this film was him proposing to Jessie after nearly 20 years of them hinting they were a item they finally leaned into and they kiss abd get married and as a long time fan it just put a huge smile on my face. If you've heard Jessie was the lead of this film you heard correct as she is the lead of the film which unlike everyone else I kind of expected this would happen at some point as she's always been like the 3rd most important toy out of all of them she's always been right behind woody and buzz and I always though there'd come a day when she'd step into the spotlight and I'll even admit I was concerned how'd that go because woody has always been the lead so you remove him will the film feel the same? I cannot tell you how much this film benefits from Jessie being the lead because they tie Jessie's fear of being abonded and threw away again and also tie her return to her former owners house into the films story and tech vs toys so well and the story benefits so much and the emotinial beats benefit so so much too from her being lead but she's also just so fun and funny that if she was the lead in the next one I wouldn't mind it. Then we have the new toys who are all great I'd say the standout was conan O'brien as smarty pants i don't like toilet humour all that much but he was hillarious in here all be it not as much as everyone else is saying but he was still great and funny. Then the "villian" of the film lilypad now I put quotations around villian because she's not that bad really yes she's portrayed as the villian but she doesn't reach like lotso or sid level of evil she's just messes up a few times because I think we were all fearing that the film would handle tech vs toys in a very cliché way where techs bad and we should give our kids toys instead but instead thr film handles it so well like lilypad is the same as the toys she just wants the best for Bonnie and yes she'll go against the toys to do that but when she realises she messes up she doesn't blame the toys she blames herself and realises her mistakes and decides to work with the toys and her development throughout the film from "villian" to another friend of the toys was really good. The film also handles tech vs toys really well likr that line from woody where he says toy are for play and tech is for everything is so true and I really like how they treat tech in a kind of horror film way where as soon as Bonnie turns on lily pad its like she becomes hypnotised by the tech and then they don't just say tech bad toys good instead they say tech can be good but we need to use it for good and instead of saying tech is bad they say its instead some of the people that use it and the film overall has such good messaging on if tech is good for kids that make I feel so relevant but also they handle it in such a not cliché way that was great. Also Bonnie in this film unlike 4 she's a actual important character with development like there is so many times in this film where they do stuff with Bonnie that broke my heart like 10 minutes in Bonnie says to her parents why does noone want to be my friend and then later on she starts being cyberbullied by these kids on lilypad and there's so many more scenes with Bonnie that benefitted her character so much but also hit me on a emotionial and personal level where I was willing to fight for this kid plus I liked blaze too she was a good addition in here. The emotionial beats in here were so good and so emotional(obviously)and this is probably the most emotional film I've watched since project hail mary or hamnet but overall there are so many scenes that almost broke my heart like when Bonnie denies taking Jessie from Blaze or when Jessie starts becoming depressed or probably I think one of my favourite scenes from maybe the entire franchise now is when Jessie finds a box from her old owner i think she's called Emily idk where she opens a card and finds out Emily has a kid who she named Jessie after her favourite toy like I almost cried that was so emotional and such a good way to put closure on Jessie feeling left by Emily that almost broke my heart. While I still think 4 has the best animation and lighting the animation here is still just gorgeous and aswell I loved the water colour animation when in Bonnie's imagination that was just a really nice touch but also its nice to see pixar experiment with their animation. I also think the 4 different stories this film has all come together really well by the end. I think if you were a long time fan of this franchise like me there are some many callbacks to the previous film like I'm pretty sure they play one if the many depressing scores from toy story 3 and then they callback zurg being buzz's dad many times with the newer buzz's plus when the newer buzz's learn to fly and take buzz and woody buzz and woody say this flying with style i don't think i need to explain the reference but this film was hitting my nostalgia again and again. I was also happy to see that this films ending was much more chill not a big twist franchise ending like toy story 3 and 4 had this one was just more chilled and more like a end to the episode then a franchise ending. The negatives I think this film is messiest of the franchise because you've got Bonnie's story,Jessie's story,buzz and woody's story and then all the other buzz's story too and we keep cutting back between all of them and especially in act 1 it feels a little messy. review: I watched Mark Kermodes review prior to viewing this, and I was a little disappointed that he didn't enjoy it. Saying it was a thrown together mess essentially, with little sentiment. However, I'm glad to report, my 6yr old and I enjoyed it. It's not without criticism. I did find the pace slow at times, the logistics of the narrative sometimes made you feel a little lost. Although, the later fell in to a positive, as it was a proper adventure with the toys, my generation, have grown up with. Now a parent, that is currently going through and seeing at first hand, the demise of imaginary play and toys, it was enlightening and disheartening hand in hand. My first born was eager to get the new toy car or figure from his favourite show. I'd even join in playing out stories with him. Onwards 10yrs, my daughter wants robux or a new game on her 'lily' pad. I thought the other older toys did get pushed out a little throughout the film, moving towards introducing more new faces/voices aka the devices, but I suppose that was required for a fresh story and move away from what may have felt stale otherwise. After just one viewing, I can safely say I'd watch it again, which is more than i did with TS4. Which is the one I did find that lacked any feeling that the previous instalments had. Go watch it, enjoy it.

review: Woody, Buzz, Jessie and the rest of the gang's jobs are challenged when they're introduced to electronics, a new threat to playtime. I grew up watching these movies and watched them tens of times, and I still remember when my Woody and Buzz plushies were my absolute favorite toys. That personal connection is exactly why the plot of this new film hit so close to home, as it introduces a brilliant idea where kids just do not play with physical toys anymore because they are completely glued to a new tablet. The execution of this concept is excellent, beautifully linking old-school nostalgia with the reality of the digital age. Just like the other parts of the franchise, it is an incredibly emotional ride that might make some tear up, balancing those sadder moments with really good character development and major arcs that breathe fresh life into the gang. The film is also incredibly funny and stands out for its very smart wordplay and clever humor that appeals to both kids and older fans. It captures the exact wit and heart that made the original films so special in the first place. Watching how Woody, Buzz, and the rest of the crew navigate a world dominated by screens is both hilarious and surprisingly moving. It is a fantastic addition to the series that proves these characters still have plenty of great stories left to tell. Score: 8/10.

review: Somehow, Toy Story 5 is dull then a stick of butter. Personally, it's pretty clear the Toy Story franchise is running on air, because despite it's colorful animation and some concepts that I did like, the emotional engagement and connection is pretty much nowhere. The concepts about cyberbullying, technology and changes are pretty good, as the movie does bring out some good messages and concepts about modern toys and connections with people. Alongside the animation colors are beautiful and some great backgrounds, and the sound designs too. Some of the new toy model designs and structures are pretty good and creative. The writing, sadly, it's not great. I'm not the ones who complain about Toy Story should have ended at 3, but just like the 4th one, the development of the characters, emotional connections and depth doesn't feel powerful, and no longer feels interesting. The character of Jessie does offer some new insightful development which I did like, but many of the other characters have little to no chemistry, developments, and felt much like filler. As if the movie is cramming too many characters at once, which ends up being forgettable, and come off annoying. The voice performances are surprisingly a mix of good and bad. There were some performances that are good, and some being really off-putting. The musical score is uninteresting, the direction is bland, and somehow, it's pretty boring. Everything about the experience felt shallow and dull, and it's just not working anymore. Overall, I'm sure the kids will like this but this is going to be one where I will forget pretty soon.

review: I did laugh during the movie, and it was beautifully presented, but not long after, I felt disappointed and increasingly so. Let me list the reasons: * The concept of the movie has been sadly lost. The original movies (1 & 2) were about the toys. Who the child was wasn't important. It was about loyality, dealing with change, finding purpose, the consequences of deception, and loyality. * Woody & gang recede into almost background characters. The first movie centred around Woody, Buzz, Rex, Hamm, Slinky Dog, Mr & Mrs Potato Head. Then Jessie & Bullseye were a delightful addition. This movie is about Jessie, an ipad-like device, her 'kid', and an additional 3 electronic characters are introduced. Woody & Buzz are supporting characters and the rest of the gang are almost entirely removed from the movie. * the movie is about the strength of girls. There is nothing wrong with that, except that it does it at the expense of males. Jessie has become the sheriff. Buzz is weakened to the point that he resembles nothing of his original character. Bo is domineering to the point of Woody appearing weak. Even in the child's play, boys are in 'female roles', dressed like girls. I am not convinced that females need to exude masculinity to be powerful, and that males must show subordination in modern society. * Pixar isn't brave enough to put technology in its place, and I find this very, very sad. A childhood can be devoid of technology and that is a wonderful thing. * every parent in the film is both irresponsible and lacking. Whilst it is sadly true, I don't think Pixar have a right to do that in a child film. Given all that, I'm disappointed.

review: Toy Story 5 is a flawed but great Pixar film! Personally, I liked it more than 4, but not by a huge margin. review: The Toy Story franchise has been incredibly special to me ever since I was a child and the original film first grazed my eyes. I loved each sequel as they were released and have continued to appreciate them as I've grown older. In my opinion, nothing will ever quite match the magic and greatness of the first three films, but I still thoroughly enjoyed Toy Story 4. Now that Toy Story 5 has arrived, I can confidently say that I enjoyed it just as much as the fourth instalment. It's a beautifully crafted animated film that, while it doesn't quite reach the heights of the original trilogy, still stands as one of my favourite movies of 2026 so far. The story wastes no time getting to the heart of its message. Technology has become an unavoidable part of everyday life, and children are being introduced to it at younger and younger ages. Bonnie, who has now had these toys for quite some time, finds herself being bullied for preferring toys over technology. When her parents eventually give in and buy her a tablet called Lilypad, her toys-and much of the world around her-begin to fade into the background. At its core, Toy Story 5 explores the idea that technology can be a wonderful tool when used responsibly, but can also lead to darker and more troubling consequences when it isn't. Without spoiling anything, I thought the film handled this message exceptionally well. Several moments genuinely got to me emotionally, and the heartfelt scenes were executed with remarkable care and sincerity. As for the toys themselves, Woody and Buzz take on more of a supporting role this time around, while many of the familiar supporting characters from the earlier films are barely featured. This is very much Jessie's story, and the film revisits her past in a way that feels meaningful rather than nostalgic for nostalgia's sake. It brought back memories without ever feeling cheap or forced. Even though key chapters of her life have already been explored, I was surprised by how much more there was to discover about her character. By the end of the film, Jessie had become one of my favourite characters in the entire franchise. The life lessons woven throughout her journey made me smile, tear up, and reflect in all the right ways. I also had a great time with the subplot involving a group of shipwrecked high-tech Buzz Lightyears. It ended up being far more entertaining and meaningful than I initially expected. Toy Story 5 is a special film that both children and adults can connect with. It never beats the audience over the head with its message about technology, yet it ventures into darker territory than I anticipated, which I give it a lot of credit for. There weren't many family films willing to tackle themes like this when I was growing up. Overall, I think this is a fantastic addition to the Toy Story franchise. Was it necessary? Probably not. But I'm tired of hearing people say the series should have ended with Toy Story 3. Yes, that film provided a perfect conclusion, but Toy Story 2, 3, 4, and now 5 all technically didn't need to exist either-and I personally think every one of them has justified its place in the series. I'm more than happy to keep following these characters wherever they go next. For me, this franchise has never missed a beat, and Toy Story 5 is yet another wonderful chapter in its story.

review: So far, It was good! So far, It was good!!! That said, the storyline felt kind of repetitive. We've already seen the consequences of kids growing up and moving on from their toys with Andy, so it didn't feel particularly fresh. I was hoping for a story that would take the characters in a completely new direction or explore something we hadn't seen before. Instead, it felt like it was revisiting familiar themes, just with different circumstances. Most of my interest came from the nostalgia factor rather than the plot itself. Seeing these characters again after so many years brought back a lot of memories from my childhood. There were several moments that made me smile simply because they reminded me of the older movies. Without that emotional connection, I'm not sure I would have enjoyed it nearly as much. To be honest, I didn't think the story was that strong, and I also didn't feel the same chemistry between the toys that made the previous movies so special. In the older films, the interactions between the characters felt natural and memorable. Here, it seemed like they spent less time together, which made the group dynamic feel weaker and less engaging. It also felt like some characters were pushed into the background while Jessie got a much bigger role. I don't mind Jessie at all-I actually like her character-but I would have preferred a more balanced focus. For example, I don't even remember Mr. Potato Head saying a single word, which honestly made me a bit sad. Characters like him have always added so much humor and personality to the series. Still, despite all that, I think the movie was absolutely worth watching. The animation was beautiful, the nostalgic moments landed well, and I never felt bored. Even though I have quite a few criticisms, I still had a good time watching it and I'm glad I gave it a chance. Hope you will enjoy as well.

review: The very existence of Toy Story 5 begs the very legitimate question of whether Pixar's iconic series is pushing its luck. After all, Buzz, Woody and the gang already had a perfect ending in the final moments of Toy Story 3, as Andy went off to college and passed his playthings on to his neighbor Bonnie. It seemed a fool's errand to return, and yet Toy Story 4 provided a charming epilogue that opened new adventures for Woody outside the toybox. For a series that often served as a metaphor for parenting, it was a reminder that life experiences don't have to end when the nest is empty. To come back might cheapen two perfectly good endings. But I've learned not to doubt the Toy Story movies. So when it was announced that a new adventure with Buzz, Woody and the gang was on the way, I withheld judgment. Yes, Disney is well-known for its endless cash grabs and brand deposits that wring all the juice out of their stories and leaving audiences to choke on the rinds. But Toy Story has somehow always evaded these pitfalls. And, well, let's just get this out of the way: Toy Story 5 continues the trend. It's an imaginative return to these characters that finds new angles from which to explore its franchise-long themes of play, the fear of obsolescence and the power of friendship. If it's not the series' best, it still maintains the charm, creativity and heart that have powered it for 31 years. Set long enough after the events of Toy Story 4 that Woody has made a life for himself in the wild but not so long that Bonnie has grown up too much, the new story finds the playthings encountering a new threat - tech. Bonnie's an imaginative kid who still loves her toys. But times have changed, and other 8-year-olds spend their days connected to a device called Lilypad that allows them to chat without leaving the couch. When Bonnie's parents buy her a Lilypad (voiced by Greta Lee) to help her make friends, the toys begin to wonder whether they'll be destined for the garage for good. Things don't bode well when Bonnie's friends make fun of her for showing up to a sleepover with her toys instead of her screen. Acknowledging that Woody has already received his ending, the story puts Joan Cusack's Jessie at the center and follows her attempts to ensure that Bonnie makes friends without succumbing to the lures of tech. In the process, she finds her way back to the home formerly occupied by her original owner and must confront her longtime fears of abandonment and uselessness. Cusack is phenomenal. Jessie is the one toy who seems to have been most affected by losing her child decades earlier, and by centering her, the story brings her to a place of healing. I guess it's a slight spoiler for something that doesn't happen, but I was really worried the film would find a way to bring back Jessie's original owner, Emily, and undercut the power of Toy Story 2's most powerful moment. Instead, the film finds another, more subtle way to give Jessie closure in a moment that moved me to tears while still keeping the series' theme that kids might outgrow their toys but they'll never forget them. Don't worry; "When Somebody Loved Me" won't lose its power. Most Toy Story movies keep the kids at the periphery and use childhood to explore existential questions of usefulness, being forgotten and growing older. Toy Story 5's toys-vs-tech story keeps Bonnie more integrated into its plot and its story focuses more directly on the challenges of raising a kid in the screen age. Except, of course, the film is wise enough to know that kids aren't the only ones drawn to tech - nearly every person, child or adult, in the film is seen constantly staring at a laptop, smartphone or other handheld device at one point or another. And you probably won't be surprised to learn that a studio like Disney - which has a lot to gain from keeping kids glued to streaming services and collecting their parents' data through apps and social media - doesn't take too hard a line on tech, eventually finding a way to allow that a balance of screens and real-life play is probably best and most realistic. That's fine; I'm sure my curmudgeonly Luddite self is just prone to complaining. And it's really hard to dislike the tech in this film, particularly when it's voiced by Greta Lee. Director Andrew Stanton - who's been involved with the script for every Toy Story film and directed two of Pixar's best films, WALL-E and Finding Nemo1 - continues to make these films a celebration of play. The moments where Bonnie and her new pal, Blaze, let their imaginations run wild with the toys are captured in fun watercolor, and some of the film's biggest laughs are the moments in which the kids' take traditional play tropes - like a wedding or a ball - and mix in some espionage, action or mystery. This is the third Toy Story film to feature Bonnie, and I like that she's developing into a character, something not even Andy really attained. She's funny and shy, and the film lets her be weird. In one of its smartest choices, the film realizes that Bonnie doesn't just need friends to be with - she needs friends to play with, who match her unbound creativity. Parents who have watched their children try to connect with others and then find the best bud who matches their weird will likely find the final moments exteremely satisfying. Toy Story 5 is possibly the funniest movie in the series. No small part of this is due to the addition of Conan O' Brien as a potty-training device ("I'm really good at pushing!"); Conan's energy and strangeness are a constant delight. The film finds new, weird toys to keep at its edges, such as Pizza With Sunglasses and a tribe of toys who sit in a derelict playhouse, religiously awaiting their young owner's return. Forky is back - and married! - and still saying the wrong thing at the wrong moments. There's a tribe of shipwrecked Buzz Lightyear toys traipsing through the woods that, at first, felt like an attempt to provide Toy Story with its own Minion-like characters, but quickly becomes a source of wonderful physical comedy that also ties organically into the plot. And pushing Buzz and Woody ever so slightly into supporting roles allows Tom Hanks and Tim Allen the chance to do some buddy comedy and cement the characters' friendship. I understand that these are CGI renderings of plastic toys, but I still found it touching when Buzz asked Woody to be best man at his wedding2. Is Toy Story 5 as good as the rest? I guess, if pressed, I'd put it right above Toy Story 4 - a movie I like quite a bit - but under the original trilogy. But it doesn't matter. What matters is that I had a smile on my face the entire time. Over the course of three decades, these characters have become old friends I'm happy to revisit, and I'm glad there are still adventures and laughs to be had in that toybox. As long as they keep making them, they'll have a friend in me. But wait!! Don't take my word for it! I was joined at my Toy Story 5 screening by my 10-year-old daughter, Cece, who informed me on the way over that during her last week at school, she did a "teach the teacher" session. I asked her what she taught her teacher and I was overjoyed when she said "how to review movies." And so, I asked her if she'd like to try her hand at this, and gave her her first assignment. So, welcome to the first edition of... Cece Sees: Toy Story 53 By Cece Williams Hello, I'm so excited to talk about the new Toy Story 5 today. And before we buzz into action4, I want you to hear why I'm writing this review! If some of you don't already know, I'm Chris' daughter, Cece. And I have loved movies ever since I met my Dad and I'm so happy that I have the privilege to write my opinion about the new movie, Toy Story 5, with you! No without a moment's ado, let's jump right into action! The beginning of the movie was really good and very sweet and thoughtful, and they go straight to Bonnie playing with her toys! This moment is really funny, yet cute (5 out of 5). This moment also shows how shy Bonnie really is to make friends as she watches kids play. This moment also introduces tech, when bonny gets a new thing called Lillypad. And moment after moment, we finally get all these problems winded up together and finally solved. This move has been really great, and there are some parts I didn't like. But it's a very thoughtful movie and I choked up. Totally recommend.

review_title: the best offering by far this summer
review: I went to this thinking that this particular franchise of the Disney/Pixar collaborations might be starting to run out of steam. But, I'm glad to admit.. I was wrong. For starters, the opening credits have a humorous homage to Tom Hanks' live-action classic "Castaway." Then, there's the refreshing focus on Jessie the tomboyish cowgirl toy (once again voiced by Joan Cusack). But, of course, the main focus is on preadolescent children becoming too addicted to their interactive games. Plus, the more widespread threat of cyber-bullying. In the midst of helping young Bonnie (now a first-grader) deal with all that, Jessie finally learns what happened to her original owner, Emily. Which made me wonder: could she have married Andy? All in all, a nice family film for this summer. Certainly better than "Supergirl" and "The Masters of the Universe" put together! review_title: a worthy addition to the toy story franchise
review: As a lifelong Toy Story fan, with Toy Story 2 still being my favorite, I was incredibly excited for Toy Story 5. I watched it on opening day knowing very little about the plot beyond the idea that it would explore toys versus technology, and overall I had a good time with it. One of the movie's biggest strengths is its concept. The conflict between traditional toys and modern technology feels relevant and fresh, especially for a franchise that has always explored what it means to be a toy in changing times. Pixar continues to do what Pixar does best: create a visually beautiful, entertaining story filled with humor, heart, and clever writing. The audience in my theater laughed throughout the movie, and many of the jokes landed perfectly. I also really enjoyed the new characters, especially Smarty Pants, who quickly became one of my favorites. He is funny, memorable, and added a lot of charm to the story. I appreciated that Jessie received a larger role as well, since she has always been one of the franchise's strongest characters. That said, some of my issues with the movie stem from that very decision. While I like Jessie, it sometimes felt as though the film focused too heavily on her at the expense of other beloved characters. Rex, Hamm, Slinky Dog, and Mr. Potato Head all felt underused. I understand that not every character can be in the spotlight, but I still found myself wishing they had more meaningful moments. My biggest criticism, however, is the pacing of the opening act. Bonnie's loneliness and her struggles making friends are introduced very quickly, and I never felt the film gave enough time to develop that situation. I would have liked to see more of Bonnie's life before the arrival of Lilypad-perhaps scenes at school showing her difficulties firsthand. Instead, the movie moves so quickly from introducing her problem to presenting a solution that the emotional impact feels somewhat rushed. Similarly, I found the storyline involving the group of Buzz Lightyears confusing and, at times, unnecessary. It occupies a significant portion of the film, and I couldn't help feeling that the time spent there could have been used to better develop Bonnie's story or give more attention to the supporting cast. One thing I absolutely loved was Woody's return. For me, Toy Story simply doesn't feel complete without him. Seeing him re-enter Bonnie's room was one of the most satisfying moments in the movie, and his presence immediately made everything feel more familiar and emotionally grounded. There were also a few plot points that left me confused, particularly regarding Jessie's former home and how that storyline connected to the present events. Perhaps I missed something, but it felt less clear than it should have been. Overall, Toy Story 5 is a funny, heartfelt, and enjoyable addition to the franchise. While I don't think it reaches the heights of Toy Story 2 or Toy Story 3, it still captures much of the charm that has made these films so beloved. I just wish some of its strongest ideas had been given a little more room to breathe. Rating: 8/10.

review: Toy Story 5 is the rare sequel that does not only continue a beloved story - it heals parts of it. For years, the ending of Toy Story 4 felt bittersweet. Beautiful, yes, but undeniably sad. This movie changes that completely. The reveal that the gang always had a way to talk to Woody through the walkie-talkies - and that he could return to Bonnie's anytime - instantly reframes everything. What once felt like a permanent goodbye now feels like a hopeful branching path. Woody didn't lose his family; he simply expanded it. And then there's Jessie. Her emotional conversation with Woody about Emily - building on the heartbreaking story from TS2 - is something I never knew I needed. It adds depth, closure, and a sense of growth that feels so earned. Jessie finally gets the spotlight she deserves, and the movie treats her history with real care. The music? Swift's performance is absolutely bravo. Her voice fits the tone of the film perfectly, adding warmth and magic without overshadowing the story. It's one of those choices that sounds surprising on paper but feels completely right in the moment. The themes about toys vs. Electronics are handled with heart, humor, and a surprising amount of nuance. Pixar once again proves they understand childhood better than anyone. Overall, Toy Story 5 is touching, funny, beautifully animated, and full of emotional payoffs that make the entire franchise feel more complete. It honors the past while giving the characters a future that feels bright and connected. A perfect 10/10. This movie reminded me why I fell in love with Toy Story in the first place.

review: Toy Story 5 (2026) is the 5th entry in the Toy Story franchise and the 31st movie from Pixar Animation Studios written and directed by Andrew Stanton which follows Jessie, Woody and Buzz Lightyear as they and the other toys deal with the presence of Lilypad, a tablet and the new favorite plaything of Bonnie. I am a massive fan of Pixar Animation Studios and I've enjoyed almost everything they've put out especially when it comes to the Toy Story franchise, but I will admit that I was very skeptical about this movie because it looked like a cash grab by Disney, but that was also the case with Toy Story 4 (2019) and I enjoyed that movie, so I went into this sequel with a open mind and I have to say this is another excellent entry in the franchise. Positives for Toy Story 5 (2026): The movie does an excellent job at continuing the story of our favorite toys as they have to deal with a tablet that is taking Bonnie away from them and it works very effectively. This is something that has become apparent with a lot of kids today as some of them are no longer playing with toys and would rather play with electronics, so it makes sense why Pixar would make this movie. The voice cast is just as fantastic with their voice performances as our favorite toys just like in the previous entries. I also liked having Jesse as the main focus and we get to explore her abandonment issues from the second movie, so you do feel for her and you don't want to see that happen again. The movie also does a good job with its explanation as to why Woody is back with the gang and that was the main thing everyone was skeptical about with this movie and they pulled it off. The banter between Woody and Buzz is just as good as it has always been in the franchise. You do get a nice arc for Buzz that was hinted at in the previous movies and I liked that for him. The new characters are a lot of fun here especially some of the new toys and they play an important part in the story. The animation still looks spectacular which is always going to be the case with anything made by Pixar Animation Studios. You still get the great use of comedy, action and emotion with one scene that hit me in the feels. And finally, the movie does a phenomenal job at closing the story perfectly and it feels like a complete story for everyone to where if this is the final adventure with our favorite toys, then I am very satisfied with it. Mixed for Toy Story 5 (2026): There is an arc given to Bonnie that I thought was good for her, but it gets handled in a way that will make Toy Story fans a little upset and there were times where I was disappointed with the decisions made by Bonnie, but I am will to forgive it because you get a nice payoff for her at the end. Negatives for Toy Story 5 (2026): There is one subplot that was shoehorned into the story for comedic reasons and plot convience and it was pretty annoying. Overall, Toy Story 5 (2026) is another spectacular adventure with our favorite toys that continues the strong streak for the Toy Story franchise and Pixar Animation Studios. So if you're a longtime fan of Toy Story and Pixar Animation Studios, then I would definitely recommend you go out with your friends and family to see this movie in theaters and then add it to your collection when it comes out on DVD.

review: Going into this film I didn't know what to really expect but I found this to be a solid and decent entry into this franchise! I mainly think this film does an excellent job at making Jessie our main character and giving her a lot of depth and character growth with this film compared to some of the other films and she finally gets a much deserved chance to shine! I also really appreciate how the film touches on a major thing now days with technology and how it's really taking kids out of the free world and making them feel confined to this technology world instead of the real world and the things kids should still be doing! I also appreciate a lot of the story and there's so many emotional and heartfelt moments throughout the film and I really enjoyed how the character explored a lot of these emotional elements to the film. I also appreciate the connection between Woody and Buzz and they still have such a strong character bond and I really appreciate how the film makes them elevate Jessie's character and they definitely take a backseat in this film but it works for me and a lot of the new characters are great like Lilypad, Smarty Pants and they definitely have a lot of strong and great moments in this film and I enjoyed the growth that Lilypad ends up having near the end of the film. The animation is also great like usual and it looks really great throughout the film and there's some great scores in the movie as well. Some of my complaints about this one is a lot of the other toys get completely thrown to the side like Rex, Slinky, Mr Potato Head and a lot of the other toys and I think these films are at their best when all of our characters are all together and not thrown to the side to feel like a cheap way to market things like merch for this film. I also don't like this weird subplot that ruins a lot of the momentum at times for me with all of these buzz light years and I just found this whole B Plot to takeaway from key moments happening in our main story. I feel like the pacing was also quite slow and I felt like we didn't really get a whole lot of adventures and the movie feels slow at times as well.

review_title: 34 year old father to a 5 year old
review: I am a 34 year old father to a 5 year old. I mention this as it is important for context. I grew up with Toy Story, I had the VHS tapes, then DVDs, then a Disney+ subscription. As my daughter came into the world, I naturally introduced her to the world of Disney and of course, Toy Story. Woody and Buzz have been a staple of my life: the connection between 2 characters, facing and fighting evil, together, where friendship always wins. The first 4 films are still relevant, emotional, and important in modern day society, and the 5th instalment is not a cash grab sequel, it is an extension of the story and aligns with today's challenges. Yes, there is agenda to it and Disney have not hidden that. But the agenda is right in my opinion. Technology has taken over our lives, and whilst it has its benefits, of course it does, but it does limit and take away some of the innocence and magic that can come from traditional and analog play time and story telling. Toy Story 5 had me crying from the opening credits and I'm not afraid to say. The characters, the music, the editing, the filming, the pace, the story line, the message, and the delivery was just perfect for me. It delivered exactly the message that I wish to pass on to my children. There is magic out there, don't be afraid to be yourself, and love will always conquer. It may not mean anything to a casual viewer, but if you are in the age bracket I am in, with children the age that I have, this is a triumph and you will not be disappointed. I created an IMDB account purely to deliver this review after reading some of the initial reviews which left me rather confused and rather angry. 10/10 for me, and would highly recommend. Just go see it, lose yourself in the magic, forget about life for a couple hours and remember what it is like to be a kid, because you blink and it's over. To infinity and beyond x.

review_title: low expectations and came out surprised
review: Toy Story 5 legitimately had a compelling theme that was a great addition to the franchise. I loved that the story focused on Jessie, a character that didn't get sunshine since the 2nd movie. If this is the ending to the Toy Story saga then I'm glad it ended with a wonderful ending like this. I can tell that this movie was made for the love of story telling despite Disney's initial intention to commercialize nostalgia, instead, the writers of this movie gave it a way to center the ideas of the last stage of grief for one of its themes, acceptance. At the end of the movie, Jessie excepts her place as a toy and how she will bring Bonnie happiness for the time she has left before she grows up, because she knows that she will always have a place in Bonnie's heart just like Andy and Emily. That said, there are also bits and pieces of the film that made me audibly chuckle, it had a lot of charm. Normally I'm not all for introducing new characters to an already huge cast, but these new additions, I feel, had an interesting add on to the franchise and had a certain charm to them I can't exactly describe but was entertained by. Timing is everything in comedy and I deal they hit the nail on the head each time. Though I do wish that we'd spend a bit more time with the original cast, but with the limited time they had I'm glad to see them in character. When the movie was looking back at past scenes in the early movies, like Jessie's flashback, I feel like it added on to a way where you can see it as a nice memory to let go of instead of trying to refurbish it for money. I can tell a lot of heart in soul was put into the production and I admire it.

review_title: still great best not to milk it
review: Toy Story 5 does a surprisingly good job of tackling the current generation of kids. One thing I appreciated was how Bonnie finally gets a meaningful character arc, emphasizing that every child is different. Not every kid is an "iPad kid," and the film understands that growing up happens in different ways for different people. At its core, the movie carries a strong message about childhood and change. Kids grow up, and the people who care about them-whether parents, friends, or in this case toys-don't get to decide when or how that happens. The best they can do is be there for them and cherish the memories they've helped create. It's a simple but effective moral that fits well within the series' themes. Making Jessie the main character was a great choice, and I had no issues with the spotlight shifting to her. The Buzz Lightyear scenes were also some of my favorites, introducing a fresh perspective on how toys can be played with in a changing world. I also think the ending works better than Toy Story 4's ending, which is something I didn't expect going in. Another pleasant surprise was Lilypad. The film doesn't villainize her despite her role seemingly conflicting with that of traditional toys. Instead, it recognizes that she's ultimately serving the same purpose: helping children. That nuance made the conflict more interesting than a simple good-versus-bad setup. That said, the plot is undeniably scattered. It feels divided across multiple storylines and lacks a strong linear progression, though to the film's credit, the different threads do connect by the end. My bigger issue is that, much like *Toy Story 4*, it lacks a truly memorable climax. The emotional highs never quite reach the level of the earlier films, and the movie leans a little too heavily on nostalgia to compensate. Even with those flaws, I enjoyed it more than I expected. I just can't shake the feeling that this is a sequel that didn't really need to exist in the first place.

review_title: a heartfelt relevant chapter that lets jessie shine
review: Going into Toy Story 5, it was hard not to wonder if another entry was truly necessary, but Pixar delivers a surprisingly thoughtful and timely story that fully justifies its existence. The decision to put Jessie at the center of the narrative is the film's single best choice. Joan Cusack gives a fantastic emotional performance as Jessie navigates finding purpose and connection in an increasingly screen-obsessed world. The central conflict-traditional toys facing off against modern technology and smart devices-feels remarkably relevant to parents and kids today without ever feeling overly preachy. While Woody and Buzz take more of a supporting back seat this time around, their presence still adds that classic nostalgia and heart we've loved for decades. The animation and scale are gorgeous, the humor lands well, and the new characters bring plenty of charm. It may not surpass the original trilogy, but it's a sweet, grounded, and emotional reflection on childhood, imagination, and staying connected in the digital age. A solid, touching addition to the franchise!

review_title: a solid entry to the toy story library
review: Minor Spoilers Below - Toy Story 5 is a bit of an understated chapter in the Toy Story saga, but all in all it's a thoroughly entertaining movie that sticks the ending. First the bad. What I didn't like about Toy Story 5: * The first half of the movie feels aimless-- both with respect to the plot and the thematic flow. You can't really quite tell where the movie is going. * I didn't care for how lightly the movie treats geographic separation. The characters (which are tiny toys) can now freely traverse different houses and even neighborhoods with the shallowest bit of plot chicanery. This actually undermines the resonance of most of the preceding TS movies. * There isn't really any animation showcase from Pixar in TS5. They chose an interesting animation style to depict the imaginative play; it's definitely more charming and cute than eye blowing. Pixar is in a tough place here. There is so much amazing and creative animation coming out from every corner of the world. Pixar knows they can no longer blow anyone away with visual wizardly. What I liked about Toy Story 5: * After quite a bit of meandering, it really nails the end. I think this particularly worked for me because Toy Story 2 has always been a favorite of mine and the close-up treatment of Jessie works fantastic here. * The resolution provides thematic clarity too. It emphasizes a very simple but easily forgotten central tenet: in the end of the day, no matter what kind of toy or what a toy even is, what is important is friendships and relationships. This was a bit cathartic after the "existential dread" introduced by Toy Story 4 (which I absolutely love too). * This was a pretty fun movie. I mean that literally; there were a lot of little chuckle moments and gags. Nothing that will bowl you over but plenty to smile at. All in all, I'd rate this in the top half of the Toy Story toy bin. It is not the best, the funniest, the most moving, the most dazzling. But it's a very solid entry and a must-see for any fan of the series.

The film maturely questions modern children's reliance on making friends online. It reflects on how, even though the digital world makes connecting easier and good people do exist online, nothing replaces the value and safety of cultivating real, in-person friendships. Another major highlight that I thoroughly enjoyed was Jessie's character arc. Furthermore, choosing her as the protagonist was an excellent decision that gave the narrative a much faster and more dynamic pace.

review_title: a movie with a lot to talk about but nothing to say
review: The biggest problem with this film is that ultimately it just doesn't have much to say. It wants to be a clever and nuanced take on tech and how it impacts the development of kids. It wants to talk about the importance of growth and change, which I guess it does somewhat. Unfortunately, it all feels hollow and superficial when you think about it for a couple seconds. I think this is encapsulated by a single moment in the film. The evil iPad uses what is clearly meant to be an ai music tool to make a song and one character says "I have ethical concerns" and that is literally it. They don't engage with the idea any further. The movie feels comfortable bringing up complex ideas but doesn't want to actually engage them because then it would have to actually say something. The movie goes out on a limb with the insanely controversial take that it's good when something is good and bad when it's bad, and I'm not even really exaggerating. That is just, as far as I can tell, the only way the movie could sit on the fence of the issue that they made the whole movie around. There is another scene where Bullseye and a real horse both move in the same way at the same time. I feel like any other toy story movie would've taken this as an opportunity to explore something about the nature of being a toy recreation of a real animal or something, but in this movie they don't do much with it. The whole movie feels like this to me, so many missed opportunities to be more interesting and the result is a kinda surface level experience. This is of course fine for a movie strictly targeted at kids, but Pixar was supposed to be the one that does good movies for the parents, too. Factor in the nostalgia plays in this movie that just don't stand alone and I'd say this movie doesn't seem to fully make sense for young kids or their parents. Stripping all of that away, you end up with an okay adventure movie for kids, but not something that justifies being made when there are already 4 other movies in this franchise. The one exception I will mention is that the scenes where we just follow the Buzz Lightyear Hi-Tech editions feel pretty fresh and clever. If only the rest of the movie was, too.

review: 1. Visual Design and Graphics (Rating: 9/10) The graphics are genuinely fantastic. Eschewing a cold, AI-like or overly sterile smoothness, the film opts for a vibrant, warm, and distinctly nostalgiac texture. I love the fact that Emily named her daughter after Jessie, but the whole movie should've been about this emotional journey. Instead it gets rushed through in one scene. We've already seen Jessie's backstory in Toy Story 2, where they did it in a much more emotional way. So why are we getting those same reheated flashbacks now if we're not adding to that story at all? It's cheap emotional manipulation, not good storytelling. The toys are not scared at getting caught at all. In Toy Story 2, Jessie literally stays under the bed for YEARS so that Emily doesn't suspect that toys are alive. The devices literally send messages and pictures to each other. Bonnie and Blaze don't even notice that their devices are sending messages they're not typing.
