The animation is nothing short of breathtaking, showcasing phenomenal visual detail that highlights just how far the medium has evolved since 1995. The script keeps a lively, never-boring rhythm that seamlessly weaves laugh-out-loud comedy with deeply resonant emotional interactions. It is a gorgeous, visual feast on the big screen that proves there was genuine passion and purpose behind returning to these characters-delivering a gold-standard message that hits adults right where it counts.

review: As a lifelong Pixar fan-and especially a massive Toy Story fan since I was a kid-Toy Story 5 meant a lot to me. It's been a long time since we've had a new entry in the franchise, and after seeing the trailers, I was really hoping this film would recapture some of the magic of the original trilogy. Toy Story 4 was a disappointment for me, so I went into this one cautiously optimistic. The first thing that absolutely blew me away was the animation. Pixar is operating on a completely different level now. At times it felt like they were showing off, and honestly, I wasn't complaining. The water animation, the way sunlight interacted with environments, the animals, and the incredible detail in every background were all stunning. Even the materials on the toys looked unbelievably realistic. Every frame felt packed with detail, and visually this may be the best-looking Toy Story film yet. Story-wise, I thought it was a significant improvement over Toy Story 4. The plot was engaging, and I appreciated the direction they took with it. However, when the credits rolled, I couldn't shake the feeling that I wanted more. The film never quite delivered that emotional punch that Pixar is famous for. Usually, Toy Story movies leave me laughing one moment and tearing up the next, but this time the emotional moments didn't hit as hard as I expected. I could clearly see what Pixar was trying to do by making Jessie more of a central character. The film leans into themes of female empowerment and gives Jessie a chance to step into a leadership role. I actually enjoyed that aspect and can understand why Pixar would want younger girls to have a character like Jessie at the forefront. That being said, I still missed Woody being the heart of the story. For me, Woody has always been the soul of Toy Story, and his reduced role was noticeable. Tim Allen's Buzz Lightyear was, as always, a highlight. He brought plenty of laughs, and some of the funniest moments in the movie involved Buzz. In fact, the comedy might have been my favourite part of the entire film. I found myself laughing out loud far more than I expected, and the jokes landed consistently throughout. One message I absolutely loved was the film's commentary on technology and children's imaginations. The way it explored the impact of iPads and screens on playtime felt incredibly relevant. Without feeling overly preachy, the movie reminded both children and parents of the importance of imagination, creativity, and the connection kids can build with their toys. It's a message that resonated with me, and I genuinely hope it has the same impact on families watching it. Overall, Toy Story 5 is a good movie. I'm not disappointed, and I certainly enjoyed my time with it. It's visually spectacular, genuinely funny, and tells a stronger story than its predecessor. At the same time, I can't help but feel slightly unsatisfied because it feels like it's missing that special ingredient that made the original trilogy so unforgettable. While it may not reach the emotional heights of the classics, it's still a worthy addition to the franchise and one that longtime fans will likely appreciate.

review_title: much more than a fun animated expedition its thoughtful message about screen addiction
review: Wow, what an exciting adventure! Toy Story 5 is much more than a fun animated expedition. Its thoughtful message about screen addiction, combined with its creative visual storytelling, makes it one of the most memorable entries in the franchise. The film follows Jessie (Joan Cusack), Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen), Woody (Tom Hanks), and the rest of Bonnie's (Scarlett Spears) toys as they navigate a world where technology is becoming an increasingly large part of their childhood. When Bonnie begins spending more time with a device called Lilypad (Greta Lee), the toys start to question where they fit into her life. As they confront this new challenge, they embark on an adventure that pushes them out of their comfort zones and forces them to adapt to a changing world. The film's animation is beautiful, and one of the most impressive production elements is the film's use of color. Scenes involving technology often feature cooler, duller tones, while moments focused on play and connection are filled with warmer, more vibrant colors. This contrast is especially noticeable when comparing Bonnie's home to her neighbor's house. The film is also incredibly funny. There always seems to be a joke at exactly the right moment, preventing heavier scenes from feeling overwhelming and keeping the story moving at a fun pace. The humor never feels forced, and many of the funniest moments come from the interactions between Jessie, Buzz Lightyear, Woody, and the other toys. Combined with strong voice performances and engaging pacing, these elements help keep the audience invested from the very beginning until the end. By combining an important message with strong storytelling, humor, and creative visuals, Toy Story 5 proves that, even after five films, this franchise still has something meaningful to say. The film promotes positive social behavior through teamwork, friendship, and empathy. At its core, Toy Story 5 is about finding balance and appreciating the world beyond a screen. The film explores a topic that is especially relevant today in a thoughtful and natural way. Rather than simply criticizing technology, it encourages reflection on how screens can sometimes distract from the experiences, relationships and moments happening right in front of us. Be forewarned that there is some mild action and suspense, but nothing that feels inappropriate for younger viewers Toy Story 5 gets 5 out of 5 stars and I recommend it for ages 5 to 18, plus adults. It releases in cinemas June 19, 2026. By Rhea S., KIDS FIRST!

review: Toy Story 5: I'm 24 years old now, and I had to see the very first screening. I'm a huge fan and a lifelong defender of *Toy Story 4*. For me, this is the best animated franchise ever made and maybe even one of the best franchises overall. Now, onto the review... In my opinion, this film misses the mark. Conceptually, it's a fantastic idea, but the execution just isn't quite there. The message of the film seems to be: buy toys for your children, but technology is okay too-just limit everything so they can coexist. Woody doesn't get any real payoff, so why include him in the movie at all? The story would have worked without him. I've seen some people say that his character arc already got its payoff in the previous films, which only proves my point. The subplot involving the 50 Buzz Lightyears also felt unnecessary to me and didn't really add much value. The film mainly follows Jessie, which I was completely fine with, but part of me hoped she would run into her former owner. There wasn't much new backstory for her-nothing we didn't already know. The ending isn't heartwarming, nor is it emotionally impactful, unlike the previous films, especially *Toy Story 3* and *Toy Story 4*. This is purely a feel-good movie. Don't get me wrong-most Pixar films are feel-good movies, but they're also realistic. For example, at the end of *Toy Story 3*, the toys get a new owner and a new life, but Andy is gone. It almost makes you cry, if you're not already crying. *Toy Story 4* is the same. Woody realizes that his mission is complete and decides to stay behind with Bo Peep. Once again, it almost brings you to tears. This film fails to achieve that. My official rating: the weakest *Toy Story* movie in the franchise. It's time to stop-they've lost their magic. A film with a message, but not one worth telling. **5/10** Screening: June 17, 2:00 PM, Belgium.

review: For this sequel, I got the opportunity to bring my daughter to see. The problem that I ran into was finding a time that worked schedule wise. Of course, I had months where there was nothing to see in the theater, then I had a free ticket to see old cartoons with her and that was the Saturday that this opened. I decided to take her on my birthday to see this as something fun to do together. Now ahead of seeing this, I did see negative reviews. I considered what was being said but came in as blank as I could. What is interesting is that I've told a few people, this feels almost like a remake of Toy Story 2. There are story elements with Jessie (voiced by Joan Cusack) that we learn. That comes back into play here. Her part of the story even takes her to the family living in her old house. There is a little girl, Blaze (voiced by Mykal-Michelle Harris). The major premise here is that due to children having too much screentime, they're no longer playing with toys. Jessie is worried because Bonnie (voiced by Scarlett Spears) is struggling to make friends. Her parents decided to get her a Lilypad (voiced by Greta Lee). She connects with girls from her dance class and thinks that she'll be able to befriend them. Things don't go as planned though as Bonnie still has her imagination. In helping her, there is a miscommunication which brings Woody (voiced by Tom Hanks) back to her house. There's once again a rivalry as Buzz Lightyear (voiced by Tim Allen) has a crush on Jessie and wants to ask her to his wife. They become separated and his question gets put on hold. It will take all the toys, working together to help Bonnie connect with a friend like her. This includes electronic toys, Smarty Pants (Conan O'Brien), Atlas (Craig Robinson) and Snappy (Shelby Rabara). Even Jessie and Lilypad need to be on the same page. Now despite me thinking this is a pointless sequel, which didn't take away from me enjoying this. What is interesting is that Woody takes a major backseat to being a secondary character. The main Buzz does as well. There is a group of newer ones that are more high-tech, that is a recurring story thread. This is truly Jessie needing to come to terms with technology and seeing that she doesn't have to do everything alone. There was a moment with a discovery she made that made me tear up, so credit there. I did want to address the major concept and it is too much screen time. This is something that we grapple with raising Mackenzie and soon, Tripp. It does concern me seeing how angry Mackenzie gets when we shut off the team. We do see her playing with her giant number of stuffed animals. She is developing an imagination. I know for myself, my father played video games and allowed my sister as well as me to watch television. Did we do it too much? Probably, but I never had issues connecting with and making friends. Mackenzie doesn't seem to either. Before moving from the story completely, the idea of children not playing with toys and being addicted to electronics could lead to them growing up faster. There was something else that hit me in the feels with watching Bonnie being bullied for still playing with toys. My fear is that my children will be bullied. I know that it is part of development, but it still makes me sad to think about. I'll then just say that the voice acting here is great once again. Hanks, Allen and Cusack along with the rest of the gang fit right back into this group of toys that Bonnie has. Lee is good as the 'villain'. I do like the character arc there. Jessie gets a good one too as she befriends tech toys that belong to Blaze. Having the likes once again of Tony Hale, Bonnie Hunt, Kristen Schaal, Wallace Shawn, John Ratzenberger, Blake Clark, Annie Potts, Keanu Reeves and Ernie Hudson. Spears, Jay Hernandez, Lori Alan and Harris rounded this out as human characters. Then all that is left would be the filmmaking aspects. Being that this is a computer animated film, it still looks great. Pixar has been able to be groundbreaking and keep what they make looking great. I still prefer classic animation but acknowledge that is the way of the past. They do good things and seeing this in the theater enhances that. It was also a fun experience to see this with my daughter there. The music didn't hold up as well as the original trilogy's did. The sound design was good though. Although initially viewed as a potentially unnecessary sequel, this film proved to be an enjoyable experience that resonated emotionally, particularly through its exploration of screen time, childhood development, and the concern regarding bullying. The production maintains high quality through excellent voice acting from both the returning cast and new additions, complemented by consistently impressive and groundbreaking computer animation. Despite the music failing to hold up against the standards of the original trilogy, the film ultimately succeeds as an engaging, heart-felt story that offers a meaningful shared experience for families. My Rating: 7.5 out of 10.

review: Toy Story 5 proves that there is still life left in Pixar's beloved franchise. While it may not reach the emotional heights of Toy Story 3 or provide the same sense of closure as Toy Story 4, the film delivers a heartfelt, entertaining adventure that successfully reunites audiences with Woody, Buzz, and the gang. The story explores how toys fit into a world increasingly dominated by technology and digital entertainment, giving the franchise a fresh theme while staying true to its core message about friendship, loyalty, and purpose. The returning characters remain as charming as ever, and the film balances humor, action, and emotion in a way that will appeal to both longtime fans and younger viewers. Visually, the animation is stunning, showcasing Pixar's continued mastery of the medium. The action sequences are energetic, the new characters are memorable, and the emotional moments land effectively, even if they feel somewhat familiar compared to previous installments. The biggest challenge facing Toy Story 5 is justifying its existence after the seemingly definitive endings of earlier films. While it doesn't completely overcome that hurdle, it offers enough heart, humor, and adventure to make the journey worthwhile. review: I went into this wanting to love it. Toy Story has been one of my favorite franchises for decades, and I genuinely believed Pixar would have a good reason to revisit these characters. Instead, I left wondering why this movie needed to exist at all. The biggest problem is that it feels like the story is running on nostalgia instead of inspiration. Every emotional beat reminded me of moments the previous movies had already done better. Rather than building naturally on what came before, it felt like the film kept revisiting old themes and expecting the audience to react simply because these are familiar characters. What disappointed me most was how some of the returning characters seemed to lose the growth they earned over the series. Their decisions often felt driven by what the plot needed instead of what made sense for who they've become. A few characters barely have anything meaningful to do, while the new additions never become interesting enough to justify taking up so much screen time. The humor was also surprisingly hit-or-miss. There were a few laughs, but too many jokes relied on repeating the same gag until it stopped being funny. Earlier films balanced comedy with genuine heart. Here, the emotional moments often felt manufactured, as if the movie was trying to recreate the magic instead of earning it. Visually, there's nothing to complain about. The animation is stunning, the lighting is beautiful, and every frame looks like an incredible technical achievement. But amazing visuals can only carry a film so far. A Toy Story movie has always been remembered for its storytelling first, and that's where this one falls short. My biggest frustration is that this sequel actually makes the ending of the previous films feel less meaningful. Those endings worked because they gave the characters satisfying conclusions. Bringing everyone back without a compelling new idea makes those emotional goodbyes feel less special in hindsight. This isn't the worst animated movie I've ever seen, but it's easily the most disappointing because of what it represents. Instead of a heartfelt continuation, it feels like a sequel made because the brand is popular rather than because there was a story worth telling. I'll happily rewatch the earlier Toy Story films for years to come. Unfortunately, this one won't be joining that rotation. Sometimes the hardest lesson is knowing when a story has already ended, and I wish Pixar had remembered that before making this movie.

review: One of the biggest missed opportunity for me was Woody's ending. The film spends time establishing that Buzz has gradually stepped into a role very similar to the one Woody once held. As Jessie's deputy, he's no longer simply the enthusiastic Space Ranger from earlier films, but someone the other toys rely on and look to for guidance. Throughout the film there's a subtle dynamic between Woody and Buzz, with Buzz proving he's capable while Woody still instinctively wants to take charge. I would have loved a final moment where Bo Peep says, "Woody, you coming?" and Woody pauses at the window, watching the room one last time as Buzz and Jessie lead the toys. Not because Woody is being replaced. Because he realises he doesn't need to be there anymore. It's the same emotional territory as the ending of Toy Story 3. A moment of quiet acceptance where Woody looks on and realises: "They're going to be okay." Woody doesn't leave because he has to. He leaves because he finally knows they're alright without him. For me, that would have been the perfect final beat to their relationship. Not a sad ending, but a proud one. A subtle passing of the torch from Woody to Buzz that acknowledges just how far both characters have come since the first film. I also felt the Jessie and Emily storyline deserved a little more room to breathe. When Jessie discovers the memory box and learns that Emily named her daughter Jessie, it's a huge emotional revelation, but the moment passes very quickly. A short montage showing Emily growing up, starting a family, and carrying those memories with her would have made the scene even more powerful. The idea that Emily never forgot Jessie is one thing, but the idea that she carried her with her throughout her life is something much deeper. Taylor Swift's song is featured during the end credits, but I couldn't help feeling that this was the moment it was made for. Used alongside a montage of Emily's life, it could have allowed the audience to truly sit with the emotion of the revelation and turned an already touching scene into one of the most memorable moments in the entire franchise. My final thought relates to the toys versus technology theme. The film begins by positioning technology as a major challenge for traditional toys, but by the end the resolution focuses more on friendship than the relationship between toys and technology. I liked Lilypad's redemption, but I would have enjoyed seeing a stronger indication of how toys and technology can coexist. Something as simple as Lilypad implementing a healthy screen time limit for Bonnie before encouraging her to go and spend time with her friends or toys would have tied the theme together nicely. A small visual moment where Bonnie puts the tablet down, runs off to play, and Lilypad gives a subtle wink to the Toy Story gang would have been a perfect way to communicate that technology isn't the enemy, it simply has a role to play alongside imagination, friendship, and play. For me, that would have provided a more complete resolution to one of the film's central themes. I really enjoyed the film overall, but there were a few moments where I felt the emotional and thematic payoffs could have been pushed just a little further. None of these points took away from my enjoyment of the film, and I'd be interested to hear whether anyone else felt the same.

review_title: toy story franchise tackles screen time in another good but unnecessary sequel
review: I was born in 2012 so I was not alive when the original 3 Toy Story movies were released. I was 7 when Toy Story 4 came out so I obviously liked it when it came out. I've not seen it since but I'm sure my opinion on it if I saw it now my opinion on it would probably something like this: "it's a enjoyable movie but it really doesn't need to exist" however, I do remember thinking that Toy Story 4 would be the last one because woody leaves. So when the trailers dropped for Toy Story 5 and it became clear woody would be in it and it was clear it would tackle toys vs tech I thought I would see it. Overall I enjoyed it, I thought it gave a relatively nuanced take on toys vs tech. It doesn't say "toys good tech bad" and they do eventually learn they can coexist to make Bonnie happy. I also thought a Jessie focused movie was interesting with getting to know more about Emily and learning that she named her daughter after Jessie. I also noticed woody, buzz and Jessie sound older which I think works because the first movie came out over 30 years ago and hanks, Allen and cusak are all in their 70s at this point. However, similar to Toy Story 4, I thought that it was kind of unnecessary and considering that this movie broke several opening weekend records, I'm sure Toy Story 6 is in the works. Considering this is a Toy Story movie, it makes it a early frontrunner for best animated film at the Oscars.

review_title: better than expected with good plots
review: Good film, the main theme about the obsolence of toys in exchange for new technologies, is a good plot point that becomes secondary to the nostalgia and history about their past and mission of Jessie; it seems to me that they directed and combined very well the focus of the plot change, since by itself it would not have been enough to give good entertainment attention to the theme of technology, with this addition that technology should be helped with old toys. For the common sake of helping their children and the importance of knowing how to choose a true friendship, it was what really made this a good film. Most of these films tend to have an excess of characters that actually become a filler when they do not usually participate and/or appear in a useful way for the plot, (many helping the problem or not being relevant), the movie literally took them out of the scene for a few minutes since they had nothing to do with it but to make it seem like there is a lot of something in the background (of course toys). On the other hand, the Buzzlightyear subplot is very good, creative and entertaining, starting and ending with them in the movie, giving it a more funny and reflective touch for new characters that will remind us of the problematic of the first Toy Story movie, a classic of the good ones. In my opinion that last with the Jessie's past was the best of the movie and the rest was just filler with the exception of the friendship of the kid, sincerely better than expected for this movie.
